items.title: DSCU Concludes 2026 Cyber Law and Hybrid Warfare Course
items.author: Jensen Stidham
items.summary: Newport, R.I. — Twenty-seven military officers and civilian defense professionals from 20 partner countries graduated July 23 from the Cyber Law and Hybrid Warfare Course, concluding a four-week program focused on the legal frameworks governing global cyber operations and critical infrastructure defense.
items.body: Newport, R.I. — Twenty-seven military officers and civilian defense professionals from 20 partner countries graduated July 23 from the Cyber Law and Hybrid Warfare Course, concluding a four-week program focused on the legal frameworks governing global cyber operations and critical infrastructure defense. Administered by the Defense Security Cooperation University (DSCU), at its Newport campus, the course examined the legal and policy aspects of cyber operations in international and domestic contexts. Participants explored topics including the foundations of cyber law, hybrid warfare concepts, and international law as it applies to cyberspace. The curriculum combined interactive case studies with expert briefings from U.S. Cyber Command, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism, the Department of War General Counsel’s office, and many others. "The most valuable parts of the course were those that integrated technological, legal, and strategic perspectives related to cybersecurity, cyberspace conflicts, and emerging technologies," noted one participating international professional. "The exchange of experiences with participants from different countries was essential to understanding diverse perspectives, strengthening international cooperation, and developing collaborative approaches to future technological and legal challenges." In today's complex security environment, understanding the legal aspects of cyber operations is critical. As state actors and organized groups exploit new technologies, the practical application of international law to full-spectrum cyber operations has become a foundational requirement for combined readiness. By aligning terminology, processes, and legal concepts, partner nations are better equipped to collaboratively address operational challenges and develop cohesive international agreements. “DSCU’s Cyber Law and Hybrid Warfare (CLHW) course is vitally important today, as it directly addresses the highly sophisticated and global threats that exploit gray-zone vulnerabilities and digital infrastructure to undermine global stability,” said Robert J. Passerello, the Cyber Law Course Director. Passerello noted that by establishing a shared legal and operational understanding of these complex challenges, the course acts as a force multiplier for international security cooperation. This shared baseline allows partner nations to coordinate defense strategies, share critical threat intelligence, and collectively uphold international norms in cyberspace. “The unique benefit of this program lies in its delivery by distinguished practitioners from the U.S. government alongside expert guest lecturers from partner countries,” Passerello said. “Their multifaceted professional perspectives equip international colleagues with an unparalleled framework to proactively defend their sovereign interests and secure the collective digital commons.” The course also included field studies in Massachusetts, New York, and Washington, D.C. The 27 graduates of the 2026 CLHW cohort now return to their respective countries prepared to translate these academic legal concepts into real-world operational success in the cyber domain.

items.title: Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam set to reactivate Navy Aiea-Halawa Shaft
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Press Release Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam CONTACT: Public Affairs Office Chuck Anthony 850 Ticonderoga Street, Suite 100 (808) 271-0712 JBPHH, Hawaii 96860 | charles.j.anthony.civ@us.navy.mil JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii – With approval from the Hawaii Department of Health (DOH), Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam (JBPHH) will place the Navy Aiea-Halawa Shaft (NAHS) back into routine operation in the coming weeks.
items.body:
For Immediate Release Release #JB026-06 Sept. 5, 2026

Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam set to reactivate Navy Aiea-Halawa Shaft

JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii – With approval from the Hawaii Department of Health (DOH), Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam (JBPHH) will place the Navy Aiea-Halawa Shaft (NAHS) back into routine operation in the coming weeks.

“We have taken every measure to ensure that drinking water from the Navy Aiea-Halawa Shaft meets or exceeds state and federal safe drinking water standards,” said U.S. Navy Capt. John Frye, JBPHH commanding officer. “Reactivation of this shaft is a key step to ensuring that the Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam drinking water system remains resilient for the long term.” Reactivation of the NAHS improves the resiliency of the JBPHH drinking water system by restoring an additional water source to the base. The Navy disconnected the NAHS in December 2021 out of an abundance of caution following the November 2021 fuel release at the Red Hill Bulk Fuel Storage Facility (RHBFSF). Extensive monitoring has shown no evidence that NAHS was affected by the 2021 fuel release.

The Navy works closely with DOH and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to ensure the safety and quality of the water. Work on NAHS included: • Extensive Water Testing: The Navy conducted a rigorous multi-phase testing program to reactivate NAHS. Between April 2024 through March 2025, the Navy took quarterly drinking water samples from NAHS which were evaluated by DOH and EPA, Test results are posted to the JBPHH Safe Waters website at https://jbphh-safewaters.org/.

• EPA and DOH also conducted independent evaluations of the Navy’s drinking water system, which mirrored the Navy’s conclusions.

• System Upgrades: A new Granular Activated Carbon/Ion Exchange filtration system was installed to treat per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), an industry standard practice to address an emerging, nationwide chemical of concern.

For more information and to access testing results, visit the JBPHH Safe Waters website: https://jbphh-safewaters.org/

items.title: US Strikes 5 Iranian Oil Tankers as More Fighter Jets Ordered to Middle East
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: In a dramatic flare-up in the hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan, according to Iranian state media. The post US Strikes 5 Iranian Oil Tankers as More Fighter Jets Ordered to Middle East appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine</
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

In a dramatic flare-up in the fighting between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan.

U.S. officials said CENTCOM took the action because Iran had fired ballistic missiles against a U.S. Navy warship twice in the past two days. The ship, which the U.S. military did not identify, was not hit, and no service members were harmed, CENTCOM said.

Nevertheless, the U.S. hit back with a major attack on Iranian shipping.

“CENTCOM destroyed the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman as well as M/T Derya near Kharg Island,” the command said in a statement, referring to ships controlled by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. CENTCOM released a video of the attacks, which shows several ships engulfed in flames.

The Iranian ships were attacked by U.S. Air Force and Navy fighters and drones.

The U.S. military said the crews were directed to abandon ship before the vessels were “rendered inoperable.”

“Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” CENTCOM added. The command also delivered a harsh warning to Tehran: “Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels.”

Repeated, escalating tit-for-tat strikes in recent days have raised the risk that the two sides might resume the all-out fighting that characterized the first weeks of the war, which is now in its seventh month.

The Trump administration has adopted a policy of striking Iranian tankers to deter Iran from firing missiles at the aircraft carrier in the region and other Navy ships . On Sept. 5, Adm. Brad Cooper, who leads U.S. Central Command, warned the U.S. would “impose an even higher economic cost” on Iran by striking a “limited and exposed oil fleet” if Tehran did not cease its attacks on U.S. forces.

But that warning went unheeded.

In response to the latest U.S. attack, the Iranian military vowed to carry out fresh strikes of its own, specifically against long-standing American allies like Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain, and videos circulating online showed ballistic missiles flying towards those countries and interceptors attempting to blunt the threats. Without providing evidence, the IRGC claimed it damaged American fighter aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a key hub for U.S. airpower. Iranian officials also warned that commercial oil tankers near ports in these countries would be targeted. Iranian officials said such attacks would be justified because those ports had been used by the U.S.

The Trump administration has hoped that stepped-up economic sanctions and its ongoing blockade would force Iranians to stop interfering with traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and to make other concessions. But Tehran has shown no sign of backing down.

The U.S. is deploying fresh warplanes to the Middle East amid the fighting. F-35 Lightning II stealth fighters from the 115th Fighter Wing of the Wisconsin Air National Guard are deploying to the region and are set to arrive in the Middle East in the coming days, people familiar with the matter said.

The Wisconsin Air Guardsmen are replacing another F-35 unit, the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard. Vermont’s “Green Mountain Boys” wrapped up a roughly nine-month deployment to South America and the Middle East, where it supported the capture of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro before heading to the Middle East to fight Iran. Airmen from the unit returned home Sept. 6 and were greeted by Chief of the National Guard Bureau Air Force Gen. Steven Nordhaus.

The fresh F-35s are not the only new fighter unit reinforcing America’s posture in the Middle East. F-16 s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing deployed to the Middle East late last week, taking the place of F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron of the 31st Fighter Wing, which returned home to Aviano Air Base, Italy. Nicknamed the “Triple Nickel,” the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since last November, a long deployment compared to the Air Force’s typical six-month rotations.

The Air Force has dozens of F-16, F-35, and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters and A-10 Thunderbolt II attack planes deployed to the Middle East, along with support aircraft and scores of tankers. More rotations are expected in the coming weeks.

The U.S. Navy also has two aircraft carriers and their embarked carrier air wings supporting operations in the Middle East: the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, along with around 20 surface vessels.

Like the Air Force, the Navy has also had extended deployments in the Middle East to carry out operations against Iran. The USS Abraham Lincoln is headed home after a nine-month deployment. Before that, the USS Gerald R. Ford was deployed for 11 months and, like Vermont’s Air Force unit, supported operations against both Venezuela and Iran.

As the U.S. and Iran exchanged blows, the U.S. Treasury Department announced it was imposing new sanctions on companies that support Mahan Air, an airline that U.S. officials say is connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Fresh fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia added to the tension in the region. The Iran-backed Houthis fired missiles and drones at energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia on Sept. 8.

items.title: Air Force EO Overhaul Lets Commanders Dismiss Some Complaints
items.author: Tobias Naegele
items.summary: The Department of the Air Force's new equal opportunity and harassment policy, rolled out to comply with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's directives, redefines key terms and empowers commanders to dismiss complaints they deem not actionable. The new rules also bar investigations based on anonymous complaints. The post Air Force EO Overhaul Lets Commanders Dismiss Some Complaints appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Department of the Air Force’s new equal opportunity and harassment policy, rolled out to comply with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s directives , redefines key terms and empowers commanders to dismiss complaints they deem not actionable. The new rules also bar investigations based on anonymous complaints.

Unveiled 11 months after Hegseth directed changes to the Pentagon’s Equal Opportunity and Military Equal Opportunity programs, the new rules are dated July 28, but weren’t announced until late August. Hegseth called for the overhaul nearly a year ago, saying the programs had been “ weaponized ” by poor performers against leaders and commanders.

“No more frivolous complaints, no more anonymous complaints, no more repeat complaints, no more smearing reputations, no more endless waiting, no more legal limbo, no more side-tracking careers, no more walking on eggshells,” Hegseth said last Sept. 30 at an all-call with hundreds of generals and admirals .

The Department of the Air Force policy follows on similar updates from the Army and Navy , also announced in August.

New Definitions

Each military department’s policy includes the same new definitions of three key terms: “bullying,” “hazing,” and “harassment.”

The new definition of harassment represents the biggest change, said retired Lt. Col. Colby Volkey, a former Marine Corps Judge Advocate General. The new definition explicitly exempts standard training programs, stating “official military or governmental activities conducted in a professional manner, such as basic military training, professional military education, physical training programs, disciplinary or corrective actions, or combat readiness exercises, do not constitute harassment.”

It also states that “behavior that is rude, ignorant, abrasive, or unkind, is not necessarily indicative of harassment, but may constitute harassment depending on the totality of the circumstances.”

The revisions appear to be “an attempt to limit the types of activities that are considered harassment, Volkey said in an email.

The new definition of hazing no longer includes the phrase “any form or initiations or congratulatory acts that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same,” language that was included in the past in an effort to stop the practice of pounding on newly earned rank or other insignia, such as aviators’ wings.

Equal Opportunity Definition Changes

Bullying

Bullying: As described in DoDI 1020.03, while not a form of prohibited harassment under equal opportunity (EO) law but is a prohibited form of conduct, bullying is a form of harassment that includes acts of aggression by service members or DoD civilian employees, with a nexus to military service, with the intent of harming a service member either physically or psychologically, without a proper military or other governmental purpose. Bullying may involve the singling out of an individual from his or her coworkers, or unit, for ridicule because he or she is considered different or weak. It often involves an imbalance of power between the aggressor and the victim. Bullying can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.

Bullying is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:

Physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.

Intimidating, teasing, or taunting another person.

Oral or written berating of another person with the purpose of belittling or humiliating.

Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning, or dangerous acts.

Playing abusive or malicious tricks.

Branding, handcuffing, duct taping, tattooing, shaving, greasing, or painting another person.

Subjecting another person to excessive or abusive use of water.

Forcing another person to consume food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance.

Degrading or damaging another’s property or reputation.

Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of bullying.

Bullying does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., command-authorized physical training). Service members may be responsible for an act of bullying even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Bullying is prohibited in all circumstances and environments, including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.

Bullying (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves repetitive, intentional hurtful conduct by an individual or a group, which intimidates, humiliates, torments, isolates, degrades, exploits, controls, or creates a risk of mental, physical, or emotional distress or harm.

Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical pain or injury.

Berating or belittling a Service member’s duty performance, professional abilities, or personal attributes.

Threatening, teasing, or taunting a Service member.

Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverable.

Excluding a Service member from work-related opportunities, information, or social activities.

Posting malicious gossip, rumors, and lies on social media, sharing humiliating photos, or sending vicious text messages

Harassment

Harassment (Military): As described in DoDI 1020.03, conduct that is unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person, whether verbal or nonverbal, written, electronic, or physical, that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment. Harassment may include offensive jokes, epithets, ridicule or mockery, insults or put-downs, displays of offensive objects or imagery, stereotyping, intimidating acts, veiled threats of violence, threatening or provoking remarks, racial or other slurs, derogatory remarks about a person’s accent, or displays of racially offensive symbols.

Types of harassment include, but are not limited to, discriminatory harassment, sexual harassment, hazing, bullying, stalking, revenge porn, and other sexual misconduct. Stalking, Revenge Porn, Other Sexual Misconduct. Formal complaints involving conduct that may be punishable under Articles 130 (stalking); 117a (wrongful broadcast or distribution of intimate visual images); and 120c (other sexual misconduct) of the UCMJ will be referred to the appropriate military criminal investigative organization or other law enforcement organization with criminal investigators who are specially trained to conduct such investigations. Harassment can be oral, written, or physical. Harassment can occur in person, through electronic communications, including social media, and other forms of communication. Activities or actions undertaken for a proper military or governmental purpose, such as combat survival training, making work assignments, or conducting performance counseling are generally not considered harassment. For the purpose of this publication, the DAF MEO program is limited to processing complaints alleging bullying and hazing as “other forms of harassment.”

Harassment (Military): Conduct by a Service member or civilian employee, without a legitimate military or governmental purpose, that would be unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person in the military environment, whether delivered verbally or nonverbally, including by written or electronic means, or in-person, that creates an intimidating, humiliating, or abusive environment.

Hazing

Hazing—As described in DoDI 1020.03, hazing is a form of harassment that includes conduct through which service members or DoD employees, without a proper military or other governmental purpose, but with a nexus to military service, physically or psychologically injure or create a risk of physical or psychological injury to service members for the purpose of: initiation into, admission into, affiliation with, change in status or position within, or continued membership in any military or DoD civilian organization. Hazing can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.

Hazing is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:

Any form of initiation or congratulatory act that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.

Pressing any object into another person’s skin, regardless of whether it pierces the skin, such as “pinning” or “tacking on” of rank insignia, aviator wings, jump wings, diver insignia, badges, medals, or any other object.

Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning or dangerous acts.

Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of hazing.

Hazing does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., administrative corrective measures, extra military instruction, or command-authorized physical training). Service members or DoD civilian employees may be responsible for an act of hazing, even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Hazing is prohibited in all circumstances and environments including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.

Hazing (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves intentional or reckless conduct by an individual or group, which humiliates, degrades, or creates mental, physical, or psychological injury or harm, or reasonably perceived as such, directly related to the affected Service member’s affiliation, entry, advancement, reinstatement, change in status or position, or continued standing within a military unit, command, or DoW or military affiliated organizations regardless of whether the affected Service member consented to the activity.

Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical violence, including striking, restraining, branding, causing body modifications, tattooing, shaving, greasing, duct taping, or engaging in any form of unwanted physical contact that causes pain or injury.

Subjecting a Service member to abusive physical discomfort or fatigue.

Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverables.

Requiring financial contributions.

Dismissing Complaints

The new policy instructs installation commanders to dismiss formal equal opportunity complaints in certain circumstances, such as if:

The complaint “does not contain sufficient or actionable information to investigate.”

“A complainant does not respond to request for information.”

“A complainant files duplicative or related complaints”

If a commander or supervisor to the service member making the complaint determines “through an adverse action or UCMJ action” that the complaint was a false official statement

Under the new policy, equal opportunity directors have five days to review a formal complaint before forwarding it to an installation commander, who in turn has 30 days to consult with the “servicing legal officer’ and determine if the complaint should be dismissed. The commander then has seven days to inform the complainant, who in turn has five days to appeal.

Giving commanders the power to dismiss complaints is a radical change, said David Sheldon, a former Navy JAG who now represents military clients from every service branch as a civilian attorney. The policy leaves it up to commanders to make a legal determination over whether the complaint is “sufficient or actionable.” Indeed, Congress only recently determined that commanders were not well suited to prosecute certain serious crimes, including murder, sexual assault, and domestic violence.

“It’s kind of a step in the wrong direction in my thinking, for the very reason that you have a conflict of interest,” Sheldon said. Commanders have a built-in incentive not to be seen as having EO problems within their commands, he said.

Dismissing or resolving a case removes the holds that have sometimes delayed promotions, held key jobs opened, or resulted in foreshortened careers. Once closed, the policy states, “all favorable administrative personnel actions (e.g., awards, promotion, retirements) for an alleged offender of an [Military Equal Opportunity] complaint will be resumed or completed.”

Similarly, an individual being under investigation for an EO complaint is no longer sufficient grounds to withhold awards, promotions, retirement and other favorable actions. In the past, EO complaints have resulted in holds that could remain in place for months.

Anonymous Complaints vs. Confidential Reports

The new policy eliminates military equal opportunity complaints based on anonymous allegations, with some exceptions. Instead of filing anonymously, service members may submit “confidential reports,” revealing their identities only to equal opportunity directors and staff. But confidential reports do not constitute either informal or formal complaints, and therefore cannot trigger an investigation. Rather, they are merely a means for service members “to disclose allegations, receive information regarding available resources and reporting options, and obtain referrals to appropriate support services,” the policy states.

Commanders may choose to “look into the matter and take appropriate action in response to a referred anonymous report of prohibited discrimination or discriminatory harassment,” and a service member can choose, within time limits, to upgrade a confidential report into a complaint.

Allegations regarding sexual harassment and those concerning bullying or hazing are not covered by that limitation, however. Anonymous allegations regarding sexual harassment must be referred to the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response office. Allegations of bullying and harassment can be anonymous, but must include “sufficient information,” such as the offender’s name and rank, date of the incident, and units involved.

Shorter Timeline

The timeline for service members to file complaints is now shorter, just 60 days versus 90 days previously. But there are exceptions:

Multiple incidents: In cases involving an alleged series of incidents or pattern of behavior, only one instance needs to have taken place within the past 60 days.

Deployments: Service members who are deployed when an incident occurs and who lack resources at their deployed locations have 60 days to file once they return.

Delays: Those who waited too long can submit a memo to their installation commander explaining the circumstances and seek an extension.

Sexual harassment: By law, these complaints are exempt from the 60-day requirement.

A service member who makes a confidential complaint and then wants to formalize it, must do so within 60 days of the incident—not the report.

Sheldon suggested this makes it harder for complainants. Whether it is 45, 60, or 90 days, he said, “obviously “I would like a longer window just to give the aggrieved party an opportunity to be heard.”

Mediation

The new policy opens the door for “facilitation,” a form of mediation in which a neutral third party meets with the accused and the complainant to try to resolve the conflict. Facilitation is “a method for resolving problematic situations before they rise to the level of misconduct,” the policy states.

The confidential process can be offered for both informal and formal complaints, so long as both parties agree; commanders are instructed to consult with their legal offices before determining if it is a suitable solution for a given complaint. Commanders may also forgo facilitation if they determine it would “negatively impact good order and discipline.”

items.title: Ukraine contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles from allies, defense chief says
items.author: Reuters
items.summary: Ukraine is contracting a supply of around 1,000 missiles for U.S.-designed Patriot air-defence systems.
items.body:
Europe

Ukraine contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles from allies, defense chief says

The 37th Air Defense Missile Squadron's Patriot missile systems, at the 3rd Warsaw Air Defense Missile Brigade's base in Sochaczew, Poland, on Dec. 18, 2025. (Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Jacek Marczewski via Reuters)

Ukraine is contracting a supply of around 1,000 missiles for U.S.-designed Patriot air-defence systems with the help of allies and through a European Union loan, Kyiv’s defense minister said on Tuesday.

Speaking at a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Yevhenii Khmara also said that the majority of the missiles would only be shipped in the coming years, and called for more urgent aid.

In comments posted later by the Defence Ministry, Khmara said Ukraine was asking its Western partners to provide more air defense missiles from their stocks in exchange for improvements in missile performance under contracts signed with Kyiv.

He said Ukraine was being hindered by a shortfall of $27 billion in financing for drone supplies.

RELATED

Ukraine asks EU to fund first Patriot missiles buy

Brussels is weighing a rare waiver that would let Kyiv tap its €90 billion loan for U.S.-made interceptors for the first time.

The ministry’s summary of the meeting said Khmara had presented a plan for Ukraine’s conduct of the war that was already being implemented along with a list of what Kyiv considered to be the biggest threats posed by Moscow.

Khmara said Russia was making no strategic gains along the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line, but Moscow was making up for its battlefield failures with “terror against Ukrainians.”

Russia resumed its near-constant drone and missile attacks on Kyiv on Tuesday after a brief halt for the visit of U.S. peace negotiators. Officials said five people were killed in the capital along with others in various regions.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told the meeting that Ukraine’s allies had no choice but to boost their support to enable Kyiv “to seize the opportunities it is creating now across all fronts and to defend itself in the skies.”

items.title: Michigan Air National Guard joins West African partners for military legal engagement in Liberia
items.author: 1st Lt. Michael Sian
items.summary: Members of the Michigan Air National Guard joined military legal professionals from Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria for a weeklong State Partnership Program engagement in Monrovia during the first week of September 2026.
items.body:
MONROVIA, Liberia — Members of the Michigan Air National Guard joined military legal professionals from Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria for a weeklong State Partnership Program engagement in Monrovia during the first week of September 2026.

The Armed Forces of Liberia welcomed the visiting delegations with a meeting with Maj. Gen. Davidson F. Forleh, AFL chief of staff. Throughout the week, participants visited military units and met with members of Liberia's legal community, providing additional insight into the country's military and civilian legal institutions. The AFL also introduced the visiting delegations to Liberian culture and hospitality, including a home-cooked meal hosted by a member of the AFL legal team.

The engagement brought together legal professionals from the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL), Republic of Sierra Leone Armed Forces, Nigerian Armed Forces and Michigan Air National Guard, to exchange ideas on the rule of law and maintaining good order and discipline within the armed forces.

Discussions focused on the administration of justice, military courts-martial, individual rights, due process, professional ethics, and the importance of the rule of law at all levels of society, including within the military justice systems.

“The hospitality we experienced and the opportunity to work directly with our African partners gave us a much deeper understanding of their military, legal system and culture,” said Lt. Col. David L. Hunter, 110th Wing staff judge advocate. “These engagements are about more than exchanging legal expertise. They build trust, strengthen relationships and take our partnership to the next level.”

The exchange provided participants an opportunity to learn from the experiences of their counterparts, while strengthening regional relationships among the participating West African nations and their long-standing partnerships with the United States.

“Bringing military legal professionals from across the region together allows us to learn from one another, while strengthening our shared commitment to justice, fairness and good order and discipline,” said Lt. Col. Joseph Palay, AFL judge advocate general. “The relationships developed through these engagements help strengthen our institutions and our partnerships for the future.”

The visit builds on several years of cooperation among military legal professionals from Michigan and West Africa. In 2024, Michigan National Guard judge advocates traveled to Sierra Leone to strengthen professional ties and observe a military court-martial.

In August 2025, legal professionals from Liberia and Sierra Leone traveled to Michigan for a State Partnership Program engagement hosted by the Michigan National Guard. During the visit, participants worked with faculty from the Michigan State University College of Law and discussed the U.S. criminal justice system, due process, jury trials and emerging challenges facing legal professionals.

The Department of Defense National Guard Bureau State Partnership Program pairs U.S. states with partner nations to conduct cooperative, mutually beneficial engagements across military, security and civilian sectors. The program supports regional stability, enhances interoperability and builds enduring relationships between partner forces.

items.title: First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: After months of delays, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore. The post First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

After months of delays from a factory strike, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore.

“This is an important next step toward bringing the F-15EX home to Kadena,” Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, said in a release. “Our team is ready to welcome the F-15EX, and this is another milestone that brings us closer to putting this capability in the hands of the Airmen who will fly, maintain and employ it from Japan.”

The F-15EX is the first Eagle II jet to feature the 18th Wing’s historic, distinctive “ZZ” tail flash and will actually arrive at Kadena sometime in fiscal 2027, which begins Oct. 1.

Spokespeople for Headquartes Air Force, the 18th Wing, and the Air National Guard did not immediately respond to queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine on Sept. 8.

This new jet is the first of 36 F-15EXs to be stationed at Kadena. The fighter, often described as halfway between fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft, will help usher in a new era in U.S. airpower within the first island chain surrounding China

The transition to the EX has been a long time coming for Kadena—the Air Force started retiring the base’s legacy F-15C/Ds in 2022 and confirmed plans to replace them with the F-15EX in 2024. The first jet was supposed to arrive in spring 2026, but a lengthy strike at the Boeing plant in St. Louis late last year slowed production until this Aug. 28 delivery.

The new F-15EX’s stopover in Oregon isn’t surprising—the Oregon Air National Guard was the first Air Force location with combat-coded F-15EXs at its Portland ANG Base. The base will conduct the final systems integration, add software updates, and other technical preparations before the aircraft can go to Okinawa.

In the interim, the Air Force has rotated F-16, F-15, F-22, and F-35 squadrons through Kadena to keep the tactical fighter presence steady at a key strategic base fewer than 400 miles from Taiwan.

Those rotational forces haven’t always matched the capabilities the F-15EX will bring. Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on the extended tour of aging F-16Cs out of the Colorado Air National Guard’s 120th Fighter Squadron, which ran from January through June. They brought a dozen fighters.

Both the squadron commander and the head of its parent wing, the 140th Wing, said in a call with the media on Sept. 3 that while the platform could keep up with fifth-gen fighters in the region, the pilots and maintenance crews were pushing the limits of the more than 30-year-old airframe

The permanent stationing of the F-15EX will “enhance Kadena’s ability to generate ready combat airpower while providing opportunities to train and integrate alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and other allies and partners,” according to the release.

The 18th Wing trains alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15s at Naha Air Base in bilateral exercises and other training, according to the release.

Pacific Air Forces has been slowly phasing out its oldest fighters and introducing more modern jets in recent years. In addition to Kadena’s F-15s, the Air Force has also recently withdrawn the A-10s at Osan Air Base, South Korea.

The 35th Fighter Wing at Misawa Air Base, Japan, meanwhile, is slated to get 48 fifth-gen F-35 Lightning IIs, but only a trickle had arrived as of April. The wing transferred its F-16s to Osan last year .

The Air Force publicly confirmed delays in getting the F-15EX to Kadena in February .

The Eagle II is the first of its kind to include digital fly-by-wire flight controls, a large-area display glass cockpit with a touchscreen interface, an APG-82 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar, a Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System, and an Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System.

The jet flies faster and farther, carries a heavier payload than its F-15 predecessors, and has two additional weapons stations.

items.title: Medical appointment coming up? Some guidance to help you prepare
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: When you have a medical appointment on the calendar, it’s best to prepare ahead of time. It doesn’t take long, and the benefits will help you make the most of your healthcare appointment.
items.body:
When you have a medical appointment on the calendar, it’s best to prepare ahead of time. It doesn’t take long, and the benefits will help you make the most of your healthcare appointment.

“It’s important to be familiar with what your TRICARE plan covers. You should have all the necessary documents available and be ready with questions for your provider before you go to your appointment,” said Dr. Ross Colt, Medical Director, Clinical Oversight and Integration, TRICARE Health Plan, at the Defense Health Agency. “Whether you’re meeting with a primary care provider or specialist, being prepared can help streamline the check-in process and maximize your time with your provider.”

Depending on where you’re getting care, check out these guidelines so you’re ready for your upcoming appointment.

If you have an appointment at a military hospital or clinic

Your military hospital or clinic will have your electronic health record through your MHS GENESIS Patient Portal . However, every time you see your provider, be sure to:

Bring your Uniformed Services ID card

Make notes to discuss with your provider, including any symptoms (with a timeline, if possible), questions, or concerns you have

Have ready a list of allergies, immunizations, over-the-counter supplements, and any lifestyle changes since your last appointment

Did you know that military hospitals and clinics worldwide have a chaperone policy ? The policy states that you or your provider can request a trained chaperone to be present in the exam room for any type of exam, including dental exams.

Chaperones are a part of the clinical team—they’re a safeguard for both patients and staff.

If you’re seeing a civilian provider

If you’re meeting with a civilian doctor, make sure you know if your provider is a TRICARE network or non-network provider. To limit your out-of-pocket costs, verify that your TRICARE plan covers the services you’re receiving.

Double check you’re carrying your Uniformed Services ID card, other health insurance card (if you have OHI), and any required copayment or cost-share .

Additionally, bring a comprehensive list of your:

Family’s medical history

Personal medical conditions of note, particularly those regarding illness, hospitalization, or surgery

Current medications, including vitamins, supplements, and herbal remedies

Allergies, especially medications

Immunization and vaccine records

If you’re meeting with a specialist

Your plan determines if you need a referral to see specialist providers. Active duty service members need referrals for any care their primary care manager doesn’t provide. Beneficiaries enrolled in a TRICARE Prime plan need referrals for most care their primary care manager doesn’t provide . In these cases, your PCM will refer you to another provider or a specialist. Those enrolled in all other TRICARE plans only need pre-authorization for certain services .

If you have Medicare and TRICARE For Life

As described in the Medicare and You Handbook , you’ll need to bring all your health insurance cards with you to your appointment. If you have original Medicare, bring your red, white, and blue Medicare card and your Uniformed Services ID card to your appointment.

If you’re enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan or have OHI, be sure to bring the plan ID cards, as well as your Uniformed Services ID card.

If any of your insurance coverages have changed, be sure to inform your provider’s office to ensure your claims are processed appropriately.

Other general reminders

Gather your medical information: Be as thorough, thoughtful, and honest as possible with your family history and personal health status.

Prepare for the type of visit scheduled.

Are you going for an annual physical or preventive or diagnostic screening? Ask ahead of time if there are any special guidelines for your visit, such as fasting for bloodwork or arriving with a full bladder for an ultrasound.

Are you ill, have symptoms, and seeking treatment? It’s helpful if you’ve tracked your symptoms. Know what your symptoms are and when they started. This helps your provider identify what you have and how best to treat you.

Do you have questions for your provider? Make a comprehensive list to get the answers you need. You may want to take notes during your discussion.

Keep in mind, there isn’t a TRICARE card to show your provider as proof of eligibility. Learn more about what identification you need to bring with you to your appointment.

And remember to check your information in the Defense Eligibility and Enrollment Reporting System and make any necessary updates. Avoid claims, billings, authorizations, and other issues by keeping your DEERS account current.

Taking some time to prepare for your appointment helps ensure a more meaningful and productive appointment with your provider.

items.title: 15 Years of Military Appreciation at the State Fair
items.author: SGT Abbygail Heinen
items.summary: Minnesotans gathered at the Minnesota State Fair to celebrate the service and sacrifice of those who have served their communities and country during the 15th annual Military Appreciation Day, Sept. 1, 2026.
items.body: Minnesotans gathered at the Minnesota State Fair to celebrate the service and sacrifice of those who have served their communities and country during the 15th annual Military Appreciation Day, Sept. 1, 2026. Held at the State Fair grounds in Falcon Heights, the event brought together service members, veterans, military organizations and fairgoers under this year’s theme, “Your Neighbors, Our Community – Honoring all Service Members.” “Minnesotans have always been ready, and always been there, to defend our nation,” said Sen. Amy Klobuchar. “These have not been actions of superheroes. They have been actions of ordinary Minnesotans who decided to put their lives on the line for the extraordinary.” Throughout the day, fairgoers had the opportunity to interact with veteran organizations, listen to the 34th Infantry Division Red Bull Band, and meet men and women who have served their country. The opening ceremony kicked the event at Luther Auto Band Shell with a C-130 Hercules flyover, and four service members were honored for distinctive actions in and out of uniform. Army Master Sgt. Ryan Kelly, of East Bethel, was recognized for being the first on scene during the tragic Annunciation School shooting, while serving as a lieutenant with the Minneapolis Police Department. Army Sgt. Jonathan Erickson, of Lakeville, was honored for his service to the community as a firefighter paramedic. Erickson previously received a Congressional Gold Medal from Rep. Angie Craig. He was also one of the Minnesota National Guard’s flight medics and supported wildfire operations this summer in northern Minnesota. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Mary Andrzejek, from Blaine, was recognized for her medical logistics coordination during the early stages of Operation Epic Fury, which aided wounded personnel in the Middle East. Army Spc. Ryan Boecker, from Becker, was also honored after helping save his civilian boss’s life during a major health event on a job site. Following the ceremony, Wells Fargo and Apple Autos presented a vehicle to former U.S. Army Staff. Sgt Blake Grienbenow at the Dan Patch Park stage. “It is a great space to engage with all branches of the military, veteran organizations who do so much great work, and honor some really great people,” said Army Lt. Col. Adam Scholze, community outreach chief for the Minnesota National Guard. Throughout the day, local veterans and currently serving service members held conversations and received support from fairgoers and community organizations attending the event, highlighting the connection between those who serve and the communities they call home.” “That legacy lives here in Minnesota,” said Maj. Gen. Shawn P. Manke, the Minnesota National Guard adjutant general. “They are your neighbors. And they make up our community.”

items.title: White Sands Missile Range Garrison Commander Provides Support to Area Veterans
items.author: Vanessa Flores
items.summary: Michael A. Lueckeman, Garrison Commander, White Sands Missile Range, was the guest speaker at the Rio Grande Honor Flight ceremony on September 05, 2026, in Las Cruces, NM, where he addressed and thanked a group of local veterans participating in the Honor Flight program.
items.body:
Michael A. Lueckeman, Garrison Commander, White Sands Missile Range, was the guest speaker at the Rio Grande Honor Flight ceremony on September 05, 2026, in Las Cruces, NM, where he addressed and thanked a group of local veterans participating in the Honor Flight program.

Honor Flight Rio Grande serves veterans from Southern New Mexico and El Paso, Texas, by transporting them at no cost to Washington, D.C., to visit the memorials built in their honor. The program focuses on veterans of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam.

“Your service came during one of the most complex and challenging conflicts our nation has ever faced. The hardships you endured—both in uniform and upon returning home—are chapters of American history that must never be overlooked,” said Lueckeman. “Today, with absolute clarity, we say: thank you.”

Lueckeman emphasized to the veterans that what they did is significant and that their story matters. “Who you are, what you did, and why you did it matters, and it must never be forgotten.”

This ceremony was part of the lead‑up to the 22nd Honor Flight, which will depart on September 24 and is scheduled to return on September 26. During this multi‑day trip to Washington, D.C., the veterans will visit:

The WWII Memorial

The Korean War Veterans Memorial

The Vietnam Veterans Memorial

Arlington National Cemetery

Additional service‑specific monuments if requested

“Our nation needs you to share your story… I encourage you to share your experiences. Share the moments that shaped you—the challenges overcome, the friendships forged, and the lessons learned and carried forward,” said Lueckeman. “It is my honor to stand with you as part of Honor Flight 22. You have more than earned this moment of recognition.”

Every veteran has a trained guardian who ensures safety, comfort, and companionship throughout the journey.

items.title: Space Force Expects to Spend $17B More on Launch as Demand Soars
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force expects the scope of its main launch program to grow by 91 missions and nearly $17 billion by fiscal 2032 as demand for national security space capabilities soars. The post Space Force Expects to Spend $17B More on Launch as Demand Soars appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force expects the scope of its main launch program to grow by 91 missions and nearly $17 billion by fiscal 2032 as demand for national security space capabilities soars.

Those increases are revealed in the latest version of the National Security Space Launch program’s selected acquisition report , drafted in April and published in September. The update brings NSSL’s total expected procurement to $76 billion for 337 launches between fiscal 2004 and 2032.

At the same time, the average cost per launch is dropping significantly, from around $422 million in 2022 to $192 million in the most recent report. That average combines a range of vehicle and payload configurations, which means some missions are much cheaper and others more expensive.

The surge in demand comes as the Space Force is planning to field large numbers of satellites in the coming years to support missions like satellite communications, space domain awareness, missile warning, and moving target indication. NSSL also supports the National Reconnaissance Office and other classified customers who are fielding proliferated constellations of their own.

The Space Force in recent months has acknowledged that its NSSL contracts will need to grow to accommodate that demand. The program has two competitive tracks, or lanes: Lane 1 is reserved for commercial-like missions with higher risk tolerance, whereas Lane 2 serves more demanding customers flying high-value payloads with less margin for error.

In July, the service announced it would triple the size of its Lane 1 contract ceiling from $5.6 billion to $17 billion, increasing the number of missions from early estimates of between 30 and 60 to approximately 170 launches over a five-year period. Likewise, “emergent requirements” are driving the service to increase the number of Lane 2 by 25—from 54 to 79.

The Space Force hasn’t said which programs these launches will support, but it has announced several contracts in recent months to buy satellites that will need rides to space over the next few years. In late May, it awarded SpaceX a $2.3 billion contract to build out its Space Data Network constellation and a $4.2 billion contract for its Space-Based AMTI program. The service also plans to launch new fleets of small surveillance and reconnaissance satellites under an effort called Andromeda, with the initial spacecraft slated to launch in 2029. The Space Force hasn’t said how many spacecraft those constellations will include, but it has set a contract ceiling of approximately $6 billion.

The growing manifest is also likely to support Golden Dome, a sprawling, layered, missile defense architecture. The Space Force is supporting that program in a few ways, including by developing space-based interceptors that can engage a missile during the boost and midcourse phases of flight. Initial prototypes of those spacecraft are expected to be integrated into the Golden Dome architecture by 2028.

The Space Development Agency is also fielding a missile defense and tracking constellation and recently announced it would add 36 more satellites to that architecture to support Golden Dome. Those satellites are also scheduled to be ready for launch by 2028.

Whether these satellites launch on time hinges, in part, on the availability of certified, ready rockets. To qualify to fly Lane 1 missions, companies need to have successfully launched their vehicle at least once. Lane 2 missions, however, require certification from the Space Force, a lengthy process that requires multiple launches. To date, only SpaceX and ULA are eligible to launch satellites for both lanes, though ULA’s Vulcan rocket is currently grounded due to an anomaly on a February NSSL launch.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn is eligible for Lane 1 flights and is on the certification path for Lane 2, but it, too, is grounded after a rocket exploded on the pad in May . Four other companies—including Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Impulse Space, and Relativity Space—are on deck to compete for missions as soon as their developmental rockets complete at least one launch.

That leaves SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy as the only rockets available to support NSSL missions at the moment. The Space Force is weighing near-term options to mitigate schedule delays caused by Vulcan’s grounding—including swapping some missions to SpaceX rockets—but several programs have already seen delays. For example, the launch of the first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellites, slated for March, has been pushed to no sooner than October.

Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space access, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July that he is “worried about timelines,” particularly for the more urgent Lane 2 missions.

“Those are vastly important national security assets that we need to get to orbit,” he said.

items.title: Team Wins Program of the Year for Rapidly Delivering Advanced C-UAS Capabilities to the Warfighter
items.author: M. Scott Bortot
items.summary: The Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies (APFIT) recently presented its Program of the Year Award to Product Manager Army Tactical Exploitation of National Capabilities (PdM TENCAP) in recognition of Polar Cascade – an effort that delivers cutting-edge counter Uncrewed Aircraft System (C-UAS) capability to the warfighter.
items.body: The Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies (APFIT) program recently presented its Program of the Year Award to Product Manager Army Tactical Exploitation of National Capabilities (PdM TENCAP) in recognition of Polar Cascade – an effort that delivers cutting-edge counter Uncrewed Aircraft System (C-UAS) capabilities to the warfighter. Polar Cascade project lead Timothy Roseberry credited his team for earning the award. “The Army TENCAP team tirelessly worked to deliver capabilities to the warfighter within budget and on time,” said Roseberry. “The team regularly worked long hours, weekends, and even deployed to austere environments to ensure Soldiers received critical capabilities in support of forward operations.” “The team’s dedication and technical expertise is truly unmatched and is a testament to their dedication to the warfighter,” he added. Army TENCAP is an office within the newly created Project Manager Space Superiority and Exploitation (PM SSE). PM SSE delivers advanced space sensing and spectrum warfare systems that leverage national capabilities to support Army commanders. Col. Carter Deekens, Project Manager for PM SSE, emphasized the significance of the award to his team. “We are proud that APFIT recognized PdM TENCAP’s efforts and provided them with the support to deliver advanced C-UAS capabilities into the hands of our warfighters as fast as possible,” said Deekens. APFIT is a government program started in 2022 to provide procurement funding for innovative projects that have completed development and are set to transition to operational use. “APFIT has fundamentally reshaped how the Department of War [DoW] accelerates the transition of innovative technologies to the warfighter,” said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, in a July 2026 DoW press release. As part of the award, APFIT provided PdM TENCAP additional funding to assist in the delivery of its C-UAS technology to the warfighter. Roseberry said the PM TENCAP technology met APFIT criteria of a fully developed, dynamic project ready for fielding. PM TENCAP and an Army Combatant Command (ACC) partnered to submit a proposal for funding through APFIT process. “We had a small business we were working with and a mature capability able to be produced, as well as the production capacity for sustainment,” Roseberry said. “One thing that APFIT does not want to do is to provide funding to deliver end items for systems that have no ability to be sustained.” Roseberry said his team worked closely with the contract vendor and Soldiers to identify a technology that identified a specific gap in their ability to combat adversaries. A description of this process played an important role in the APFIT proposal submission. “We were able to mature that system's capabilities based on feedback and continuously working with Soldiers on the ground,” Roseberry said. “Over the course of time, we were able to get the system to the point where it was highly effective.” PM TENCAP received its first tranche of funding for initial delivery of the system in 2025 and to date has provided the unit with 30 of the 49 systems. Roseberry attributes the additional funding from APFIT pivotal to rapidly and effectively delivering the capabilities through Polar Cascade. “By diligently working with APFIT, we were able to have a product that has significantly increased the capability that's being delivered to the warfighter in use today,” Roseberry said.

items.title: New furniture filling spaces as West Point modernization continues
items.author: William Farrow
items.summary: Currently, New England District is managing the 15-year effort to modernize academic infrastructure at the historic campus. As the brick-and-mortar renovations and construction projects are continuing the U.S. Army Engineering and Support Center, Huntsville (Huntsville Center) is filling the spaces with furniture.
items.body: REDSTONE ARSENAL, Ala. --The United States Military Academy (USMA) at West Point and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) share a foundational, historical, and ongoing operational relationship rooted in the birth of American military engineering. USACE manages major military construction, renovations, and modernization programs on the West Point grounds, such as upgrading historic cadet barracks and academic facilities. The USMA 2035 Modernization Plan is a 15-year effort to modernize the academic infrastructure including the renovation of seven dated facilities on campus and one major military construction project. The modernization plan also included the Cadet Barracks Upgrade Program (CBUP). The CBUP is a 10-year effort to completely renovate and modernize all cadet barracks, including the construction of Davis Barracks in 2017. Currently, New England District is managing the 15-year effort to modernize academic infrastructure at the historic campus. As the brick-and-mortar renovations and construction projects are continuing the U.S. Army Engineering and Support Center, Huntsville (Huntsville Center) is filling the spaces with furniture. Huntsville Center's furniture program is driven by standardization partnerships with the General Services Administration, and significant cost savings achieved through centralized bulk purchasing. In the early 2000s Huntsville Center was designated as the executing agency of the Centrally Managed Administrative Furniture Program to streamline procurement across installations. A major ongoing modernization project is the 136,000 square foot Goethals Hall as it becomes the Academy’s Cyber and Engineering Academic Center (CEAC). Tiffany Torres, Centralized Furnishings Program Project Manager is leading the furniture outfitting requirement for the CEAC. She said as construction is ongoing at Goethals Hall, desks, chairs and office furniture are filling classrooms, offices and collaborative areas as fast as the construction crews can complete their work. However, Torres explains the process to procure and contract for the installation of furniture isn’t like purchasing furniture from a retailer - manufacturing lead times need to be taken into consideration as these items are not ready-made off-the-shelf items sitting in a furniture warehouse. Torres has been the project manager since 2024 and she said there has been a lot of thought put into ensuring the USMA gets exactly what they want; quality furnishings that enhance the overall instruction provided to Cadets in the cutting-edge classrooms and laboratories. Along with Huntsville Center Interior Designers Stacey Sapp and Nancy Williamson, Torres said there were many discussions with West Point end users and stakeholders to ensure the activities in each space were thoroughly understood so that the product specifications could be tailored to provide a beneficial product that supports the rigorous instruction. “Over a 12 month span, our team conducted comprehensive in-person and virtual design reviews to refine space layouts, balance end-user requirements, and adhere to program procurement regulations,” Torres said. “Through close coordination with our contracting project development team (PDT) members and project stakeholders, we navigated complex procurement challenges to successfully award contracts in September 2025 and February 2026 totaling more than $3 million.” Following contract award, the PDT and stakeholders held an onsite post-award kickoff meeting where end users collaborated directly with the vendor to finalize all furniture finishes and verify site conditions prior to manufacturing of the product. The phased on-site delivery and installation commenced in August 2026 and remains on schedule for full completion by October 2026. “We (Huntsville Center Centralized Furnishings PDT) provided not only project management support but design and acquisition expertise that resulted in approximately 10% cost savings and successfully delivered an end product that will ensure Goethals Hall’s impact on USMA for years to come,” Torres said. To oversee day-to-day furniture delivery and placement, Jason Mielke, New England District project manager, oversees the furniture installation at West Point and works with Huntsville Center to make sure everything stays on schedule and is installed correctly. “If any issues come up, I work with them (Huntsville Center) to find solutions and keep the project moving,” Mielke said. He said working with Huntsville Center makes his project manager’s work easier. “Their (furniture) program is really robust and they (Huntsville Center) are the experts with navigating GSA rules when procuring furniture.” After construction, CEAC will serve as a modern academic facility that will enable and inspire collaboration across engineering disciplines. The CEAC will house the engineering laboratory functions of the Departments of Civil & Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering & Computer Science, and Systems Engineering together under one roof.

items.title: TRICARE authorizes temporary prescription refill waivers for Hawaii due to Tropical Cyclones
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: FALLS CHURCH, Virginia – The Defense Health Agency announced that TRICARE beneficiaries in Hawaii may receive emergency prescription refills now through Sept. 14, due to Tropical Cyclones.
items.body:
FALLS CHURCH, Virginia – The Defense Health Agency announced that TRICARE beneficiaries in Hawaii may receive emergency prescription refills now through Sept. 14, due to Tropical Cyclones.

All counties are affected.

To receive an emergency refill of prescription medications, TRICARE beneficiaries should take their prescription bottle to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy. If the bottle is unavailable or the label is damaged or missing, beneficiaries should contact Express Scripts, Inc., or their retail network pharmacy for assistance.

To find a network pharmacy, beneficiaries may call Express Scripts at 1-877-363-1303, or search the https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/find-pharmacy.

If possible, visit the pharmacy where the prescription was filled. Prescriptions filled by a retail chain may be filled at another store in that chain. If the clinician who prescribed the medication is available, beneficiaries can ask them to call in a new prescription to any network pharmacy.

As a reminder, TRICARE beneficiaries, other than active duty service members, may receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider and do not need a referral. This allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency care for illnesses or injuries if their primary care provider is unavailable because of emergencies. Any TRICARE beneficiary who reasonably believes they have an emergency should always call 911 or, go to the nearest emergency room.

Beneficiaries are advised to visit Express Scripts’ https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/notices/weather/2026-sep-4/state-emergency-alert-tropical-cyclones-hawaii for updates.

The Defense Health Agency provides health services to 9.5 million beneficiaries, including uniformed service members, military retirees, and their families. The DHA operates one of the nation’s largest health plans, the TRICARE Health Plan, and manages a global network of more than 700 military hospitals, clinics, and dental facilities.

items.title: Food and Drug Administration approves lifesaving, shelf-stable plasma for far-forward battlefield care
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: In a major advancement for military medicine and battlefield survival, the Defense Health Agency helped secure Food and Drug Administration approval for a lifesaving product designed to stop uncontrolled bleeding in the most remote environments.
items.body: In a major advancement for military medicine and battlefield survival, the Defense Health Agency helped secure Food and Drug Administration approval for a lifesaving product designed to stop uncontrolled bleeding in the most remote environments. Marketed under the name EZPLAZ Freeze-Dried Plasma and manufactured by Teleflex, the product provides front-line military medical providers with a stable, highly portable treatment for severe injuries when traditional blood products are unavailable. "Securing FDA approval for freeze-dried plasma is a key step forward for military medicine, and it speaks directly to our primary mission: keeping our joint force ready and bringing our warfighters home alive,” said DHA Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin K. Via. “The reality of future conflict means our medics will be operating in highly distributed, austere environments where traditional supply chains may not reach. By turning a fragile, refrigerated blood product into a rugged, shelf-stable tool that fits in a medic's pack, we are effectively pushing lifesaving capabilities right to the point of injury.” Plasma is the liquid portion of blood that contains essential proteins necessary for clotting. When a warfighter suffers severe trauma, rapid transfusion of plasma is critical to prevent fatal blood loss. However, traditional liquid plasma requires freezing or strict refrigeration, making it nearly impossible to transport and store in austere environments. Freeze-dried plasma, or FDP, solves this long-standing logistical challenge: It is shelf-stable, easily carried by medics, and can be rapidly reconstituted with water for field use. In addition, unlike other FDP products stored in glass containers, the new product utilizes a patented, flexible plastic bag. This eliminates the risk of bottle breakage and simplifies repacking, making the product far more durable and better suited for the harsh physical realities of far-forward combat operations. Uncontrolled hemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable death on the battlefield, especially when time and distance impede immediate evacuation. Recognizing that early transfusions of blood components dramatically improve survival rates, the Department of War has long championed FDP as a key capability to bridge the gap between the point of injury and surgical intervention in expansive theaters like the Indo-Pacific and Arctic regions. The urgent need for a field-deployable plasma supply was the primary catalyst behind Public Law 115-92, which was enacted in 2017 specifically to facilitate enhanced engagements between the DOW and the FDA to accelerate the development of critical military medical products. Development and management of FDP over the past decade was spearheaded by the Warfighter Protection and Acute Care Program Management Office. Operating under DHA’s Research, Development & Acquisition/Component Acquisition Executive office, the WPAC team used the authorities of P.L. 115-92 to work closely with the FDA, addressing regulatory hurdles to bring this capability to the front lines. "The WPAC PMO collaborates with companies to develop products to address the Department of War’s mission-critical medical priorities,” said Kendra Lawrence, Ph.D., WPAC’s project manager. “Warfighter emergency medical care relies, in part, on bringing shelf-stable and easy-to-transport blood products to the front lines of the battlefield where they are most needed.” WPAC is now actively managing the procurement and distribution of EZPLAZ FDP alongside the Armed Services Blood Program. A key partner in the rollout process, ASBP manages the blood and blood component supply for the military. The ASBP is the central driver of collection, manufacturing, storage, and delivery of blood products for the individual service branches globally. Moving forward, FDP will be added to the blood provision capabilities of the military. Because this is the first FDP product to receive full FDA licensure rather than an Emergency Use Authorization, it eliminates the administrative reporting burdens previously placed on medical staff, allowing them to focus more on patient care. According to Army Col. Jason Corley, director of ASBP, this full approval will have immediate impact in both civilian and military healthcare systems at home and abroad. “FDP is a huge step forward at ensuring our warfighters at and near the front lines have the lifesaving supplies they need to address uncontrolled hemorrhage in far-forward, austere environments,” said Corley. “The military has focused heavily on developing this capability because it is widely needed and broadly applicable in both military and civilian healthcare settings when whole blood is unavailable or in short supply.” By mitigating the challenges of time and distance, the FDA-approved FDP product is expected to have an immediate impact on front-line combat casualty care. “Blood products are a critical and urgent need across the Department of War and the service branches, and FDP is a game changer,” said Andy Atkinson, the FDP product manager with WPAC. “Because it is so user-friendly, portable, shelf-stable, and rapidly reconstituted, it is form-fitted for use by both conventional and special forces anywhere in the world.”

items.title: Nevada Guard Honor Guard supports dedication of state’s first national cemetery
items.author: SSG Adrianne Lopez
items.summary: Members of the Nevada Army National Guard Honor Guard provided ceremonial support during the dedication of Elko National Cemetery on Sept. 4, helping mark the establishment of Nevada’s first Department of Veterans Affairs national cemetery.
items.body:
Story by Staff Sgt. Adrianne Lopez

106th Public Affairs Detachment

ELKO, Nev. — Members of the Nevada Army National Guard Honor Guard provided ceremonial support during the dedication of Elko National Cemetery on Sept. 4, helping mark the establishment of Nevada’s first Department of Veterans Affairs national cemetery.

The Honor Guard represented Nevada’s military community as veterans, families and officials gathered to recognize the future burial site.

Located at 3602 Jennings Way in Elko, the 15.37-acre cemetery will accommodate casketed burials, in-ground cremation burials and urn placements in columbarium niches.

Developed through the National Cemetery Administration’s Rural Initiative, the cemetery will give qualifying Nevada Guardsmen and other rural veterans in northeastern Nevada closer access to VA burial benefits. Once fully developed, it is expected to serve more than 3,705 veterans and their eligible spouses and children within a 75-mile radius.

items.title: Cryopreservation Demonstration Program launches, allowing for flexibility in warfighter family planning
items.author: Robert Hammer
items.summary: The Defense Health Agency’s Cryopreservation Demonstration Program, a three-year pilot created to reimburse certain costs for sperm or egg freezing, aims to give eligible service members options for family planning when facing the unique demands of military service.
items.body:
The Defense Health Agency will launch a three-year pilot on Sept. 14, 206, to support eligible service members who want to freeze sperm or eggs through the Cryopreservation Demonstration Program — 30 days after being listed in the Federal Register.

Mandated by the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025 , the demonstration program will reimburse certain costs tied to sperm or egg freezing, giving eligible service members more choice in family planning.

The program, overseen by the DHA medical affairs directorate, “offers support for members who face unique military demands,” said Air Force Maj. (Dr.) Kathleen Pombier, chief of DHA’s women’s health clinical management team. “Military service has an impact on how people build their families, with deployments and long separations affecting when troops decide to have children.”

Cryopreservation safely freezes eggs or sperm with liquid nitrogen to stop the aging process. The frozen eggs and sperm can be thawed, even years later, so service members can use them when the time better fits their family planning objectives, said Pombier.

Designed to give active duty service members “flexibility in choosing when to build their family,” cryopreservation can provide them with more “options in their reproductive future, or if there are issues with getting pregnant,” she said. By providing these family planning possibilities, the program ensures the delivery of high-quality care to all beneficiaries, Pombier added.

In DHA’s effort to deliver joint warfighting capabilities, the pilot covers all active duty forces — U.S. Army, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Air Force, and U.S Space Force. To be eligible, a service member must meet one of three conditions:

Have orders for duty that qualify for hazardous duty pay

Be likely to receive orders for duty that qualify for hazardous duty pay within 120 days

Who will, under orders, be geographically separated from a spouse, domestic partner, or dating partner for more than 180 days, including sea duty

The program is voluntary and not a TRICARE benefit, Pombier noted. Participants can be reimbursed up to $500 per year for sperm preservation and capped at $10,000 per year for egg preservation. The demonstration program will also reimburse for related medications, medical tests, lab work, and imaging. Storage and shipping causes may also be reimbursed. Embryo creation, in vitro fertilization, or other elective procedures are not covered.

“We encourage participants to use a participating military hospital or clinic ,” said Pombier, but a civilian fertility clinic may also be used, and doesn’t have to be TRICARE-authorized.

Participants must follow timing guidelines: All testing, retrieval, and freezing generally must occur before orders begin. Beneficiaries who face a qualifying long separation may receive services before the separation or while it continues, if care is available.

Pombier said those interested should begin with the DHA’s program website to get started. All service members must get confirmation of eligibility from their commander before seeking reimbursement. An advance medical directive is also required of all participants stating how they want their stored sperm or eggs handled if they die.

Throughout the demonstration program phase, DHA will track use, costs, claims processing, patient experience, and impact on readiness and retention — all part of a feasibility assessment, Pombier said.

The program is set to end after the initial three-year mandate, unless it’s extended. Pombier said eligible participants should expect to pay storage and shipping costs after the pilot ends if the program doesn’t continue.

In providing “eligible service members options to choose when to begin a family,” the program delivers warfighter medical readiness by allowing them to “focus more on being mission-ready rather than worrying about family planning,” said Pombier.
