items.title: Driving Army innovation: ALTESS’ transition to NETCOM
items.author: Kevin Dietz
items.summary: In a strategic realignment of the Army’s enterprise systems and digital infrastructure, the department is moving the Acquisition, Logistics and Technology Enterprise Systems and Services (ALTESS) product office out of the acquisition community and into the Network Enterprise Technology Command (NETCOM), which falls under the U.S. Army Cyber Command (ARCYBER). This organizational transition aims to streamline operations and secure the Army’s digital infrastructure.
items.body: FORT BELVOIR, Va. -- In a strategic realignment of the Army’s enterprise systems and digital infrastructure, the department is moving the Acquisition, Logistics and Technology Enterprise Systems and Services (ALTESS) product office out of the acquisition community and into the Network Enterprise Technology Command (NETCOM), which falls under the U.S. Army Cyber Command (ARCYBER). This organizational transition aims to streamline operations and secure the Army’s digital infrastructure. Barry Nichols, ALTESS product lead, said that “in June 2025, Army Cyber Command released an execution order that would bring some missions within the Assistant Secretary of the Army (Acquisition, Logistics and Technology) (ASA(ALT)) portfolio into NETCOM.” He explained that among ARCYBER’s many functions, the command secures, operates and defends (SOD) the Army network. ALTESS does similar work, so it made operational sense for these ALTESS SOD functions to pair with NETCOM. Historically, Nichols said, ALTESS has been unique because it is “more focused on operational tasks rather than acquisition ones,” despite the ALTESS workforce consisting of acquisitions professionals. The Army created one of its first data centers at the Radford Army Ammunition Plant in the 1950s. These early data centers processed and stored massive amounts of data on Universal Automatic Computer (UNIVAC) systems and tape machines. By the 1970s, the data center was designated as Research, Development and Acquisition Information Systems Activity (RDASIA), under the U.S. Army Computer Systems Command (USACSC), until November 1985, at which time it became part of U.S. Army Information Systems Command (USAISC). USAISC was the predecessor to much of what is now NETCOM. ALTESS runs one of the 12 designated Army Enterprise data centers, further emphasizing the organization’s focus on operations instead of acquisition. Moving under an operational command ensures data centers align with their operational and information-processing identity. NETCOM will tentatively assume operational control of ALTESS on October 1, 2026, and will oversee daily operations. Capability Program Executive Enterprise Software and Services, however, will maintain administrative control of ALTESS for approximately one year as the positions are transitioned from acquisition-coded positions to cyber-excepted service positions. The transition is expected to be completed by the end of fiscal year (FY) 27. The transition, which has already begun and is “progressing smoothly,” according to Nichols, directly answers Army directives governing organizational boundaries. Under standard guidelines, acquisition bodies are designated to manage procurements while ARCYBER secures, operates and defends the Department of War Information Network – Army (DOWIN-A). "This move,” Nichols said, “is the Army getting ALTESS into the operational side of the Army because the ALTESS mission does not align with traditional acquisition programs." Data center tasks will experience no service interruptions, and systems embedded in data centers or cloud environments will continue normal operations. ALTESS will continue providing infrastructure support for 55 DoW organizations and approximately 75 unique systems. This support includes on-premise systems and those within the Army commercial cloud. Team members’ daily tasks will not significantly change, though reporting structures and issue escalations are likely to change as well as the ALTESS name. Nichols anticipates the organization will be renamed once the transition is complete by September 2027, which will provide support to data centers and all on-site computing systems. The new name will become effective by the end of FY27, Nichols noted. Change can be challenging, and Nichols said that “taking care of the ALTESS team is our number one priority. We want to make sure people are informed, have timelines and expectations are clearly stated.” As realignment progresses, ALTESS and Army Contracting Command Rock Island plan to release two solicitations in the first quarter of FY27. The first will focus on ALTESS facility requirements, and the second will address information technology services followed by an industry day. The solicitations will be under the ALTESS name and posted on [sam.gov/](https://sam.gov/).

items.title: NPS Students Apply Graduate Research to Real-World Fleet Challenges During RIMPAC 2026
items.author: SN Katherine Eldridge
items.summary: A team of nine NPS students across several departments and programs traveled to RIMPAC 2026 for an invaluable opportunity to take their graduate education and research from the classroom into the operational environment. Supported by nearly a dozen faculty and researchers, the NPS team advanced several student/faculty driven research efforts, working directly alongside fleet operators and industry partners during the world's largest international maritime exercise.
items.body: A team of nine NPS students across several departments and programs traveled to RIMPAC 2026 for an invaluable opportunity to take their graduate education and research from the classroom into the operational environment. Supported by nearly a dozen faculty and researchers, the NPS team advanced several student/faculty driven research efforts, working directly alongside fleet operators and industry partners during the world's largest international maritime exercise. Led primarily by NPS’ Consortium for Advanced Manufacturing Research and Education (CAMRE), the effort allowed students to test research against real operational challenges while collaborating with military operators and industry partners. The experience helps shape future research, and ensures students are directly supporting fleet needs. U.S. Navy Ensign William Schleper, a student in the NPS Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering researching advanced manufacturing alloys, served as the officer in charge of CAMRE’s additive manufacturing team embarked aboard the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) and MV Asterix (A147). In addition to coordinating personnel, equipment, and shipboard integration efforts, he operated a Metal Powder Works M-175 Direct Powder system capable of producing metal powder from bar stock while at sea. The team also demonstrated multiple additive manufacturing technologies as part of a broader effort to evaluate a complete shipboard manufacturing workflow. Moving that work from a controlled laboratory to an operational ship presented challenges that are difficult to reproduce in an academic environment. “In a laboratory, we generally have stable power, controlled environmental conditions, readily available tools, and relatively unrestricted access to equipment,” Schleper said. “At sea, those assumptions no longer hold.” Ship movement, heat, equipment placement, power requirements, safety restrictions, communications, logistics and the ship’s operational schedule all affected how the team conducted its work. As team leader, Schleper also had to balance the technical objectives of the research with the practical requirements of working aboard an operational vessel. “That experience gave me a much better understanding of the difference between demonstrating that a technology works in a laboratory, and demonstrating that it is actually useful and sustainable for the fleet,” Schleper said. The experience also shaped how he views his own research. “Instead of viewing the printer as an isolated piece of equipment, I now think much more about the complete manufacturing system: raw material, feedstock production, printing, post-processing, inspection, and ultimately getting a usable component into the hands of the operator,” Schleper said. While Schleper was focused on shipboard manufacturing, U.S. Navy Lt. Evan Humphreys, also an NPS mechanical engineering student, supported another part of CAMRE’s RIMPAC effort involving autonomous logistics and unmanned surface vessel operations. Humphreys coordinated operations between CAMRE and USS Essex (LHD 2), Theodore Roosevelt and Asterix, while also working with industry partners Splash and HavocAI. He coordinated the movement of components between ships, shore locations, and unmanned surface vessels, as well as supporting spectrum coordination and access approvals required for operations in and around the Hawaiian Islands. “I was able to apply the knowledge I gained in the classroom to inform decisions directly in support of USV operations,” Humphreys said. “The conversations were with Navy shore, ship, and industry stakeholders, requiring a tailored approach for each.” During the exercise, CAMRE and its partners launched and recovered unmanned surface vessels from shore and ships while using the vessels to transport components between operating locations. Humphreys supported operations involving Splash's Typhoon and HavocAI's Kaikoa systems, including an evolution that brought the Typhoon aboard Essex through the ship's stern gate. The operations revealed practical considerations involving communications reliability, cargo stowage, and vessel control during launch and recovery evolutions. “The operations showed me that technology has progressed to the point where uncrewed systems can be relied upon to transit independently and arrive at a designated rendezvous point on time,” Humphreys said. Working directly with industry representatives also gave Humphreys a firsthand look at how commercial developers help the Armed Forces adapt emerging technologies to operational requirements. Although Schleper and Humphreys supported different parts of CAMRE’s work, their experiences reached the same point — having NPS students advance their research in the fleet allows them to better apply what they have learned, work through operational challenges firsthand, and carry those lessons back to campus, and ultimately, back to the fleet and force. “The benefit of having NPS students participating is that we have the technical training to ask appropriate questions and think critically about the responses provided in order to provide accurate assessments of the operations at hand,” Humphreys stressed. Schleper and Humphreys’ participation was part of a broader NPS presence at RIMPAC that included eight researchers and faculty members from multiple academic departments, with several students representing multiple military services, curricula and research domains. Together, they supported a broad portfolio of CAMRE experimentation working with military, government, academic and industry partners throughout the exercise. Their experience reflects a unique strength of NPS: operationally experienced officers confronting real-world challenges, working alongside faculty and industry partners to develop solutions, and returning to the force with deeper understanding and practical insight. By connecting graduate education and research directly to fleet operations, NPS helps ensure its students are prepared not only to study complex defense challenges, but also to help solve them. NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters andleaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

items.title: Poland’s in-development fighting vehicle carries newfound defense-export drive
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Polish officials hope a new infantry fighting vehicle design will propel the country's weapons-export business.
items.body:
Europe

Poland’s in-development fighting vehicle carries newfound defense-export drive

Visitors look at armored vehicles on display at the MSPO defense show in Kielce, Poland, on Sept. 8, 2026. (Jaroslaw Adamowski/staff)

KIELCE, Poland — As Poland’s defense spending has reached record levels , the country aims to increasingly shift from the role of a buyer of foreign military gear to its exporter, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and National Defence Minister, said on the opening day of this year’s MSPO show here.

The technology demonstrator for a new heavy tracked infantry fighting vehicle, developed by Poland’s industry and presented during the event, reflects this ambition.

“Poland is becoming a country that not only buys military gear from the world, but is also its major producer,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said at the show’s opening ceremony on Sept. 8.

The deputy prime minister said the Polish defense industry can benefit from the European Union’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) scheme. Under the instrument, Poland has been allocated up to €43.7 billion ($50.8 billion) worth of low-interest loans for military acquisitions.

“We have reached a level of fifty-fifty [between domestic military gear purchases and imports]. This would not happen without the SAFE mechanism,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

The Polish sector is dominated by state-owned defense group PGZ but also features a group of emerging private companies.

Kosiniak-Kamysz named PGZ’s new heavy tracked infantry fighting vehicle (IFV), whose technology demonstrator was officially presented during this year’s MSPO event, as one of the examples of the Polish industry’s potential flagship export products.

“This is a modern platform, with a weight of between 40 and 43 tons, which maximizes troop protection,” a PGZ representative told Defense News. “We plan to present the vehicle’s prototype next year, and it could enter serial production in 2029.”

The heavy IFV is to be added to PGZ’s offer alongside the group’s light tracked IFV, the Borsuk (Badger) , that is already in production. To date, the Polish Ministry of National Defence has ordered 257 Borsuks from the group, with deliveries of up to 1,400 units of the platform in different variants envisioned ina 2023 framework agreement.

Military officials expect around 700 heavy IFVs could be procured for the Polish Army.

While Poland’s pro-European Union government is advancing efforts to ramp up domestic weapons, equipment and ammunition production, while also intensify cooperation with European partners, the country remains a major buyer of gear from the United States.

Over the past years, Poland has placed orders for Abrams tanks , F-35 fighter jets , AH-64E Apache helicopters , Patriot missiles and M142 HIMARS rocket launchers , among other equipment.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: ‘North Star’ of Defense Health Agency is data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support, declares director
items.author: Robert Hammer
items.summary: Navy Vice Adm. Darin Via, director of the Defense Health Agency, opened the Tri-Service Chapters Annual Scientific Meeting in Bethesda, Maryland, Aug. 26, by underscoring the agency will “be synchronized and data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support.” The meeting is a joint medical education conference hosted by the American College of Physicians for military internal medicine professionals, which includes military physicians, residents, fellows, and other emerging military healthcare l
items.body:
To a cohort of emerging military healthcare leaders at the 2026 Tri-Service Chapters Annual Scientific Meeting, Defense Health Agency Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin K. Via positioned the agency as a source of “problem solvers and solution providers” to optimize combat support in generating and sustaining global warfighter readiness.

In his remarks at the meeting in Bethesda, Maryland, Aug. 26, Via called upon future leaders across the military healthcare enterprise to own risk, solve problems at the right level, and focus on ensuring service members are medically ready for the future fight.

“Military medicine faces a more complex future than it did during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan,” Via said. “The enemy has changed the tactics on us, and we have to adapt,” in delivering care to warfighters.

The joint medical education conference is hosted by the American College of Physicians for military internal medicine professionals, including physicians, residents, fellows, and other healthcare professionals.

Via said since the first day he became director of the agency, his goal was to make “the entire DHA a combat support agency.”

His viewpoint shapes how DHA leaders will measure success, Via said, emphasizing the agency must look beyond healthcare delivery and ask how each part of the system supports combat power. He noted his fiscal year 2027 campaign order will finalize “the plan to deliver my four strategic priorities ” — the agency’s “North Star” in optimizing operational medical readiness.

“To achieve our North Star, DHA should be synchronized and data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support,” Via said.

Agency’s focus on keeping warfighters healthy and lethal

Via stressed DHA needs to find ways to return the warfighter to the fight more quickly.

He described studies of musculoskeletal injuries finding gaps between healing and nondeployability, saying the insights offer a “chance to return more people to the fight faster.”

“We have to deliver the readiness of the warfighter,” Via declared.

He tied this goal to better access to care, faster referrals, and clearer measurable outcomes on meeting the mission, mobilizing leaders to use data to find root causes of illness or injury instead of only treating symptoms.

Via referenced the vital work of Dr. Jesus Caban, DHA’s chief data and analytics officer, and his team to make data more accessible, using artificial intelligence to translate a wealth of information into useful knowledge quickly. He noted this data and access to the Joint Medical Planning Tool , a computer-based simulation tool that models patient flow from point of injury through more definitive care, which can help predict casualties, support treatment and evacuation decisions, and guide supply and resupply in future battles — enhancing medical warrior currency across the enterprise.

Accountability and ‘smart risks for the warfighter’

In his intent to give network and military hospital and clinic leaders more authority to make and execute decisions, Via underlined, “Everyone should feel empowered to solve the problems at their lowest level. Period.”

“Find the root cause, identify solutions, execute and learn,” he said, while urging leaders to challenge assumptions: “Be willing to speak truth to power.”

Leaders should push risk up the chain, not down it, he added: “It is taking risk at the right levels … if we’re going to take the risk, I’m happy to own the risk.”

Preparing combatant commands for tomorrow’s fight

He highlighted plans to strengthen support for combatant commands and casualty receiving facilities. DHA is working to set requirements for medical supplies in the fight, using planning tools to estimate casualty needs, and expanding spaces inside military hospitals and clinics currently used for other purposes.

“We’re going to get those opened up. We’re going to get them functional. We’re going to have them ready,” he said.

Aligning with his warfighter-first focus, Via briefly mentioned working with the Joint Trauma System to optimize the military’s trauma learning system, ensuring the joint force can adapt faster to modern battlefield threats. JTS plays a critical role in delivering joint warfighting capabilities through unified trauma clinical care standards and data-driven medical logistics.

“We are also going to stand up a Joint Warfighter Health System — we're going to learn from the JTS. We’re going to use those same models to drive mental health, TBI (traumatic brain injury), and infectious disease,” he said. “We’re going to use the same continuous, data-driven process improvement to keep and save warfighters and keep them in the fight.

He closed by emphasizing the role of military medical leaders in battlefield success and ensuring all beneficiaries receive the high-quality healthcare they deserve.

“You all will save more lives on the future battlefield … you will keep more fighters in the fight, and that is how we will win the war.”

items.title: Hanwha plans to build armored vehicle carrying a counter-drone laser
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Hanwha representatives said the vehicle is fitted with a more powerful version of the stationary Cheongwang laser that protects the presidential compound.
items.body:
Europe

Hanwha plans to build armored vehicle carrying a counter-drone laser

South Korea's Hanwha brought models of the company's air-defense products to the MSPO defense trade show in Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. (Hanwha)

KIELCE, Poland — As Poland and numerous other NATO eastern flank countries are looking for inexpensive ways to bolster their counter-drone capabilities, South Korea’s Hanwha is pitching a new product to militaries across the region: a 50 kW laser mounted on an armored vehicle.

Speaking on Sept. 8, the first day of the annual MSPO defense industry show in Kielce, Poland, company representatives said the vehicle is fitted with a more powerful version of the stationary Cheongwang laser that South Korea’s military has used since 2024.

Cheongwang has been deployed at strategically important sites, including near the Blue House, the office and residence of the nation’s president.

“We are currently in talks with a number of countries over potential exports of the Cheongwang laser, including potential clients from Europe, Asia and the Middle East,” Hyungun Park, the manager of the laser system business team at Hanwha Systems, told Defense News.

One of the biggest advantages of the Cheongwang results from the fact that each laser shot costs around 2,000 Korean won ($1.5) which makes the weapon a highly cost-efficient way to counter drones, Park said.

To cater to the needs of militaries seeking a mobile laser solution capable of tracking fast-moving targets, the company has combined its laser technology with a wheeled platform, using the Tigon eight-wheel-drive armored personnel carrier.

“Our new product is the 50 kW Laser Armored Vehicle. We have developed a prototype, and we plan to launch serial production of this vehicle by the end of 2027,” according to the executive.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: US Air Force seeks air-defense guns to protect overseas bases
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: The U.S. Air Force plans to acquire anti-aircraft guns to protect its overseas bases following Iranian attacks on U.S. bases in the Middle East.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

US Air Force seeks air-defense guns to protect overseas bases

Smoke rises after Iran launched a missile attack targeting the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet in Manama, Bahrain, on Feb. 28, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

In the wake of Iranian attacks that devastated U.S. bases in the Middle East , the U.S. Air Force wants portable air-defense guns that can destroy drones and cruise missiles.

The Ground-Based, Medium-Caliber Gun Weapon System project is aiming for a weapon “that fires affordable munitions, enables defense against air and missile threats with an initial focus on subsonic cruise missiles (CM) and Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) to provide persistent defense in support of United States Air Force assets,” according to the Air Force’s Request for Information published Thursday. The deadline is Oct. 9.

Iran has unleashed retaliatory strikes at U.S. military installations and civilian infrastructure across the Middle East amid bombardment by U.S. and Israeli forces.

U.S. troops were killed when an Iranian one-way attack drone evaded U.S. air defenses and struck a makeshift operations center at a civilian port in Kuwait. More troops were killed in attacks on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia.

The Iranian strikes have also damaged U.S. aircraft , including five KC-135s on the ground at Prince Sultan Air Base.

The Air Force’s RFI doesn’t request a specific caliber for the new weapons system, but “ medium-caliber ” suggests a weapon in the 20mm to 50mm range. In August, the U.S. Army published a Sources Sought notice for a 50mm anti-drone cannon and ammunition. The Army plans to conduct a live-fire test using Northrop Grumman’s XM913 Bushmaster 50mm chain gun, with companies supplying 50mm ammunition.

The Air Force’s weapon will have 15 baseline parameters, including its probability of kill, or PK, against subsonic cruise missiles, as well as Group 1 to Group 5 UAVs, meaning small drones all the way up to very large unmanned aircraft flying above 18,000 feet.

Contractors “must carefully select the organic sensor capability and phenomenology—integrating the right mix of radar, electro-optical, infrared, or radio-frequency sensors—to ensure reliable target acquisition and tracking across varying weather conditions, environments, and countermeasure scenarios,” the Air Force emphasized.

Weapons will also be assessed for range and elevation, magazine capacity, number of crew needed and integration with other sensors and command networks. They must also be capable of stopping saturation attacks by drones and missiles.

The Air Force is also looking for a portable air defense weapon with “a lightweight, modular, and transportable footprint that can be swiftly projected into austere theater environments to meet emergent threats.”

Based on the RFI, the Air Force appears cognizant of modern air defense’s biggest challenge : air defense systems that are either much more expensive than the drones and missiles they are trying to stop, or systems that run out of ammunition before an attacker does.

The new weapon “must optimize munition performance versus munition cost and gun capability, ensuring that the interceptor’s velocity, maneuverability, and terminal effects are maximized without driving the cost-per-engagement to unsustainable levels or exceeding the physical constraints of the host platform,” the RFI said.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Ready at a Moment’s Notice: Marine Forces Reserve Assesses Rapid-Response Capabilities During Reserve Mobilization Exercise 26
items.author: LCpl Breysson Villacortacampos
items.summary: NEW ORLEANS -- Marine Forces Reserve conducted Reserve Mobilization Exercise 26 this summer, testing the rapid mobilization and combat readiness of units across its major subordinate commands nationwide.
items.body:
NEW ORLEANS-- Marine Forces Reserve conducted Reserve Mobilization Exercise 26 this summer, testing the rapid mobilization and combat readiness of units across its major subordinate commands nationwide.

The annual exercise serves as a critical benchmark to gauge how quickly and efficiently MARFORRES can activate and deploy ready forces if called upon. This year's iteration saw active participation from units within the 4th Marine Division, 4th Marine Logistics Group, 4th Marine Aircraft Wing and Force Headquarters Group. Designed to simulate a large-scale, short-notice activation, RMX 26 required thousands of Reserve Marines to transition from their civilian careers, assemble at their home training centers, inspect their equipment, and rapidly deploy to training sites across the country.

"The Reserve Mobilization Exercise is in place to gauge the readiness of the Reserve in a specific unit, to see any effect of mobilization, see what shortfalls we may have, or where efficiencies are and find where we could tighten up our plans," said U.S. Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Jared McCarty, company gunnery sergeant for Company C, 4th Law Enforcement Battalion, Force Headquarters Group.

McCarty emphasized that while smaller-scale mobilization drills occur regularly, the expanded scope of RMX 26 reflects a direct response to current global operational requirements.

"The Marine Corps is a force in readiness, and the Reserve is a force in readiness to that force," McCarty said. "It's a reminder of what we're really here for. To be ready at a moment's notice."

A premier showcase of this collective readiness spanned across the United States, demonstrating the mobilization capability of the ground combat, aviation, logistics and command elements.

In the East, Marines with 4th Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion, 4th Marine Division, executed strategic embarkation procedures at sites across Maryland and Pennsylvania. Personnel staged, inspected and loaded Light Armored Vehicles onto transport platforms, preparing the combat assets for rapid coast-to coast movement to Camp Pendleton, California.

On the West Coast, Marines and Sailors with 4th Medical Battalion, 4th Marine Logistics Group, validated rapid-readiness processing pipelines and conducted cargo-loading operations at Camp Pendleton to guarantee immediate medical operational capability. Simultaneously, Marine Wing Support Squadron 473, 4th Marine Aircraft Wing, stood up operational infrastructure at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar, California, executing rigorous cargo validation and tactical equipment repositioning to sustain distributed aviation logistics.

In the Midwest, Company C, 4th Law Enforcement Battalion, Force Headquarters Group, integrated with Airmen from the U.S. Air Force's 87th and 89th Aerial Port Squadrons at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Marines and Airmen conducted joint cargo inspections and staged vital assets inside strategic transport aircraft, verifying all gear complied with strict weight, balance, and hazardous material protocols before flight.

"We're checking to make sure that all of our personnel are accounted for and that the gear is serviceable," said U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Keaton Dennis, a squad leader with Company C, 4th Law Enforcement Battalion. "Making sure that basically we have beans, bullets, and band-aids -- everything that we're going to need for this deployment, and we're ready to be operable as soon as we hit the ground."

Leaders across Marine Forces Reserve will utilize the logistical and operational data collected throughout RMX 26 to refine future mobilization procedures, ensuring that the Reserve force remains an agile, lethal, and seamless extension of the active-duty component.

items.title: ENCAP project builds relationships during Super Garuda Shield 26
items.author: SGT Isaac Copeland
items.summary: U.S., Indonesian, Canadian and Singaporean service members renovated SDN 12 Martapura during Super Garuda Shield 26, improving the school through roofing, painting, masonry, electrical work and other infrastructure upgrades. The Engineer Civic Assistance Program project strengthened multinational cooperation while providing students and the local community with an improved learning environment.
items.body:
MARTAPURA, Indonesia — U.S., Indonesian, Canadian, and Singaporean service members renovated SDN 12 Martapura as part of an Engineer Civic Assistance Program project, helping improve the school and strengthen relationships between participating forces and the local community during Super Garuda Shield 26, from Aug. through Sept., 2026.

The ENCAP project brought together multinational service members to repair and improve the elementary school through painting, masonry, electrical work, roof repairs, and paver installation. The renovations addressed infrastructure needs affecting the school's learning environment during Indonesia's wet season.

U.S. Marine Staff Sgt. Benjamin Means, supporting civil affairs with Marine Rotational Force - Darwin, said Indonesian forces selected the school because of its condition before construction.

"It was badly in need of a roof, especially during the wet season," Means said. "It makes the learning environment kind of hard for the students to focus and pay attention."

As the ENCAP project progressed, service members worked side by side to complete the final details of the renovation, including painting, masonry, and laying pavers. Means said the improvements provide upgraded infrastructure, additional space for sports and outdoor assemblies, and an area the surrounding community can use for events.

For teachers and students at SDN 12 Martapura, the improvements create a more comfortable learning environment.

Novia Nurcahyani, principal of SDN 12 Martapura, said the renovation will allow students to learn in a better-suited school.

"The reconstruction that we received is very beneficial for the students so that they can learn comfortably, joyfully, peacefully, and happily," Nurcahyani said, according to a translation provided by Yulianniza Marshanda. Nurcahyani also saw the cooperation between Indonesian and international service members during the project, describing their teamwork, discipline, and commitment to improving the school.

The ENCAP project also gave participating forces another chance to build interoperability beyond traditional military training.

"This project supports Super Garuda Shield because it allows us to be interoperable," Means said. "We're still learning lessons here, working alongside our partner forces on how we can work together not only now, but in the future."

For U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Ed Matthaidess, the ENCAP project shows how the relationships strengthened during Super Garuda Shield extend beyond military training.

"Our partnership extends beyond defense and includes education, youth and the communities that form the foundation of our two nations," Matthaidess said. "This new facility stands as a lasting symbol of what the United States and Indonesia can build together."

The ENCAP project culminated with a ribbon cutting ceremony, Sept. 7, 2026.

Super Garuda Shield brings U.S. forces together with the Indonesian National Armed Forces and partner nations to strengthen interoperability and cooperation. Projects like the renovation of SDN 12 Martapura provide another way for those relationships to have a lasting impact beyond the training area.

items.title: Mid-Atlantic Regional Maintenance Center Delivers USS Mesa Verde Following a Selected Restricted Availability
items.author: Harrison Cox
items.summary: NORFOLK, Va –Mid-Atlantic Regional Maintenance Center (MARMC) successfully concluded a Selected Restricted Availability for the amphibious transport dock ship USS Mesa Verde (LPD 19) Sept. 4, delivering a fully modernized combatant back to the fleet.
items.body:
NORFOLK, Va –Mid-Atlantic Regional Maintenance Center (MARMC) successfully concluded a Selected Restricted Availability for the amphibious transport dock ship USS Mesa Verde (LPD 19) Sept. 4, delivering a fully modernized combatant back to the fleet.

Executing a project of this scale requires sustained momentum and tight coordination. The project served as a Lead Maintenance Activity pilot availability, a significant milestone where major modernization was accomplished directly by Marine Hydraulics International (MHI) and its subcontractors rather than traditional government Alteration Installation Teams.

Working in close coordination, MARMC and its industry partners executed complex upgrades across the entire ship.

“Maintaining momentum on a multi-year project comes down to establishing a unified battle rhythm on day one,” said Blake Nipper, MARMC project manager, USS Mesa Verde. “From the start, MARMC and MHI refused to operate in a vacuum; we functioned as an Integrated Project Team (IPT). We maintained that momentum through transparent, open and honest communication, tackling problems together on the deckplates, and constantly reminding ourselves of the ultimate goal: returning a fully capable warship to the fleet. The sheer stamina and professionalism of both workforces kept driving us forward.”

This effort was bolstered by a “One Navy” partnership, utilizing teamwork across multiple commands, including the Naval Information Warfare Center (NIWC), Naval Surface Warfare Center (NSWC) Port Hueneme Division (PHD), the Shore Intermediate Maintenance Activity (SIMA) Norfolk and the Mesa Verde crew to restore and modernize the ship’s critical communication, combat and propulsion systems.

“Amphibious warships like USS Mesa Verde are incredibly complex platforms. While MARMC and MHI tackled the Hull, Mechanical, and Electrical (HM&E) work, we relied heavily on the specialized expertise of NSWC PHD, PMS (Program Manager Ships) 321, Planning Yard, Huntington-Ingalls Industries (PY-HII) and NIWC to modernize the ship's 'nervous system' and combat capabilities. This 'One Navy' approach allowed for seamless handoffs and parallel execution. We simply could not have synchronized the testing and integration of these advanced systems without that enterprise-wide alignment.”

Reflecting on the successful completion of the multiyear project, Nipper highlighted the dedication of the workforce as the defining element of the availability's success.

“As the MARMC project manager,managing an availability of this magnitude is a marathon not a sprint, but my proudest moment wasn't crossing off a specific milestone or key event. It was watching the ship light off her various systems and come back to life. My praise for the RMC COC, MHI, Code 900 (SIMA) and other partner workforces is boundless. Every single day, they brought their blood, sweat, and unmatched technical skill to the deck plates. They took a massive, complex project and turned it into a modernized, lethal asset. They are the reason USS Mesa Verde is now fully mission capable and will be ready on arrival to answer the Nation's call.”

The successful completion of the USS Mesa Verde’s maintenance highlights the Navy’s innovation in delivering ready assets back to the fleet to meet operational demands. Through disciplined planning, strategic partnerships and the dedication of skilled Sailors and civilians, MARMC continues to ensure the fleet is a ready and lethal force.

MARMC, a field activity under Program Acquisition Executive Industrial Operations (PAE IO), provides surface ship maintenance, oversight of private-sector repair work and fleet technical assistance to ships throughout the Mid-Atlantic region.

items.title: New space strategy will bolster UK defences against threats from space
items.summary: New UK space strategy to bring government's investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies
items.body:
New national space strategy brings together UK’s plans for growth, defence, and national security to help reindustrialise the UK

Government will design a resilient, integrated national satellite communications system to boost our security and defence

Strategy also brings everyday benefits to Brits from better connectivity on trains to stronger phone signals

Safeguarding our national security and defence capabilities are the key pillars of a new strategy launched today (Tuesday 8 September) which puts the UK’s space sector to work in reindustrialising the country over the coming years.

Backed by a record £7.8 billion until 2030, the UK Space Strategy brings government’s space investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back the technologies that underpin modern life.

It also recognises space as an increasingly important domain for keeping our country safe. Work to strengthen Space Domain Awareness – the study and monitoring of objects like satellites, rockets and debris orbiting our planet – is being backed by projects including £149 million for the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. UK funding will see British tech offer earlier warnings of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms, helping protect the power, communications and navigation services people rely on every day.

Meanwhile £880 million will help beef up the UK’s space control and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies that can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites, meaning we can act quickly and decisively to protect our way of life on Earth and our assets in space.

A further £2.8 billion meanwhile will go towards strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.

These benefits will also be felt in everyday life, helping bring faster, more reliable connectivity to rural communities and reducing mobile signal dropouts on trains by using advanced satellite communications.

Together, these investments will help grow a UK space sector worth £18.6 billion and supporting over 55,000 skilled jobs – cementing Britain’s place as a global space leader from satellite services that underpin the economy to landmark missions such as the UK-built Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover.

Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said:

“As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.

“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”

Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said:

“This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.

“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”

The Strategy also offers an opportunity to deliver the jobs and companies of the future, with £40 million to support pioneering in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies (ISAM). These will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by space debris, solar storms or hostile interference, while helping clear dangerous objects from orbit – all while continuing to operate in space.

That support will help bring new products online that are directly developed in the unique environment of space, from new semiconductors that underpin our power grid to pharmaceuticals and drug delivery tools that could transform outcomes for patients.

Additional support for the UK’s wide-ranging space sector includes:

£148 million for European rocket programmes and £30 million for SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland – helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.

£163 million in space science and exploration missions, including the delivery of the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built in Stevenage. These missions power world-leading research while boosting this government’s mission to reindustrialise the UK with high-skilled jobs and new tech in areas like AI and autonomous systems.

£57 million from the Department for Transport to improve rail connectivity, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) for astronomy and space science research, and £9 million from the Met Office to strengthen space weather forecasting.

For the first time, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, starting with satellite communications, helping British firms win more work, strengthening UK supply chains, supporting skilled jobs and delivering capabilities faster and better value for taxpayers.

The new Strategy formally replaces the previous National Space Strategy, published in 2021, and will play a key role in the delivery of the Modern Industrial Strategy to deliver reindustrialisation and good growth in every postcode.

Alongside the Strategy, we’re reforming space regulations to reduce costs, reward responsible operators and make it easier for UK firms to invest in cutting-edge missions from satellite servicing to lunar exploration.

Supportive comments:

Doug Liddle, Chair of the trade association UKspace, said:

“UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”

Kevin Craven, CEO of the ADS Group, said:

“We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals. “Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration. ADS looks forward to supporting government on the crucial next steps for implementation.”

Professor Anna Hogg and Professor Mark Sims, Space Academic Network (SPAN) Co-Chairs said:

“SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. Space technologies and services are integral to modern life, from secure communications to monitoring and responding to environmental change. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”

Joanne Wheeler MBE, Managing Partner at Alden and Director of the Earth & Space Sustainability Initiative, said:

“In addition to enhancing UK security and defence, the UK Space Strategy brings together world-leading innovative regulation and insurance opportunities to enable and drive growth and investment, whilst encouraging responsible and sustainable operations.”

Simon Brown, Met Office Managing Director, said:

“Space based observations are critical for delivering weather forecasts and climate intelligence that people rely on every day to stay safe and grow the economy of the UK. Advancements in space observations are allowing us to improve our weather forecasts and also give us new imagery which helps us show the impacts of other hazards such as wildfires and drought which we have seen this summer.

“Delivering new and innovative space capability is important to enhance our preparedness for extreme weather and exploit the latest advances in our prediction capability using both physics and AI models. We welcome the new UK Space Strategy and its recognition of the vital role space plays in supporting weather and climate services, as well as the Met Office’s role as the UK’s space weather forecasting centre.”

Notes to editors:

The Strategy details how government will go further and faster to develop capability and deliver outcomes in our four priority subsectors:

Satellite Communications

In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing

Space Domain Awareness

Assured Access to Space

The package of space regulatory financial tools contains measures which have been proposed by government, as well as those received in response to the previous consultation on orbital liabilities, insurance, charging and space sustainability . The package covers the following announcements:

Adopting a world-first variable liability limits approach for orbital operations to incentivise uptake of government priorities of security and space sustainability, reduce cost burdens on UK companies and stimulate increased commercial investment in the UK’s space sector.

Waiving operator liability for innovative and novel space missions launched before the end of 2030 (In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly & Manufacturing and lunar missions) to help support development of high potential technologies.

Adoption of new world-first models for the provision of third-party liability insurance to support innovation in the City of London space insurance market.

Abolishing decommissioning funds for operators of constellations in favour of a more proportionate approach to monitoring operators’ financial health.

Further detail on the measures can be found in the government response to the consultation in the link above.

items.title: Sweden to buy HIMARS rocket artillery for around $730 million
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: The Swedish government said it needs more rocket artillery fast, signing off on a $733 million purchase of HIMARS weapons from the United States.
items.body:
Europe

Sweden to buy HIMARS rocket artillery for around $730 million

An M142 HIMARS operated by the U.S. Army launches a missile from Palawan, Philippines, during an exercise on Apr. 27, 2026. (Staff Sgt. Brandon Rickert/U.S. Army)

PARIS — Sweden signed off on the purchase of Lockheed Martin’s M142 HIMARS rocket-artillery system for around 7 billion Swedish kronor (US$733 million), with the government saying the security situation is such that it needs rapidly available capabilities to complement its Archer self-propelled howitzers.

The first deliveries of the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System are scheduled for 2027, the Swedish Ministry of Defence said on Monday . Buying the American-produced rocket artillery will allow the Swedish Armed Forces to operate over larger areas and with greater long-range capacity than with the current artillery systems, the ministry said.

“The introduction of rocket artillery clearly demonstrates that Sweden is taking responsibility for security in Europe,” Defense Minister Pål Jonson said.

While Estonia in April expressed concern about possibly delivery delays for HIMARS ammunition due to the Iran war, the Swedish calendar indicates potential bottlenecks may not affect launcher production.

Sweden’s neighboring Norway in January picked Hanwha to supply its Chunmoo rocket artillery system, preferring the South Korean system over HIMARS due to the availability of longer-range munitions.

“The fact that we are now procuring HIMARS and getting long-range precision combat capability on the ground is important not only for the Army but for the Armed Forces as a whole and for our allies,” said Swedish Army chief Maj. Gen. Johan Pekkari in a separate statement .

With Europe currently lacking a home-made equivalent to HIMARS, the Swedish purchase of the U.S. system and Norway acquiring Chunmoo reduces the commercial space for a French rocket artillery system being developed by MBDA and Safran.

The HIMARS systems will be organized in a rocket artillery unit in accordance with plans announced in 2024, Pekkari said. Sweden’s defense bill for the 2025-2030 period , published in 2024, set plans for a rocket artillery unit alongside two Archer battalions.

In parallel with the purchase, Lockheed Martin and Saab are signing a joint declaration on potential integration of Saab’s Ground-Launched Small Diameter Bomb and production of munitions for HIMARS, as well as other systems such as the Patriot air-defense system, the ministry said.

Additionally, Sweden and Finland signed a declaration to cooperate on rocket artillery, including on training, security of supply and production, with Finland’s Multiple Launch Rocket System using the same munitions and components as HIMARS, according to the Swedish ministry.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

items.title: Policy paper: UK Space Strategy
items.summary: The UK Space Strategy sets out the UK’s enhanced intentions for the space sector, focussing on defence, national security and economic growth, backed by £7.8 billion of investment to 2030.
items.body:
Space is fundamental to our economy, national security and daily lives. It enables critical services, strengthens our defence, powers innovation and connects people and businesses across the United Kingdom. As the space domain becomes more contested and competitive, where activities and capabilities are continuously subject to threats and hazards, the UK must act with greater focus and ambition to protect its interests and capture the opportunities ahead.

Our vision is for the UK to be a competitive space power; assertive in protecting our interests and driving our growth.

To achieve this, the UK Space Strategy sets out a new approach to investments, operations, and partnerships. We will focus our resources where they can have the greatest impact, strengthening the capabilities that matter most for national security, defence and economic growth. With that ambition, we are prioritising the acceleration of four subsectors, where we will focus effort and resource to build capability faster, at greater scale:

Satellite Communications

Space Domain Awareness

In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing

Access to Space

Through this Strategy, we will build a stronger, more competitive and more resilient space sector; enhance the UK’s security and sovereign capabilities and ensure that space continues to support growth and prosperity across the whole country.

Details

Following a review, ‘Overseas Accompanied Service Assessments’ replaces ‘ Assessment of Support Needs for Accompanied Assignments Overseas ’.

This policy applies to Service personnel planning to take their families on an overseas assignment, particularly those with additional medical, social care, or educational needs. The assessment process is designed to take a holistic judgment about whether the host location can reasonably meet the family’s needs and whether associated risks to their health, education, safety, or well-being can be appropriately managed.

MOD civilians and their families should instead follow the Overseas Relocation Policy .

For further information or advice on this publication please contact the AFFS Families Policy team by emailing People-AFFS-FamiliesTeam@mod.gov.uk .

items.title: EU abruptly shelves Kallas-led defense panel after pushback from Berlin, Paris, Rome
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas scrapped plans to launch a high-level advisory group on European defense just hours before its scheduled unveiling.
items.body:
Europe

EU abruptly shelves Kallas-led defense panel after pushback from Berlin, Paris, Rome

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas (L) speaks with Irish Minister for Defence Helen McEntee (R) during an informal meeting of European Union defense ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, on Sept. 1, 2026. (Mostafa Darwish/Anadolu via Getty Images)

VIENNA — EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas scrapped plans to launch a high-level advisory group on European defense just hours before its scheduled unveiling, after several member states, reportedly including Germany, Italy and France, pushed back against the initiative.

The group, first announced by Kallas at an informal defense ministers’ meeting in Wicklow, Ireland, on Sept. 1, was meant to bring together former political and military leaders to draft recommendations for closing Europe’s capability gaps faster. Former NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen was expected to chair the panel, with ex-defense ministers Jüri Luik of Estonia and Florence Parly of France among the anticipated members, according to diplomats familiar with the plans. The United Kingdom and Ukraine were also expected to take part.

The formal launch, a fireside chat with Kallas planned for Sept. 7 at Brussels’ Bibliothèque Solvay with roughly 150 invitees, was called off on the afternoon of Sept. 6, before the group’s membership had even been officially confirmed.

“Some member states felt this was not the right path to pursue at this moment,” Politico quoted an unnamed EU official as saying, adding that Kallas’s office would instead pursue “new ways of engaging with member states.”

German news agency dpa reported that Berlin’s objections were central to the reversal, and Euractiv reported that France, Germany and Italy jointly rejected the plan, which had been informally likened to a “Draghi report for defense.”

Speaking to reporters on Monday, a German defense ministry spokesperson said the government did not want to comment on consultations by EU countries, while also highlighting that Germany considers NATO the first and foremost venue for military capability planning.

“Fundamentally, defense and armaments policy are the responsibility of the member states, while capability planning and defense planning are derived from NATO planning,” the spokesperson said. Various EU initiatives such as meetings of defense ministers, PESCO, EDF, SAFE and Military Mobility are valuable “to accompany all of this,” he said.

“The EU has regularly launched various such initiatives in the past. Some find approval, some less so,” the German military spokesperson said.

The episode is the latest sign of friction between Kallas’ diplomatic service and the European Commission over who controls the bloc’s defense agenda. Some capitals are said to have worried the group would duplicate work already underway under Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, while Berlin has separately pushed to fold parts of the European External Action Service into the Commission itself.

The collapse comes as Kallas has repeatedly warned that Europe cannot keep “outsourcing” its defense to the United States and must move faster to rearm as Russia escalates hybrid and, increasingly, kinetic pressure on the continent’s eastern and northern flanks.

One EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, acknowledged the underlying problem remains unresolved regardless of the group’s fate: “Europe still needs to confront the question the group was designed to address — how to strengthen European defense faster.”

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
items.summary: Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
items.body:
Misconduct hearings

To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.

Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour ( PSPB )’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.

Accelerated Misconduct Hearings

Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:

that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct

it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay

Police Appeals Tribunals

Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.

The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.

This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).

^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.

What happens at a misconduct hearing

At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:

written warning (only if misconduct only found)

final written warning

reduction in rank

dismissal without notice

What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing

An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:

What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal

Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.

Attending a misconduct hearing

Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.

When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).

Please note the following conditions of entry:

any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the MDP misconduct hearing registration form ( PDF , 178 KB , 2 pages ) they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)

any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time

priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)

any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing

members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session

no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing

any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing

where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment

no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time

no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient

we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible

members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted

If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.

Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.

Private hearings

Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.

Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:

all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private

a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing

specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness

specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome

If a decision is made to hold a hearing in private the reasons will be published below and, where conditions are placed on any person’s attendance, that person will be notified prior to commencement of the hearing.

Upcoming hearings

Subject Officer: PC Voke

Hearing date: 16 September 2026

Alleged Conduct (& PSPBs breached):

PC Voke is to attend an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing which will be heard 10am at RAF Wyton on 16 September 2026.

PC Voke will appear to answer allegations relating to breaches of the Standards of Professional Behaviour in respect of the following standards: Authority, Respect and Courtesy; Discreditable Conduct; and Confidentiality.

It is alleged that PC Voke posted a video to social media where he conveyed threatening and/or intimidatory and/or untrue messages regarding police officers and his colleagues.

It is further alleged that the conduct of the officer, if proven, amounts to Gross Misconduct and is so serious as to justify dismissal.

How to Attend: Members of the press or public wishing to attend the Misconduct Hearing must register to do so. Anyone who has not pre-registered will not be allowed to access the hearing. Those attending are not allowed to record or film the proceedings.

Members of the media and public may attend subject to the following:

The taking of photographs and the use of film or sound recording equipment during the hearing, except for official use, is prohibited;

Any accredited member of the media attending the hearing by the video conference link must produce valid identification if required to do so and,

There may be parts of the hearing which are held in private session; if that is the case, any accredited member of the media or public attending the hearing will be asked to leave during the private session and will be informed by the Hearings Officer when they can return.

To register, email MDP -PSD-GMB@mod.gov.uk with the following details:

Your name

Contact telephone number

Your email address

All requests to attend must be received on or before 11 September 2026.

Upcoming police appeals tribunals

There are currently no upcoming police tribunals.

Previous hearings and outcomes

Subject Officer: FPS Kay

Hearing date: 1 September 2026

Alleged Conduct (and PSPBs breached):

It is alleged that former PS David Kay breached the following standards of professional behaviour:

Honesty and Integrity

It is alleged that the officer breached the standards of professional behaviour by, whilst still serving in the MDP , misrepresenting that he was not a serving member of the force on LinkedIn, in order to benefit his personal electrical company.

It is alleged that this conduct, if proved, amounts to gross misconduct.

Finding : Gross Misconduct

Outcome : Dismissed without notice if still serving

Read the full outcome report: FPS Kay MDP Chair's Finding and Outcome ( PDF , 92.2 KB , 11 pages )

Subject Officer: PC Cleary

Hearing date: 22 July 2026

Mr Cleary is to attend an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing which will be heard remotely on 22 July 2026.

Mr Cleary will appear to answer allegations relating to breaches of the Standards of Professional Behaviour in respect of the following standards: Honesty and Integrity, Orders and Instructions, Duties and Responsibilities and Discreditable Conduct.

It is alleged that Mr Cleary improperly retained examination questions and answers from an examination he had failed to complete in order to gain an advantage in his resit.

Read the full outcome report: FPC Shaun Cleary MDP Hearing Outcome ( PDF , 197 KB , 13 pages )

Subject Officer: PC Colling

PC Colling is to attend an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing which will be heard remotely on 22 July 2026.

PC Colling will appear to answer allegations relating to breaches of the Standards of Professional Behaviour in respect of the following standards: Authority, Respect and Courtesy, Duties and Responsibilities, Fitness for Duty and Discreditable Conduct.

It is alleged that PC Colling engaged in a sexual act while on duty.

Read the full outcome report: FPC Benjamin Colling MDP Hearing Outcome ( PDF , 71.2 KB , 13 pages )

Subject Officer: PC Murphy

Hearing date: 21 July 2026

On 21 July 2026 an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing is taking place to hear an allegation against former-PC Hywell Murphy that on 24 March 2026 he was subject to a random drugs test that subsequently tested positive for the presence of cocaine, a Class A controlled drug.

It is alleged that by failing a drug test former-PC Murphy has breached the Standards of Professional Behaviour at the level of gross misconduct.

Read the full outcome report: PC Murphy MDP Hearing Outcome ( PDF , 117 KB , 8 pages )

Subject Officer: PC Jones

Hearing date: 8 July 2026

PC Jones is to attend an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing which will be held remotely on 8 July 2026.

PC Jones will appear to answer allegations relating to breaches of the Standards of Professional Behaviour in respect of the following standards: Honesty and Integrity, Authority, Respect and Courtesy and Discreditable Conduct.

It is alleged that PC Jones sent messages of a sexual nature to a 13-year-old child.

Outcome : Dismissed without notice

Read the full outcome report: PC Reece Jones MDP Outcome Report ( PDF , 255 KB , 19 pages )

Subject Officer: PC Grafton

Hearing Date: 14 – 22 May 2026

It is alleged that while off duty PC Grafton:

was aggressive and used homophobic language towards a member of the public

harassed and/or sexually harassed a member of the public

assaulted and/or sexually assaulted a member of the public

consumed alcohol such that he was reckless and/or unfit for duty early the next morning

Thereby, he failed to adhere to the expected Policing Standards of Behaviour. PC Grafton’s alleged conduct was in breach of the Standards of Professional Behaviour of Equality and Diversity, Authority, Respect and Courtesy, Use of Force, Orders and Instructions, Duties and Responsibilities, Fitness for Duty and Discreditable Conduct.

Finding: Gross Misconduct

Outcome: Dismissal Without Notice

items.title: Russia’s Enduring Role in Latin America and Its Implications for U.S. Hemispheric Interests
items.author: Samantha Perez Davila
items.summary: The authors examine Russia’s activities in Latin America and the Caribbean, how these efforts have advanced Russia’s strategic aims across the region as a whole and with key partners, and the implications for U.S interests in the Western Hemisphere.
items.body:
Elina Treyger , Samantha Perez Davila

Expert Insights Published Sep 8, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered sweeping international isolation for Russia and stretched the nation’s resources. Nonetheless, Moscow has intensified its engagement with several countries in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). In this paper, the authors examine Russia’s activities in LAC—specifically in Cuba, Venezuela, Nicaragua, and Brazil—and how these activities have advanced its strategic aims across the region as a whole and with respect to its key partners. The authors also describe the implications of these activities for U.S. interests in light of the broader geopolitical context of the Western Hemisphere.

The authors find that Russia’s activism in LAC suggests that neither the resources needed for its costly war of aggression nor international isolation prevent it from pursuing objectives far from home. Deepening ties with key partners and opportunistic engagements across the Western Hemisphere help Russia marshal support in the Global South for its anti-Western vision of a multipolar world order and for its unlawful territorial claims. To prevent and respond effectively to these challenges, the U.S. government needs to assess Russian activities in the Western Hemisphere holistically—in the broader context of Chinese and Iranian influence and the direct connections between regional developments and effects on the U.S. homeland.

items.title: UK pledges winter air defence package to boost Ukraine's defences
items.summary: The UK will supply air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery rounds and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against barbaric Russian attacks this winter, as part of Britain’s commitment to help Ukraine defend its freedom and sovereignty.
items.body:
The UK commits £100 million to air defence package including Patriot missiles to help Ukraine defend against Putin’s attacks.

Defence Secretary chairs his first Ukraine Defence Contact Group, the 50-nation strong group providing military kit for Ukraine.

Builds on recent UK backing of Ukraine’s domestic production of long-range missiles and landmark AI deal to boost military capabilities.

The UK will supply air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery rounds and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against barbaric Russian attacks this winter, as part of Britain’s commitment to help Ukraine defend its freedom and sovereignty.

Through a £100 million contribution to NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) the UK will support Ukraine with Patriot missiles and other air defence equipment that will be delivered before the winter, helping Ukraine defend its critical national infrastructure, innocent civilians and armed forces from Russian attacks. This follows the Prime Minister and Defence Secretary’s visits to Kyiv, where they heard from President Zelenskyy on the importance of additional support going into the winter.

Britain’s commitment to provide over 120,000 drones to Ukraine this year continues, with 25,000 delivered to date, a figure set to ramp up ahead of the winter. These include interceptors that take out Russian drones, reconnaissance drones that enable the Armed Forces of Ukraine to see what is happening on the battlefield and behind enemy lines, as well as attack drones that help Ukraine take the fight to Russia.

This comes as military support for Ukraine reaches another milestone, with the UK recently delivering its millionth round of large-calibre artillery ammunition to Ukraine, vital to its defence against Putin’s war. Building on this, the UK will deliver tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds in the coming months with funding from Britain, Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:

Both the Prime Minister and I heard loud and clear on our first visits to Kyiv the importance of supporting Ukraine through this winter, as Putin prepares to use winter as a weapon by continuing barbaric attacks against civilian and energy targets. We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can. Today, we are delivering on that, strengthening Ukraine’s defences and, alongside 50 allies, converting commitment into capability. We will stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine until they win. Ukraine’s frontline is the frontline for freedom everywhere and our support will not waver.
