We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can. Today, we are delivering on that, strengthening Ukraine’s defences and, alongside 50 allies, converting commitment into capability.

We will stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine until they win. Ukraine’s frontline is the frontline for freedom everywhere and our support will not waver.

This military support follows the Prime Minister’s announcement that the UK has agreed that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP, also known as Storm Shadow, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine.

The Prime Minister recently travelled to Kyiv to meet President Zelenskyy and sign a landmark AI deal that will see the two countries join forces to develop new military capabilities and the technology of the future.

Today’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group co-chaired by the Defence Secretary and his German counterpart Boris Pistorius, brings together nearly 50 nations. Taking place for the 36th time, it focuses on Ukraine’s urgent battlefield requirements and helps to sustain long-term military support for Ukraine.

items.title: 25 Years After 9/11: Lessons for Securing the Homeland
items.summary: Reflecting on 25 years since the September 11 terror attacks, RAND experts answer questions about protecting soft targets, the role of the TSA, mitigating risks from emerging technologies, and more.
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 8, 2026

The Tribute in Light rises above the New York skyline from the Brooklyn waterfront across the East River in New York, on September 9, 2025

Friday marks 25 years since the September 11 terror attacks. Americans are spending the week remembering those who lost their lives and honoring the first responders and others who sprang into action to help. The attacks cast a long shadow, stretching beyond Ground Zero, the Pentagon, and Flight 93 to transform not just the United States but the world.

RAND experts are reflecting on one of the most enduring aspects of this transformation: what we've learned about homeland security in the quarter-century since the attacks. Below, our researchers answer questions about protecting soft targets, mitigating risks from emerging technologies, and more.

What has stayed with you most about September 11, 2001? How did that day shape the way you think about protecting the homeland?

Heather Williams My professional trajectory has been shaped by many events, but it was set in motion by September 11. The attacks led me to focus on the Middle East and to join the U.S. Intelligence Community. That day stays with me as a reminder that solidarity is interwoven into the American fabric. This is comforting as we grapple with the current national divisions.

My thoughts on September 11 as a policy expert are more nuanced. Policymaking is so difficult because bureaucracy is complex and people are naturally resistant to change. September 11 allowed leaders to overcome much of the resistance, and I lived the positive effects of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act. At the same time, the reactionary nature of those changes created a patchwork of organizations working on homeland security, largely focused on terrorism as the threat.

That enterprise is now reorienting toward today's multi-hazard environment but without the catalyst that September 11 provided. Like many others, I'm motivated to build the necessary protective institutions before another tragedy strikes.

Ryan Consaul I think back to the tremendous sense of patriotism and unity born from the great tragedy of 9/11. Sadly, that unity has given way to controversy and division. Congressional oversight remains diffuse, and past bipartisan efforts to enact meaningful legislation to protect the homeland have given way to more-partisan priorities. Given the multitude of threats we continue to face, we need to stand together to tackle ongoing and emergent homeland security challenges.

Given the multitude of threats we continue to face, we need to stand together to tackle ongoing and emergent homeland security challenges.

What have we learned in the years since 9/11 about how best to protect soft targets? What does the evidence say about safeguarding communities from mass attacks by nonstate actors and others?

Brian Jackson For protecting soft targets, we often think first about technology: cameras, weapon-detection systems, or other physical protection measures. But some of the most effective protection comes from the community working together to identify and respond to potential threats. This is called behavioral threat assessment and management, or BTAM, and it's now one of the ways that the majority of K–12 schools , many workplaces, and some police departments or community safety efforts protect themselves. Teams respond when someone's behavior suggests they may become violent. Much of what the teams using this approach do doesn't look like security. For example, they might get the people referred to them into counseling or other programs to redirect them from whatever is moving them toward violence.

BTAM is effective, but it relies on everyone buying in. You can't intervene with a kid who's reading violent websites or making threats if their classmate doesn't let the teacher know what's happening or if the kid's parent refuses to let the child work with a counselor. Building and maintaining trust is tough. We tried to use this approach in the years after 9/11; it was a central part of efforts to respond to radicalization to violent extremism. But because many of the other counterterrorism approaches undermined trust with key communities, the strategy was never able to strengthen homeland security as much as it could have.

John Hollywood The evidence supports starting with layered security strategies in which multiple measures work together to improve the chance that an attack will be stopped or at least mitigated.

These security layers start with prevention. Tips from the public to police or on-site security have often helped to foil plots. Look for warning signs that incorporate a strong motivation to attack with concrete actions to prepare. Things like creating attack plans; researching how to attack; seeking to learn from extremists (including traveling to receive paramilitary training); accumulating large quantities of weapons or materials used in the construction of improvised explosives; and probing or breaching potential attack sites. Be aware that most motivations for mass attacks have been personal rather than ideological or partisan.

For on-site security, focus on the basics. Cases where attackers had direct access to a large crowd have tended to have the highest lethality, so consider how to put distance, barriers, and crowd movement between would-be attackers and crowds. Access-control systems—notably exterior and interior door locks, secured windows, and securable entryways—have all been effective and efficient. However, all require training and maintenance.

Be aware that most motivations for mass attacks have been personal rather than ideological or partisan.

Bystanders and security have stopped attacks. Groups of bystanders tackling shooters has been extremely effective. Again, training can make responses even more effective. That said, training needs to be low-stress and empowering without causing psychological injuries.

For communities, use interagency teams to support prevention, security training, and response planning. We need to establish and fund teams responsible for both educating the public about what to report and conducting diligent follow-up on reported cases. (Brian mentioned an approach for doing so, BTAM, above.) We then need to ensure advance planning and joint training with those agencies that will respond locally to a mass attack.

For many Americans, the creation of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and changes to airport screening remain among the most visible legacies of 9/11. What has research found about the TSA?

Kelly Klima Research over the past 25 years suggests that TSA has played a vital role in reducing the risk of terrorist attacks against U.S. aviation. Since 9/11, there has been no successful terrorist attack on a U.S. commercial flight that passed through TSA screening. This record reflects a layered defense-in-depth approach to screening passengers, baggage, and cargo, alongside intelligence, law-enforcement, and industry partners.

TSA has also balanced security with the need to move millions of travelers and large volumes of cargo efficiently and at reasonable cost. The passenger fee is less than $6 per flight, and the total TSA budget (which includes the development and procurement of screening technology) is about $8 billion in 2026.

That balance of security and reasonable cost continues to improve through better physical and chemical screening technologies, changes in checkpoint design and procedures, and risk-based approaches that focus attention where it's needed most.

But the threat continues to evolve. Terrorists and insiders may seek to conceal firearms, explosives, or other weapons in new ways. Emerging cyber and other nontraditional threats require constant assessment. Continued investment in advanced detection technologies, process redesign, and responsibly developed AI can help TSA identify threats more accurately and quickly, strengthen aviation security, and improve the passenger experience.

Continued investment in advanced detection technologies, process redesign, and responsibly developed AI can help TSA identify threats more accurately and quickly.

Williams Americans associate TSA with the blue shirts they encounter at the security checkpoint, but the organization has a broader mandate than many realize. One of the other programs TSA manages is the Security Threat Assessment for multiple security credentials, including the Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) and Hazardous Materials Endorsement for commercial driver's licenses. RAND research has found that TSA generally executes these programs effectively, at cost, and with timely resolution, in a way that reduces internal threats. For example, TWIC applicants who have no flags for possible disqualifying factors could find a physical card in their mailbox less than six days later.

Many anti-terrorism technologies and capabilities require collaborations between government and the private sector. What have we learned about how to effectively navigate those partnerships?

Thao Liz Nguyen One of the enduring lessons is that the development, maturation, and operational adoption of anti-terrorism technologies can proliferate in well-structured public-private collaboration. After 9/11, the Support Anti-terrorism by Fostering Effective Technologies Act of 2002, enacted as part of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, established the Office of SAFETY Act Implementation and created a statutory framework for evaluating and incentivizing anti-terrorism technologies. From a technology-evaluation perspective, the SAFETY Act not only encourages innovation in the abstract but applies a rigorous process to assessing technical performance, operational utility, and real-world deployment considerations of mature technologies to emerging capabilities.

Designation and Certification protections under the SAFETY Act have helped mature the market for proven security technologies and services by reducing liability uncertainty and signaling that a capability has undergone meaningful DHS review. At the same time, the Developmental Testing and Evaluation Designation protection has been especially important for emerging technologies, because it allows developers to generate operational evidence, refine concepts of use, and test performance in relevant environments before a capability is fully fielded.

What we've learned is that effective public-private partnership requires more than funding or policy encouragement; it requires credible evaluation pathways, clear incentives for participation, and mechanisms that help bridge the gap between innovation, validation, and scalable adoption for anti-terrorism technologies.

The development, maturation, and operational adoption of anti-terrorism technologies can proliferate in well-structured public-private collaboration.

Of course, new technologies have also transformed the threat landscape. Let's start with unmanned aerial systems, commonly known as drones. How have drones emerged as a potential threat to people and infrastructure, and what do we know about how to mitigate that threat?

Brendan Toland Drones have rapidly emerged as a threat because these systems have become more capable and more available. Parallel advances in a series of technologies (batteries, electric motors, precision manufacturing, optics) have shrunk the airframe for drones, increased their speed and endurance, and lowered their cost. Additionally, improvements in lightweight cameras, guidance via GPS waypoints, and wire-guided control have made it more difficult to detect and take over hostile drones. Finally, drones come in various forms. This lets bad actors select a drone that is optimal for the intended objective, whether that's maintaining an eye in the sky or delivering compact items (contraband, bombs) virtually anywhere at speed.

As part of RAND's work operating the Homeland Security Operational Analysis Center, we evaluated the capabilities of commercially available drones. We found that these systems continue to lower in cost while improving on operationally relevant metrics, such as speed, flight time, and payload capacity. We also developed several high-threat scenarios in which bad actors could use drones to threaten the homeland, including bombing a federal building or delivering a chemical agent outside a major sporting event. Looking across the market, we found more than 500 systems capable of conducting at least one of our high-threat scenarios. This number has only grown in the six years since our research was conducted.

The speed of drones and the ability to launch these systems from virtually anywhere constrains the response time for those working to defend the homeland. In our more recent simulation modeling, we found that defenders had only seconds to a few minutes to detect and defeat incoming drones, depending on the situation. If the adversary uses a drone to provide aerial surveillance, then in many cases the onboard camera enables a stand-off range that undermines detection. Any effective defense requires deploying layered mitigation capabilities in advance, putting these capabilities in the hands of trained personnel, sharing detection information across the homeland security enterprise, and empowering defenders on the ground to make quick decisions.

Christopher Scott Adams Advances in drone technology have made the threat more salient, but the homeland security enterprise has some tools to help mitigate that threat. The Preventing Emerging Threats Act and the SAFER SKIES Act have given key counter-drone authorities to federal and state/local/tribal/territorial law enforcement, respectively. These include permissions, under certain circumstances, to intercept communications between drones and their operators, track and monitor drone flights, and disable, down, or destroy potential threats.

These authorities have allowed DHS and its partners to invest in counter-drone technologies. At RAND, we've advised our DHS sponsors on the requirements for effective counter-drone capabilities and the right technology mix. This analysis has informed ongoing counter-drone investments at the border and in defense of major events, such as the World Cup and the Olympics.

Advances in drone technology have made the threat more salient, but the homeland security enterprise has some tools to help mitigate that threat.

Across these assessments, we've found a few consistent effective practices to mitigate, though not eliminate, the threat. First, defense-in-depth is key; having multiple types of sensors and effectors (kinetic and non-kinetic) in the same location gives the best chance of detecting and defeating a variety of drone threats. Second, defenders need to plan ahead. This includes resolving authorities issues, developing rules of engagement that are well understood by all operators, and creating information-sharing agreements across responsible agencies. Third, employing automation in defense can provide the speed to respond to a similarly automated threat.

What about artificial intelligence? For example, concerns are rising that AI could enable biological attacks. What do we know about this emerging risk and how best to mitigate it?

Steph Guerra Historically, biological attacks have been rare, unsuccessful, and difficult to execute. That's because of the technical, operational, and motivational barriers that bad actors face. But AI is increasingly able to lower these barriers by democratizing biological expertise, driving laboratory workflows, raising the ceiling of biological novelty, and circumventing existing biosecurity controls like gene synthesis screening . At RAND, we seek to assess these capabilities to help inform policy action that reduces the risk of misuse while still enabling beneficial scientific innovation.

Our team recently published a biosecurity strategy for the AI era to prevent AI-enabled biological attacks. The strategy is deliberately layered, because different mitigations stop different threat actors. For example, access controls like gene synthesis screening may stop a lone terrorist, but they probably can't stop a state bioweapons program. But a state program might be deterred from developing bioweapons by credible attribution and rapid response capabilities. Each layer is critical, but only having one is insufficient.

We know AI capabilities in biology are advancing fast, but thankfully the most hazardous thresholds haven't yet been crossed. That gives us a narrow window to build protective infrastructure before misuse becomes demonstrably easy.

Nguyen Detection technology is being pushed to do more than it was originally built for. This is true for any emerging unforeseen threat. As AI lowers the barrier to entry of designing novel biological agents or even modifying existing ones, screening systems must improve at spotting unusual patterns, not just known signatures stored in their static reference libraries. In practice, that means detection equipment needs to keep pace with new compounds, new delivery methods, and changes in how material may be packaged or concealed.

The challenge is that detection is only as good as the data, calibration, and reference libraries it relies on, so if the libraries are outdated, then the equipment can miss something that doesn't look like the “expected” threat. That's why DHS and other stakeholders should continue investing in research, development, testing, and evaluation; field testing; and recalibration of sensors and screening tools. We also need to think about how these systems are integrated across layers of screening, because no single device is going to catch everything. We need to invest in innovative detection systems and the algorithms behind them so they can stay adaptive and agile as threats evolve.

David Luckey The convergence of AI with advances in biotechnology and chemistry represents one of the most significant emerging risks to homeland security since 9/11. AI is rapidly lowering technical barriers in synthetic biology, genomics, and chemical engineering. This means that malicious actors could potentially leverage AI tools to design, synthesize, or optimize biological or chemical agents with unprecedented speed and precision.

This risk is not hypothetical. AI-driven platforms can already assist in protein folding, gene editing, and even the design of novel chemical compounds. Used by a bad actor, these capabilities could be repurposed to engineer pathogens or toxins that evade current detection and mitigation strategies. The dual-use nature of AI in life sciences poses unique governance and oversight challenges; the same tools that accelerate medical breakthroughs can also facilitate weaponization.

Mitigating this risk almost certainly requires a multi-layered approach that includes strengthening oversight, promoting responsible innovation, enhancing detection and response, and building cross-sector partnerships. Effective mitigation will likely depend on seamless collaboration between government, industry, and the research community. Proactive risk assessment, horizon scanning, and anticipatory governance are essential to stay ahead of adversaries who might exploit AI for catastrophic ends.

Proactive risk assessment, horizon scanning, and anticipatory governance are essential to stay ahead of adversaries who might exploit AI for catastrophic ends.

Twenty-five years later, what lesson from 9/11 feels most urgent in your work today?

Jackson Responding to threats requires thinking about how we will maintain defenses in the long term, even when the need to respond is most urgent.

The human and financial costs of 9/11 were catastrophic, and so there was pressure to do everything possible to make sure that such a tragedy couldn't happen again. As time passed, it became clear that the costs of all the security and other measures added up over time—and that one of the most effective responses to that specific threat (reinforcing airplane cockpit doors) was one of the cheapest. While government needs to spend to protect the nation, the more expensive security measures are, the harder they are to maintain over time.

Though thinking about the cost-effectiveness of security may seem odd when we're concerned about the risk of disasters like 9/11, doing so is critical, particularly since it's often much cheaper for attackers to try something new than it is for defenders to update protections.

Hollywood We need to stay vigilant but not overreactive.

This means maintaining a focus between overreaction to what have been extremely rare events and inattention to ongoing threats. Similarly, we must avoid getting distracted by a single part of the threat (e.g., focusing on a specific ideology when most attacks are personally motivated) or by a single security technology. Instead, what's needed is a strategic, layered approach that counters the full range of violent threats. Perhaps most importantly, vigilance means maintaining and developing partnerships between the public, security groups, and local, state, and federal agencies to provide ongoing prevention and protection.

Luckey It's imperative to have imagination and adaptability in the face of evolving threats.

9/11 exposed the dangers of “failure of imagination,” specifically the inability to anticipate how adversaries might exploit emerging or unexplored vulnerabilities. Today, as we confront the intersection of AI and biological or chemical weapons, that lesson is more urgent than ever.

Our adversaries are agile, opportunistic, and increasingly technologically sophisticated. The tools of mass disruption are no longer confined to nation-states or well-resourced groups; they're becoming accessible to a broader spectrum of actors. This reality demands that we continually reassess our assumptions, update our risk models, and foster a culture of innovation and vigilance across the homeland security enterprise.

I'm reminded daily that security is a dynamic process, not a static end state. The post-9/11 era amplified the value of intelligence sharing, public-private partnerships, and resilience. But it also illuminated that the next threat might not look like the last. Our greatest asset is the ability to anticipate, adapt, and act—before the unimaginable becomes reality.

items.title: Novel technologies for security-sector governance and management
items.author: Elizabeth Moisan
items.summary: RAND Europe scoped technology use in security-sector governance and management, mapping opportunities and risks from real-world cases and distilling lessons and good practices to embed good governance in the adoption and use of these tools.
items.body:
RAND Europe conducted a scoping study to explore the use of technologies in security sector governance and management (SSG/M) with the aim of examining opportunities and risks stemming from use cases identified through the research, as well as identifying lessons learned and good practices to foster good-governance efforts when leveraging technological solutions in the security sector.

Novel technologies for security-sector governance and management

Pauline Paillé , Sarah Winder , Elizabeth Moisan

Research Published Sep 8, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

RAND Europe conducted a scoping study on the implications of novel technologies for security-sector governance and management (SSG/M) supported by the Security and Stabilisation Department of the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).

The study explored how emerging solutions such as artificial intelligence (AI), biometrics, machine learning and enhanced surveillance systems are being adopted by security-sector actors and how their use affects public acceptability and consent, institutional accountability, financial sustainability and ethics.

Through a targeted literature review and semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders, the study investigated how technologies can strengthen efficiency, effectiveness and transparency across SSG/M while introducing significant risks, including privacy and data-protection concerns, algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and challenges related to data sovereignty and reliance on private suppliers. The study identified cross-cutting lessons and good practices to guide responsible adoption and foster good governance by emphasising early engagement with end users, adaptation to local context, clear data governance, layered human oversight of automated processes, complementary internal policies and external regulation, and continuous training.

Key Takeaways

Exploring novel technologies and their impact on SSG/M

Nine technology areas were identified as being increasingly used in SSG/M: Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality (AR/VR), Automated decision support, Biometrics, Blockchain, Digital ID platforms, Data management solutions, Satellite imagery, Social media monitoring, and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs).

These solutions can provide gains in efficiency, effectiveness, situational awareness, and, where designed transparently, strengthened accountability and traceability. However, there are also cross-cutting risks to consider: privacy and data-protection concerns, algorithmic bias and opaque models, cybersecurity and data-sovereignty vulnerabilities, exclusion of digitally marginalised groups, and diluted accountability when private vendors or automated systems shape decisions.

Enhancing good-governance practices for the use of technology in SSG/M

Six cross-cutting practices were identified to embed governance into the full technology lifecycle in the context of SSG/M: 1. Co-design with end users and communities to ensure fit-for-purpose tools and accountability 2. Justify and adapt adoption to local context, infrastructure and perceptions, anticipating misuse 3. Assess need and balance risk appetite and tolerance, including lifecycle costs, while governing data provenance, ownership and cross-border sharing 4. Move beyond human-in-the-loop to multilayered oversight that counters automation bias, allows time to intervene and clarifies responsibility 5. Pair internal policies with external regulation and oversight (transparent approvals, logging/auditing, public consultation and after-action reviews) for accountability 6. Provide continuous and dedicated training for operators and leaders to support the use of technologies in SSG/M.

Recommendations

There is a need to bring key stakeholders together, including private-sector companies developing technological solutions as well as state and non-state actors involved in the delivery and management of security services. Relevant actors from adjacent sectors who are also using these technologies, such as humanitarian or disaster-response bodies, could also benefit from widespread engagement.

Technological solutions evolve very rapidly and often simultaneously across contexts. As a result, there are limited opportunities to learn from past or ongoing experiences in other contexts in order to replicate good practices and avoid pitfalls that may have been previously identified in different settings .

SSG/M good-governance principles should be embedded when considering the use of technologies. To do so, the principles of good governance outlined above should form part of the requirements when considering technological solutions for the provision and management of security services. In addition, the development of a risk-assessment model could be used across fragile contexts to assess the suitability of these technological solutions.

items.title: UK expertise to bolster Polish air defences in boost to NATO security
items.summary: A new defence centre built with UK expertise opens today in Poland, strengthening the country's air defences and reinforcing NATO’s eastern flank against Russian aggression.
items.body:
New repair and logistics centre opened in Czosnów will help protect Poland’s airspace, using UK expertise.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP opens new defence facility in Poland, supporting jobs in Bristol, Stevenage and Bolton.

Part of UK’s commitment to protecting NATO’s eastern flank against increasing Russian aggression.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP joined the Polish Deputy Minister of National Defence, Paweł Zalewski to open the MBDA missile logistics facility in Czosnów, Poland.

UK personnel will work alongside Polish counterparts at the site to help protect Poland’s airspace. Its development will also support jobs in Bristol, Stevenage and Bolton, with more than 400 UK MBDA staff working on programmes that support Poland’s defence.

The centre will enable faster and more direct maintenance, support and training for Poland’s PILICA+ programme - a multi-billion-pound project building an integrated air defence network to defend Poland’s skies in conjunction with the UK.

MBDA’s expanded footprint in Poland will drive innovation and investment into the Czosnów region, while reinforcing stability across NATO’s eastern flank.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:

The UK is proud to stand alongside Poland as a close friend, trusted ally, and partner in security, industry collaboration and defence. At a time when Europe faces its most serious security challenges for generations, the opening of MBDA’s new site demonstrates that the relationship between our two nations has never been more important. Stronger Polish air defences means stronger NATO air defences, and that work is taking place while also backing jobs in both nations.

The UK is proud to stand alongside Poland as a close friend, trusted ally, and partner in security, industry collaboration and defence.

At a time when Europe faces its most serious security challenges for generations, the opening of MBDA’s new site demonstrates that the relationship between our two nations has never been more important.

Stronger Polish air defences means stronger NATO air defences, and that work is taking place while also backing jobs in both nations.

MBDA UK Managing Director, Chris Allam, said:

We are very pleased the Minister was able to attend the opening of our new facility in Poland. items.title: Croatia buys South Korean rocket artillery after HIMARS purchase from the US
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: In the aftermath of the Iran war, the U.S. government has flagged possible delays in deliveries of military gear, including HIMARS ammunition.
items.body:
Europe

Croatia buys South Korean rocket artillery after HIMARS purchase from the US

The K239 Chunmoo multiple launch rocket system fires a munition. (Courtesy of Hanwha Defense)

WARSAW, Poland — The Croatian government has approved the acquisition of 18 K239 Chunmoo multiple-rocket launchers from South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace. Croatia is joining other European countries that have also ordered the weapon which is considered an alternative to Lockheed Martin’s M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, or HIMARS.

“Due to the relatively short delivery times of 24 to 36 months, better availability, lower prices, openness to industrial cooperation, the European countries Poland, Estonia and the Kingdom of Norway are increasingly deciding to equip themselves with this unique system,” said Croatian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Ivan Anušić, as quoted in a statement released by the country’s government.

The procurement is worth around €544.1 million ($631.9 million). Deliveries to the Croatian military are scheduled for the years 2026 to 2029, according to the statement. Hanwha Aerospace is to supply launchers, ammunition and accompanying equipment to Croatia. The company’s Polish partner, WB Group, will deliver a command-and-control system to connect all components into a single operational unit.

Under the plan, the South Korean launchers are to replace the Croatian Army’s outdated Yugoslavia-made M-92 Vulkan and Soviet-designed GRAD BM-21 systems.

Anušić said that, alongside the nation’s 2021 purchase of 12 second-hand Dassault Rafale F3-R fighter jets from France, the acquisition marks one of the most important military procurement since the end of Croatia’s independence war in 1995.

In December 2024, the Croatian government approved the purchase of eight HIMARS launchers from the United States under a contract worth around $351 million.

In the aftermath of the Iran war, the U.S. government has flagged possible delays in deliveries of military gear, including HIMARS ammunition, to a number of countries in the region, triggering concern in capitals on NATO’s eastern flank.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: National Armaments Director appoints new Chief Financial Officer
items.summary: The National Armaments Director (NAD) has appointed Ian Brimicombe as the new Chief Financial Officer (CFO) for the NAD Group.
items.body:
Ian brings more than 40 years of finance leadership experience spanning professional services, global pharmaceuticals and luxury retail to the NAD Group.

As CFO, Ian will join the NAD Group Executive Committee and play a crucial role in how the NAD Group delivers the Defence Investment Plan (DIP), reacting to Defence’s new capability priorities. Under his leadership, the Group’s finance professionals will support the NAD Group teams responsible for developing, delivering, sustaining, housing and harbouring the UK’s ‘national arsenal’ and defence estate.

Ian has a history of crafting smart financial strategies and improving performance in both FTSE 100 and private international companies, and has helped solve financial business challenges for FTSE 100 firms.

Commenting on his appointment, Ian Brimicombe said:

I’m delighted to be joining the National Armaments Director Group as Chief Financial Officer. Having spent my career in the private sector, I’m excited by the opportunity to bring that experience to the Ministry of Defence at such an important time for the organisation, for defence and for the UK. I look forward to working with the team to build on its foundations and support its future growth and success.

On graduating from King’s College London, Ian completed his accountancy and tax qualifications at Coopers and Lybrand (now PWC). After building a strong technical foundation across audit, tax and corporate finance, he moved into the pharmaceutical industry, joining what later became AstraZeneca, where he spent over 20 years in increasingly senior leadership roles.

Ian subsequently joined the British fashion house, Burberry, where he spent nearly seven years supporting finance and business transformation, including navigating the organisation through the COVID-19 pandemic and leading refinancing activities. Most recently he was CFO at Abercrombie & Kent Group.

Rupert Pearce, National Armaments Director, said:

I am delighted to welcome Ian to the NAD Group. He brings with him a wealth of experience from the high-tech world of pharmaceuticals and the fast-paced retail arena. As UK Defence continues its transformation, and we look to drive greater efficiency into our systems, these are skills we really value. David Johnson, who retires this Autumn, leaves an exceptional legacy as our first Group Finance Director. He has been a stalwart member of the MOD for 37 years. His professionalism, rigour and sharp eye for detail have helped make our armed forces and country more secure. We wish him all the best for his retirement.

items.title: An analysis of Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in the labour market
items.author: Linda Slapakova
items.summary: This RAND Europe research explores UK Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in civilian labour markets, including economic participation, underemployment and barriers to, and facilitators of, good employment outcomes.
items.body:
This RAND Europe research explores UK Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in civilian labour markets, including economic participation, underemployment and barriers to, and facilitators of, good employment outcomes. While Veterans and Reservists have similar employment rates and hourly wages to non-Veterans they face distinct labour market challenges, including barriers at the individual, employer and structural level.

An analysis of Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in the labour market

Catherine Galley , Sean Flanagan , Linda Slapakova

Research Published Sep 7, 2026

Includes Executive Summary; Supplementary Annex

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Approximately 960,000 working-age Veterans and 30,000 volunteer Reservists live in Great Britain, and they participate in the labour market at broadly comparable levels to the wider civilian populations. However, the nature of their economic activity often differs: Veterans are over-represented in sectors such as manufacturing, transport, construction and public administration. Despite the high employment rate, some Veterans and Reservists also face barriers to securing meaningful work and some Veterans and Reservists experience underemployment where their skills and experience are not being fully utilised.

Despite growing policy attention, including the 2026 Veterans’ Strategy commitment to ensuring Veteran’s skills are properly recognised and utilised, and that these skills contribute to UK national security, there are significant evidence gaps on Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in the labour market. Research has historically focused on whether individuals are in employment, overlooking phenomena such as underemployment and positive economic contributions.

To address these gaps, RAND Europe was commissioned by the Office for Veterans' Affairs, via the Armed Forces Covenant Fund Trust, to conduct a mixed-methods study combining statistical analysis of three national datasets (the Census, Annual Population Survey, and Family Resources Survey) with an international literature review and stakeholder interviews. This report presents new evidence on the employment profile and earnings of Veterans and Reservists, underemployment and the barriers and facilitators to Veterans and Reservists gaining successful employment, informing five recommendations for the OVA.

Key Takeaways

Veterans and Reservists have similar levels of employment and hourly wages to comparable non-Veterans

The data shows that Veterans and Reservists have similar levels of employment and hourly wages to non-Veterans with similar characteristics, indicating that Veterans and Reservists do not face systemic labour market disadvantage. However, Veterans and Reservists are concentrated in different industries and occupations to non-Veterans, making them vulnerable to economic shocks in different ways to non-Veterans.

Employers increasingly recognise that Veterans and Reservists bring valuable skills to the labour market

However, some Veterans and Reservists still face challenges in translating their skills and qualifications and having them recognised in civilian workplaces, and can face barriers to employment at the individual, employer and structural level. These barriers include poor awareness and understanding of the Armed Forces, military roles and skills among hiring managers and other decision makers, and a lack of clear policies to support Veterans and Reservists consistently.

Underemployment remains an underexplored but potentially significant issue for both Veterans and Reservists

The limited evidence suggests that underemployment may affect a substantial number of Veterans, particularly during their transition from military service to civilian life. For Reservists, underemployment is more complex and can occur in both their military and civilian roles.

Minority subgroups within the Veteran community tend to experience the disadvantages faced by their non-Veteran counterparts

Female, ethnic minority, and disabled/poor-health Veterans generally experience similar labour-market disadvantages as their non-Veteran peers with the same characteristics, rather than being either protected or uniquely disadvantaged by Veteran status alone.

Recommendations

This report makes five recommendations for the Office for Veterans’ Affairs:

Continue providing through-life career support to Veterans and Reservists with a focus on encouraging engagement and exploring promising avenues for strengthening support.

Continue to promote understanding of military service among employers and the broader public, focusing on gatekeepers (e.g. hiring managers) as well as senior leadership.

Ensure policymakers and service providers consider regional differences and ensure that policies and support are inclusive to all members of the Armed Forces community.

Monitor trends and shocks impacting the labour market and work with other stakeholders across national and local government, industry and the third sector to effectively align support provision.

Work with stakeholders across the sector to address priority evidence gaps and ensure the continued inclusion of Veteran and Armed Forces identifiers in large-scale national surveys.

items.title: UK forces join trilateral Arctic exercise in strategic High North operation
items.summary: UK Armed Forces have deployed to the remote Arctic island of Jan Mayen alongside Norwegian and US allies, in a demonstration of NATO's enhanced capability to operate jointly in the High North.
items.body:
Royal Marine Commandos and RAF personnel have deployed alongside Norwegian and US allies to Jan Mayen for Operation Atlantic City.

The operation tested NATO’s ability to operate in harsh Arctic conditions, where weather and terrain demand meticulous planning.

Striking imagery showcases UK’s contribution to enhanced deterrence in the Arctic Region.

UK Armed Forces have deployed to the remote Arctic island of Jan Mayen alongside Norwegian and US allies, in a demonstration of NATO’s enhanced capability to operate jointly in the High North.

As part of Operation Atlantic City, personnel from LXX Squadron, Royal Air Force, deployed alongside detachments from UK Commando Force, running from 26 August to 4 September 2026. The trilateral operation formed part of Arctic Sentry, NATO’s enhanced vigilance activity for the High North.

Jan Mayen sits in an isolated stretch of the Norwegian Sea, roughly 620 miles from mainland Norway. The island occupies a critical geostrategic position north of the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, an area of water vital to the defence of northern Europe and the wider Euro-Atlantic area.

The operation has seen UK forces work alongside the Royal Norwegian Navy, the Norwegian Home Guard, and US Marine Corps units integrate various sensor and communications systems, allowing NATO to be better prepared for potential threats.

The UK’s participation in this deployment reflects its commitment to NATO’s collective security and its ability to adapt to the unique challenges of Arctic operations.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:

The High North is vital to the security of the UK and our NATO Allies. This operation demonstrates the strength of our partnership with Norway and the United States, and the ability of our Armed Forces to operate together in even the most demanding Arctic conditions. It is a clear signal of our enduring commitment to NATO security and to defending our shared interests in the High North.

The High North is vital to the security of the UK and our NATO Allies. This operation demonstrates the strength of our partnership with Norway and the United States, and the ability of our Armed Forces to operate together in even the most demanding Arctic conditions.

It is a clear signal of our enduring commitment to NATO security and to defending our shared interests in the High North.

Operation Atlantic City ran concurrently with naval manoeuvres during Operation Northern Viking 26, allowing the trilateral force to maximise overlapping maritime and sensing resources across the European theatre, while also supporting NATO’s broader Arctic Sentry activities.

The exercise has built on similar Allied training conducted around Jan Mayen last year and draws on the island’s history.

Arctic training provides UK forces with practical experience in maritime operations, surveillance, movement, survival and joint operations in some of the world’s most challenging weather conditions.

Forces operating in the High North must be prepared to overcome the challenges posed by distance, extreme weather, limited infrastructure and rapidly changing conditions.

items.title: US Fighters, Drones Strike 3 Iranian Oil Tankers After Iran Fires on Navy Ships
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: The U.S. military struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept. 5, as the Trump administration and Iran battle for control over the Strait of Hormuz. The post US Fighters, Drones Strike 3 Iranian Oil Tankers After Iran Fires on Navy Ships appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The U.S. military struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept. 5, as the Trump administration and Iran battle for control over the Strait of Hormuz.

A mix of Air Force and Navy aircraft carried out the attacks using both fighters and drones, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine. The American strikes followed an unsuccessful Iranian ballistic missile attack on a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer. Neither U.S. ship was hit.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, referring to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. “If you shoot at our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost—take out three of yours.”

Cooper’s statement continued: “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

The three Iranian tankers included the M/T Downy, which was hit near Kharg Island, and the M/T Stark 1, which was struck near Jask, a coastal city in Iran. The M/T Downy and the M/T Stark 1 were “permanently disabled,” according to CENTCOM. The third Iranian tanker, the M/T Kylo, was hit in the Gulf of Oman. Struck in multiple locations, that tanker was rendered inoperable and “completely destroyed,” according to CENTCOM. It later sank. The Iranian crew was warned that it should abandon ship before the strike, the command said. CENTCOM released videos of the attacks on the ships and the sinking of the M/T Kylo.

The M/T Downy and the M/T Stark 1 were impacted by weapons fired at the stern, while the M/T Kylo suffered a more significant bombardment.

The U.S. attacks on the Iranian oil tankers are part of a new Trump administration policy to deter Iranian attacks on U.S. military forces and commercial vessels. Previously, the U.S. had focused its attacks on Iranian military targets, such as radars and surface-to-air missiles.

Iran’s foreign ministry called the attacks on oil tankers a “war crime” intended to further America’s “economic war” on the Iranian homeland. Cooper said the attacks on Iran’s oil carriers are justified because they generate revenue for the IRGC.

The IRGC said in its own statement that it would follow suit and that it targeted “three oil tankers traveling through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three vessels affiliated with the United States in other areas.”

The U.S. is seeking to use economic sanctions and a blockade to pressure Iran to give up its attempt to control international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and to agree to limits on its nuclear program.

items.title: Future Airmen to Get Less Sleep, More Stress in Basic Training
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: The Air Force has begun depriving new trainees of more sleep and will soon ramp up the stress level in Basic Military Training to better prepare Airmen for the increased strain of combat operations such as Epic Fury. The post Future Airmen to Get Less Sleep, More Stress in Basic Training appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-LACKLAND, Texas —The Air Force has started challenging new trainees with less sleep and will soon ramp up the stress level in Basic Military Training to better prepare the future Airmen for the increased strain of combat operations such as Epic Fury.

The service’s 7.5 weeks of BMT already forced Airmen to endure the high stress of constant corrections, long hours of training, and sleep periods interrupted by guard duty.

But in late August, BMT officials here began an effort that will force trainees to handle additional sleep deprivation by increasing the frequency of nocturnal training. In the coming weeks, officials hope to add “stress inoculation” to the effort that’s designed to increase training stress but also teach trainees techniques to function more effectively under it, Col. Kellie Courtland, commander of the 37th Training Wing that oversees BMT, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach directed BMT officials to make the new training changes after combat operations—such as the recent air campaign against Iran—showed that some young Airmen struggled under the strain of the increased operational pace, Courtland added.

The Air Force is “realizing that there are people that are not responding to being able to perform well when they’re sleep deprived, or there’s a lot of stress, … or hard events happen; they’re having a hard time recovering from that,” Courtland said. “The idea is to practice that a little bit more and get used to that level of stress and sleep deprivation because it’s going to happen at different points throughout your career but definitely when you’re out in those wartime environments.”

This is the latest change in a larger effort to overhaul BMT to instill a mindset of “airmindedness” in all Airmen to ensure they know how to work in small teams to defend, operate, generate, and sustain airpower.

Less Sleep

The first week of BMT will remain unchanged since new trainees are already “sleep deprived” from the complete culture shock of the new environment, Courtland said. Beginning in week two, military training instructors, or MTIs, will increase the amount of nighttime entry-control procedures, or guard duty, that each 60-member flight must share. In the past, shifts were two hours long. Now they are one hour each, which requires more trainees to be up on any given night.

Before “you would only have four to eight people basically getting woken up during the night that would do their entry control procedures,” Courtland said. “Now you’ve got 21 trainees that have to get up, spend an hour doing entry control procedures.”

On top of guard shifts, more nighttime training activities are added in the fourth and fifth week in the lead up to PACER FORGE, the final field training exercise that stresses trainees’ agile combat employment skills.

In the fourth week, “we will do different exercises, like maybe an accountability exercise,” said 37th Training Wing Command Chief Master Sgt. Caleb Vaden, describing how all trainees fall out of the dorm, so leaders can ensure everyone is present.

“That usually takes about an hour, and they’ll fall back into their sleeping area,” Vaden said. “Everything we do here is tied to a training objective.”

During the fifth week, trainees will see more nocturnal training events as they begin to prepare for PACER FORGE, where trainees traditionally get little sleep during the 57-hour training event, Vaden said.

“We are working on an exercise where they would fall out, work on that F-16, fall under attack, have to go to a bunker, and then they’re going to go forward to their forward site,” Vaden said. “So essentially, they’re getting additional sleep deprivation before they even get to the PACER FORGE site. We’re getting them up early, keeping them up, not letting them sleep very much. … it just keeps amping up as you get closer and closer to PACER FORGE.

More Stress

The plan to prepare trainees to endure more stress effectively is still under review, Courtland said, but the idea is to not only introduce more stress into training activities but also teach trainees techniques for recognizing and coping with extreme pressure.

“It’s more understanding how you work through stress when you are stressed out,” Courtland said. “The idea is they get stressed out more here. It’s intense. They get that stress, but then we are walking them through it— ‘hey, you probably felt really stressed in that moment, here’s something you could have done, or here’s something that may have helped.’”

For example, trainees may be taught to use box breathing, a technique that uses equal counts of inhaling, holding, exhaling, and pausing to calm the nervous system, said Courtland, who would not discuss the list of techniques that is currently under review. If all goes well, the new stress portion of training could be approved by the end of September, she added.

“At the same time that we’re teaching them how to deal with stress, we are going to be turning up the stress and turning up the intensity,” she said.

MTIs will use regular after-action reviews of training events to ensure trainees understand how the increased stress affected their performance, Vaden said.

“I will more than likely see degradation in teamwork. I’ll see degradation in leadership. I’ll see degradation in situational awareness; I’ll see degradation in a lot of things,” Vaden said. “We’re just going to use those performance measures when we’re assessing.”

Courtland added that the success of the effort will involve seeing if trainees use the new stress techniques under increased pressure. “The goal is to teach them the tools, stress the hell out of them, and see if they know how to use the tools correctly.”

In other changes to BMT, training officials have partially completed a portion of the new air base training range that includes a non-flying F-16 Fighting Falcon . Trainees have begun learning and practicing how to re-arm the fighter with mock AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles and other training munitions that mock Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System rockets. The new air base training range will soon include two retired C-130 Hercules aircraft which arrived here in August .

items.title: Ukraine asks EU to fund first Patriot missiles buy
items.author: Katie Livingstone
items.summary: Brussels is weighing a rare waiver that would let Kyiv tap its €90 billion loan for U.S.-made interceptors for the first time.
items.body:
Europe

Ukraine asks EU to fund first Patriot missiles buy

A PAC-3 interceptor fires from a Medium Extended Air Defense system launcher during a test. (John Hamilton/U.S. Army)

KYIV, Ukraine — The European Union is reviewing Kyiv’s request to spend billions of euros on PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its Patriot batteries — the first time Ukraine has formally asked to tap a €90 billion support loan approved earlier this year to buy the U.S.-made systems, European officials announced this week.

“We will keep supporting Ukraine, including with European air defence and PAC-3 Patriot systems,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X on Sept. 2, confirming the request alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. “We will work closer than ever with NATO. And deter anyone who attacks our freedom and security.”

The statement comes a day after Ukraine’s defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara, pressed allies for more aid. Russia is continuing a second week of launching near-nonstop aerial strikes on Kyiv, Odesa and other cities as Ukraine faces a dire antiballistics interceptor shortage .

“Ukraine calls on partners to allocate national budget funds for the procurement of Ukrainian drones, expedite the provision of the EU loan, and resume discussions on the use of frozen Russian assets,” Khmara said in a statement .

He said Ukraine currently faces a $27 billion defense budget deficit, but emphasized that supporting Kyiv is a “win-win” for Europe.

“Every euro invested in Ukraine’s defence is an investment in European security,” he said.

The €90 billion loan Kyiv hopes to tap into — finalized by the Council of the EU in April after months of delay — sets aside roughly €60 billion for defense procurement and €30 billion for budget support.

But the loan’s rules were written to prioritize European and Ukrainian-made weapons, capping non-EU/Ukrainian content at 35% of a given purchase’s value.

Because PAC-3s are built in the U.S., Kyiv’s request needs to receive a formal exemption to access the funds.

Ukraine already secured a similar carve-out in April for Chinese-made drone components, a precedent officials are pointing to as EU member states weigh the latest request.

Von der Leyen said in her Sept. 2 statement that the exemption review “is moving in the right direction,” and that EU representatives were due to decide on the exemption on Monday.

items.title: US Air Force speeds Reaper successor timeline after Iran losses
items.author: Michael Scanlon
items.summary: The Air Force is accelerating its timeline for a cheaper, more expendable successor to the MQ-9A Reaper after combat losses.
items.body:
MilTech

US Air Force speeds Reaper successor timeline after Iran losses

An MQ-9 Reaper, armed with GBU-12 Paveway II laser guided munitions and AGM-114 Hellfire missiles, flies a combat mission over southern Afghanistan. (Lt. Col. Leslie Pratt/U.S. Air Force)

The U.S. Air Force is accelerating its timeline for a cheaper, more expendable successor to the MQ-9A Reaper, officials said Sept. 3, after combat losses left the service unwilling to wait out the rest of the drone’s life.

Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s chief modernization officer, told reporters at the Pentagon that a follow-on was already under discussion as the MQ-9 aged out.

“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” he said, according to Breaking Defense , which covered the briefing.

Defense Daily reported that Air Force Secretary Troy Meink directed the acceleration, and that the fiscal 2031 target of 20 mission-ready aircraft could be pulled forward by about two years.

In May, Lt. Gen. David Tabor told the Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Airland the fleet was down to about 135 aircraft , roughly 54 below the service’s 189-aircraft floor. Niemi did not update the inventory.

Backfilling the fleet is difficult. General Atomics shut down MQ-9A production in 2025, and Tabor said the service was pursuing a short-term buy of existing MQ-9A airframes in fiscal 2026. Niemi said Sept. 3 that budget constraints make buying a large number of upgraded MQ-9B SkyGuardians unrealistic. It is a misconception, he said, that the Air Force could write a check and take delivery of 100 aircraft.

A Congressional Research Service Insight updated May 13 cited an April 9 news report of 24 Reapers lost since military operations against Iran began in February, and said it was unclear whether the Pentagon had given Congress an accounting. The Washington Post reported Aug. 13 , citing three U.S. officials, that at least 45 had been lost, roughly 25% of the fleet.

Niemi signed requirements in May for a cheaper, modular, mass-producible aircraft.

That program, Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA, opened as a Defense Innovation Unit competition July 7 with the Air Force as partner. The solicitation, which closed July 23, asked for a drone that could fly Reaper-class strike, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare and communications-relay missions cheaply enough to absorb losses. It called for at least 2,800 pounds of payload and an 8,000-nautical-mile one-way ferry range.

That is the aircraft Niemi now prices against Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCA. He put CCA air vehicles near $20 million and MMA at about half that, Defense Daily reported.

An Air Force spokesperson said those figures are for the air vehicle only, not a fully missionized aircraft, according to Breaking Defense . In May, Niemi told senators a Reaper with a full sensor package can cost up to $50 million. At the Sept. 3 briefing, he said the Air Force will probably field at least 180 MMA drones.

Niemi argued the Reaper’s value is not the airframe.

“What makes the MQ-9 special has nothing to do with the aircraft itself,” he said, calling its speed, altitude and range decades-old technology.

Initial MMA versions, he said, will rely on proven technology rather than new systems to hit the price. He described a long-aspect-wing turboprop in the “4,000 miles-type class,” farther and heavier than a CCA but slower. Officials did not say how that class relates to the 8,000-nautical-mile ferry range in the July notice.

General Atomics is bidding a design it calls Wildfire, first reported by Aviation Week in August. Spokesman C. Mark Brinkley told Air & Space Forces Magazine it “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” but declined to give capabilities or cost. The company has not released images.

Brinkley told The War Zone in August that treating MMA as a Reaper replacement misses the immediate need for a backfill. Wildfire does not depend on winning the competition, he said, and “we can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”

He framed the design targets as considerations rather than specs, among them a 10,000-nautical-mile ferry range, four Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles and 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control.

Col. Todd Dye, senior materiel leader in the Air Force’s medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance division, said awards for MMA concept refinement were expected in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Breaking Defense reported .

Officials did not announce a new date at the Sept. 3 briefing.

Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

items.title: Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft. The post Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.

Back in July, the Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit announced plans to develop a low-cost drone to do all the missions that an MQ-9 can do today, and when necessary fly in groups to overwhelm an enemy’s anti-drone capabilities and force them to expend large numbers of munitions. They called the effort Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA .

At the time, officials said they wanted to have a prototype to test fly within 21 months of a contract, and then 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031 to achieve initial operating capability.

Now, though, officials are targeting a more ambitious timeline. During a media roundtable at the Pentagon, DIU military deputy Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel said the MMA program will try to follow DIU’s typical timeframe of prototyping a system within a year of a contract, and then fielding it at scale within three years—as soon as 2029.

Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said those goals changed “fairly recently,” when Air Force Secretary Troy Meink “called us in and said ‘You need to move faster.’”

That urgency, Niemi acknowledged, came at least partly in response to the significant losses the MQ-9 fleet has taken in the past year or so during operations against Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Since the start of the Iran war, the Air Force has lost at least 45 MQ-9s, roughly a quarter of its fleet. The service was already thinking about what it needed to succeed the MQ-9 as a medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platform, but Niemi said the combat losses pushed it to move faster.

“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” Niemi said.

Replacing, Not Reinventing, the MQ-9

The MQ-9 has long been a workhorse of the Air Force fleet, valued by combatant commanders for its long endurance, loitering ability, and ability to combine strike and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach called the Reaper the “most valuable player” of Operation Epic Fury in a May congressional hearing.

Unsurprisingly, then, officials said they were eager to replace the ones lost in combat. Niemi said the Air Force has “spent a lot of time and energy” in recent months trying to figure out how to do so and found “there’s not a lot of good options to immediately replace those aircraft.”

The Air Force considered General Atomics’ MQ-9B, a larger and more complex—and more expensive—version of the MQ-9A, Niemi said. Ultimately, officials concluded the MQ-9B was not the right choice because the Air Force needed something more “attritable,” or inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.

“If you don’t like losing an MQ-9A that cost on the order of $50 million, with the sensors, you’re probably not going to like losing an MQ-9B at a higher price point,” Niemi said.

For that reason, the Air Force decided to go all-in on the MMA concept. The Air Force plans to field at least 180 of the drones, Niemi said, but probably more than that.

In order to move fast and keep costs down, Niemi said the Air Force plans to “accept prudent risk” on the MMA program. Kunkel also said the Air Force wants “significantly increased levels of competition” to keep costs down.

As the Air Force wrote out what attributes MMA drones would need, Niemi added, it tried to allow as much flexibility as possible and not include hyper-specific requirements that “push technology to the very edge.”

“When that happens, you’re going to pay a lot for it, because it’s hard to do,” Niemi said. “It takes a lot of engineering, cutting-edge science, emergent technologies, things like that. So we’re trying to be more aligned with sort of an ‘80 percent is good enough,’ [using] mature technologies” approach.

That means MMA won’t have the latest and greatest flight control systems, engines, or manufacturing processes, he said—and they’ll actually resemble the MQ-9 in some key ways: they’ll likely have long-aspect wings and will likely be powered by turboprop engines.

One way officials are looking to differ from the MQ-9, though, are higher levels of autonomy and automation than the MQ-9A has today, Niemi said—“more mouse clicks and keyboard strokes instead of a stick and throttle.” That will reduce the number of Airmen needed to operate MMA drones and allow a single Airman to operate multiple drones simultaneously.

At the same time, Niemi said MMAs won’t have the same level of autonomy as the Air Force’s flagship autonomous drone program, Collaborative Combat Aircraft.

“It’s not going out and autonomously finding targets and employing weapons,” Niemi said of the MMA drone. “It’s more like a truck that’s carrying packages, whether it’s a sensor package or whether it’s a weapon, to a point where it can be employed.”

CCAs and MMAs

While CCAs and MMAs will both be unmanned and have some kind of autonomy software, Niemi was quick to note there will be major differences between the two.

“They’re going to look very different,” Niemi said. The MMA is “going to look like an MQ-9, and [CCA is] going to look more like a fighter, like you’ve seen in the current too CCAs that we’re flying.”

The Air Force wants MMA drones to be able to fly about 4,000 miles—more than twice the expected range of autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft drones—and carry a heavy payload, although they will be slower than CCAs, Niemi said.

Those differences extend to price, too—while the Air Force is targeting $10 million for an MMA drone, it’s hoping for $20 million per CCA once they reach full production. Those costs are for just the base aircraft, excluding sensors, weapons or other equipment that might be loaded onto them.

From an acquisition perspective, the Air Force is hoping to use the same methods across the CCA and MMA programs to keep costs down and production simple.

That includes moving quickly to award contracts and keeping several vendors on contract to provide a variety of drones. Like CCAs, MMA drones will also use open architecture , Niemi said. That will ensure the drones have standardized interfaces and could be easily upgraded with newer sensor packages or weapons capabilities, even from different vendors, he said. This would also allow MMAs to be tailored with the gear needed for a particular mission.

“If you want to build a package that’s going to go on this new aircraft, as long as it conforms to this [standardized interface], we can do it very speedily and very readily,” Niemi said. “That’s something we struggle with at the opposite end of the spectrum, something like the F-35, where it’s very very hard to incorporate new things onto it, because of the construct and the architecture of that system.”

The Air Force also wants manufacturers to be able to produce MMA drones in large numbers, Niemi said, but also be able to ramp production up or down as needed, such as if the Air Force started losing large numbers in a heated conflict. Keeping MMAs simple is the best way to ensure that production flexibility, he said.

“If you wanted to suddenly ramp up production of something like an F-35, it’s not a limiting factor so much as money, as the ability to build out your production capacity and actually crank more of those things out,” Niemi said. “And the more complex the aircraft, the harder that problem is. … In major combat operations, depending on who you’re fighting, we could be losing dozens [of MMA drones] a day, and so you have to figure out how do you adjust the industrial capacity in order to make [necessary production levels] happen.”

General Atomics, which also makes the MQ-9, is planning to pitch a newly designed drone it calls Wildfire for the MMA program.

“Our new Wildfire aircraft addresses all of the concerns posed by the MMA solicitation,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement to reporters. “We can deliver years earlier and maintain the same high quality. You can have everything that makes Reaper special, plus more, at a price that doesn’t break the bank.”

items.title: Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended campaign of economic and military pressure against Iran. The post Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended pressure campaign against Iran.

The move will free up units that have been based in the region far beyond the Air Force’s usual six-month deployments. More fighter unit rotations are expected in the coming weeks.

Units on their way home include the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard, which flies F-35 Lightning II aircraft, and F-16 Fighting Falcon s from the 555th Fighter Squadron based at Aviano Air Base, Italy, are also returning, according to people familiar with the matter and data collected by the open-source research group the Military Air Tracking Alliance .

The departing units have been deployed overseas since last year. The Vermont F-35s first deployed to Puerto Rico in December 2025 and supported the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, before deploying to the Middle East ahead of the U.S. air war against Iran. The Vermont ANG’s F-35s were spotted transiting through RAF Lakenheath, U.K., on their way back home. The F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since November.

Arriving in CENTCOM are F-16s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing. Twelve F-16s from the Ohio ANG departed Lajes in the Azores on Sept. 4, according to local aircraft spotters. The planes, which arrived on the Portuguese island on Aug. 29, are due to head to the Middle East.

Other units likely to deploy in the coming weeks include the 115th Fighter Wing of Wisconsin Air National Guard, which flies F-35s, sources said.

A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not respond to a request for comment.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month that the U.S. is stepping up its economic sanctions campaign to try to stop Iran from interfering with oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz while pressing Tehran to make concessions on its nuclear program. That is in addition to the ongoing American maritime blockade.

“If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart,” Bessent told CNBC last month.

But U.S. officials also say that the increased economic pressure might lead Iran to retaliate militarily. Fighting in the region flared up late last month when the U.S. struck Iranian launchers that were preparing to launch rockets with mines into the strait, and Iran retaliated by firing ballistic missiles at American forces in Jordan.

The new U.S. pressure campaign is likely to reduce the need for defensive and offensive munitions in the near term. But it still requires an ongoing military presence in the region and efforts to manage operational demands on the force.

The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand earlier this week after spending nine months at sea. The Lincoln took part in Operation Epic Fury—which officially lasted from Feb. 28 to early April—and then helped enforce a U.S. military blockade of Iranian ports and partook in tit-for-tat clashes against the Iranians for months.

Dozens of Air Force and Navy fighter jets remain deployed to the Middle East.

items.title: Trump to travel aboard Qatari-donated Air Force One to Ireland
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump will use the Qatari-donated jet to travel to Ireland next week, the plane's first international trip since the swap in Turkey.
items.body:
Daily News Roundup

Trump to travel aboard Qatari-donated Air Force One to Ireland

U.S. President Donald Trump arrives aboard the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S., July 9, 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

U.S. President Donald Trump plans to fly to Ireland next week aboard the Boeing 747 Qatari-donated jet for the first time since security concerns caused the president to leave Turkey on a different aircraft, The Washington Post first reported.

In July, Trump unexpectedly left the NATO summit in Turkey on a different plane , citing a potential threat as the conflict with Iran escalated. He switched to a smaller military aircraft in secret, using a catering truck for deception.

The swap raised further questions about the modified Qatari jet’s security as a presidential aircraft. That same month, Trump announced that the jet would be soon sent to be “maxed out” for security upgrades.

Trump said the alterations would begin in roughly a month, but no official statement has been made about the schedule.

“We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force One,” a senior administration official told Military Times. “We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture.”

Trump will be in Ireland on Sept. 12 and 13, attending the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg. The BBC reported that he is scheduled to meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin during his two-day trip.

Ahead of the midterm elections, Trump is also scheduled to headline the Republican midterm convention next week in Texas, and he has promised to campaign for Republican candidates across dozens of battleground states.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.
