items.title: US Marine Corps plans to use 3D scanners to detect cracked body armor
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: The U.S. Marine Corps is looking to acquire high-resolution 3D scanners to detect cracked body armor.
items.body:
MilTech

US Marine Corps plans to use 3D scanners to detect cracked body armor

Weapons and body armor are staged for members of the U.S. Army, Navy and Marine Corps during the Fleet Combat Camera Pacific’s Winter Quick Shot 2014 combined field training exercise in the Angeles National Forest near Azusa, California. (Spc. Philip Diab/U.S. Army)

The U.S. Marine Corps is looking to acquire high-resolution 3D scanners to detect cracked body armor.

The goal is to develop sensors that can “scan individual hard armor plates for cracks and delaminations,” according to a Marine Corps Request For Information , which is due Oct. 2. More specifically, the devices will inspect Enhanced Small Arms Protective Inserts and United States Marine Corps Lightweight Plates.

The Enhanced Armor Inspection System will use computed tomography , or CT, scanners. CT scanning, commonly used for tasks such as medical imaging and airport bomb detection, creates 3D images that are more detailed than traditional 2D X-ray images.

The Marine Corps intends to set up 10 CT scanners for body armor inspection. This includes six devices in the continental United States, two in Japan and one each in Hawaii and Guam.

The Marine Corps currently uses two techniques to spot defects in body armor, as explained in a 2023 Small Business Innovation Research solicitation that sought new methods of examining cracked ceramic plates and delaminated polyethylene layers. Cracked ceramics are detected by X-rays and deformed polyethylene by tapping the armor and determining whether the sound is like a chime (good) or a thud (bad).

The SBIR did point to CT scanning as an alternative, but noted that “this method is extremely expensive and requires highly trained personnel.”

The new RFI seeks an automated commercial system. It should include an “automated material custom conveyance & sorting system, imaging system, and data processing/handling that is fully equipped with customized Automated Defect Recognition (ADR) software to meet the USMC’s requirements.”

Contractors should specify how many plates per minute their systems can examine. They are also asked to describe how well the scanners can handle “materials with varying densities or compositions, such as the blend of boron carbide and silicon carbide, or the presence of metal crack arrestors.”

In 2011, a Department of Defense Inspector General audit found that the U.S. Army had purchased 5.1 million ballistic inserts that might have been defective. Army tests sometimes failed to use the correct-sized armor plates, the proper velocity for bullets fired at the plates or assess the effects of weathering and altitude.

The Army replied that there was “no case in which the military’s body armor has failed to do its job in protecting troops in Iraq and Afghanistan.”

There have also been claims of defective military body armor in Britain and Taiwan , as well as for U.S. police departments .

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Buying Time Against AI Proliferation
items.author: Tobias Sytsma
items.summary: The author describes a formal model of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and proliferation that focuses on the demand for AI capability.
items.body:
Much of today’s policy debate over artificial intelligence (AI) revolves around instruments designed to change the costs of access to AI; this report describes a formal model of AI adoption and proliferation that focuses on the demand for AI capability.

Buying Time Against AI Proliferation

The Economics of Governed Access

Tobias Sytsma

Research Published Sep 3, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Much of today’s policy debate over artificial intelligence (AI) focuses on efforts to change the costs of access to AI—to shift relative costs such that AI adoption is steered toward channels that society can monitor and away from channels it cannot.

Policy analysis has concentrated on the supply side of this problem, with such mechanisms as export restrictions, licensing requirements, and controls on computing hardware. But where AI capabilities end up depends on the choices of organizations and individuals about what to adopt and through which channels, and it is on this demand side that cost-shifting instruments operate. This demand side of the problem has received far less systematic analysis.

This report addresses this gap with a framework for judging when cost-shifting steers adoption as intended, when it accomplishes little, and when it backfires and makes proliferation worse. The author details a formal model in which AI adoption is driven by relative costs across access channels, and governance instruments operate by manipulating those relative costs. The central question is: When policy changes the relative cost of AI access, how do users reallocate across governed and ungoverned channels, and under what conditions does that reallocation reduce, fail to affect, or accelerate uncontrolled proliferation of AI?

Key Takeaways

Compliance burdens on governed AI access channels can make uncontrolled AI proliferation worse

Raising the cost of controlled frontier access without corresponding pressure on ungoverned alternatives can redirect user adoption toward ungoverned access channels. In simulations conducted by the author, this occurred in roughly one-quarter of relevant scenarios.

Whether AI access governance can sufficiently delay or suppress ungoverned access growth depends on three demand-side conditions

Three indicators predict whether policies can suppress ungoverned AI access: (1) how responsive adopters are to cost differences across channels, (2) how effectively policy can raise the cost of ungoverned AI access, and (3) how costly it is for users to switch between access channels.

AI access governance policies are no longer able to shift users toward governed access channels once AI capabilities are sufficiently strong

Once AI capabilities become sufficiently valuable to users, policies that attempt to shift the relative costs of governed vs. ungoverned AI access lose their traction. Once AI capabilities advance far enough, no policy evaluated in the modeling framework can suppress ungoverned access.

The distinction between AI capability dynamics and access-cost dynamics matters for governance of the technology

A framing centered on capability thresholds implies that governance should track and respond to specific technical milestones; a framing centered on price dynamics implies that governance should track and respond to the cost of access. The latter may be more observable, more amenable to policy intervention, and more predictive of who adopts what and through which channels.

Topics

Artificial Intelligence

Science and Technology Legislation

Science, Technology, and Innovation Policy

items.title: Iran war escalation raises concern over civilian death toll
items.author: Menna AlaaElDin and Kanishka Singh, Reuters
items.summary: The recent escalation of the Iran war has cast renewed attention on its civilian toll after Iran reported four killed and dozens wounded at a wedding.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

Iran war escalation raises concern over civilian death toll

Rubble lies around a damaged house on Sept. 2, 2026, following a reported attack near a wedding gathering in Kuhistik, Sirik, Iran. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via West Asia News Agency via Reuters)

The sudden recent escalation of the Iran war has cast renewed attention on its civilian toll after Iran reported 18 dead in the last U.S. assault, including four killed and dozens wounded at a wedding.

Iran’s health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 wounded in Tuesday night’s U.S. strikes across Iran. The Iranian Red Crescent said four people were killed and 67 wounded at a wedding ceremony near the coast of the Strait of Hormuz.

The return of combat operations has alarmed countries throughout the region, as Iran launched missile and drone attacks against what it said were U.S. assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq.

The guns had largely gone silent since the previous exchange in July, although peace talks failed to advance in the interim. President Donald Trump threatened to unleash yet more military force, even though the war is unpopular at home and has driven up the cost of gasoline.

Iran, for its part, has remained defiant, despite suffering heavy military and economic losses.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran,” and called for an immediate cessation of military action, his spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.

“The Secretary General condemns all attacks against civilians. He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution,” Dujarric said.

The deaths would be in addition to the 3,636 people documented as killed in Iran as of April 7, including 1,701 civilians, according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), an independent Iranian rights group.

The U.S. has reported 18 military personnel killed and more than 750 wounded.

“We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” U.S. Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for the U.S. military’s Central Command, said in an email.

The Iranian Red Crescent Society released video showing debris strewn on the ground next to a building with a large hole in the roof, accompanied by still images showing people, some in Red Crescent vests, at a damaged building and a utility tower lying on the ground.

Reuters was able to verify the location using satellite imagery, which showed the fallen tower was 136 metres (149 yards) from the damaged building.

The wedding incident recalled the blast at a school in Minab that killed 160 people at a girls’ school on the first day of the war.

The Pentagon has yet to issue an official finding on the Minab strike, which would be the U.S. military’s largest civilian casualty incident in decades. It may have been the ‌result of U.S. use of outdated targeting data, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Democratic members of the U.S. Congress have called on the administration to release findings of its investigation of the incident, but the report has not been sent to lawmakers.

RELATED

Lawmakers demand Pentagon release findings from probe of Iran school strike

Lawmakers demanded Monday that the Pentagon release its findings from an investigation into the Feb. 28 strike at a girls’ school in Iran.

U.S. defenders of the Iran war also point to civilian deaths that resulted from Iranian attempts to put down street protests that embroiled the country in December and January, before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. HRANA has put that death toll at more than 7,000, while Iranian exile groups claim the number is much higher.

Trump has cited an incentive for Iranians to overthrow their government as one reason for the war, in addition to seeking to halt Iran’s nuclear program and ending its support for militant groups abroad such as Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis.

Iran has also responded to the U.S. attacks by threatening any oil tankers that transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorization, severely curtailing traffic in a waterway that before the war carried 20% of the world’s oil supply.

items.title: US Army awards $192M to Palantir, Anduril for TITAN production
items.author: Leigh Giangreco
items.summary: The Army moved its TITAN program from prototyping to production with a $192 million award to Palantir and Anduril this week.
items.body:
Industry

US Army awards $192M to Palantir, Anduril for TITAN production

The U.S. Army chose Palantir in 2024 as the prime contractor to develop the next-generation Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

The U.S. Army moved its Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node (TITAN) program from prototyping to production earlier this week with a combined $192 million award to Palantir Technologies and Anduril Industries.

A cornerstone of the Army’s ground system modernization effort, TITAN was designed to simplify the data-gathering process for soldiers aiming at far-off targets.

The Army chose Palantir as the prime contractor to develop the next-generation targeting system in 2024 .

Palantir, which received $127 million, will lead TITAN’s production, alongside L3 Harris Technologies, Sierra Nevada Corporation, Strategic Technology Consulting and World Wide Technology.

Anduril, which received $65 million under the award, will manufacture the ruggedized, vehicle-mounted systems and integrate the power and thermal subsystems that allow TITAN to operate in austere environments.

The TITAN program will create an advanced variant of the system to be mounted on the Army’s tactical trucks and have the ability to gather data from space sensors , as well as a basic variant for the service’s Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.

The award covers procurement and integration of four advanced and four basic variants, which are slated for delivery over the next 18 months. Those will buttress the Army’s nine existing prototype units that the service uses today.

The Army expects to award additional production orders in fiscal 2027.

items.title: U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground hosts Arizona Commanders Summit
items.author: Mark Schauer
items.summary: With the purpose of sharing information and building relationships, military commanders and senior leaders from across Arizona gathered for a day of discussions at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground (YPG) on Sep. 2, 2026. The summit, the first hosted by YPG Commander Col. Charles Seaberry, was the first held on post since 2022.
items.body:
Effective communication is a vital commodity, something of which one can never have too much.

With the purpose of sharing information and building relationships, military commanders and senior leaders from across Arizona gathered for a day of discussions at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground (YPG) on Sep. 2.

The summit, the first hosted by YPG Commander Col. Charles Seaberry, was the first held on post since 2022.

“It gives me an opportunity to meet my fellow commanders in Arizona,” said Seaberry. “It is good to collaborate and learn about the creative things they are doing that I could potentially leverage with YPG. I think we are going to have a lot of opportunities to synergize our initiatives and be less duplicative in areas where we are resource constrained.”

The Arizona Commanders Summit is a semi-annual event in which commanders and senior leaders from YPG, Marine Corps Air Station-Yuma, Fort Huachuca, Luke Air Force Base, Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, the Arizona National Guard’s Papago Park Military Reservation, and other Arizona and California-based military units along with local and state government representatives to discuss mission and installation sustainment. Though not a decision-making body, the group hears presentations on key topics throughout the day.

“I like the ability to go to all of the installations and see what they are like,” said Chas Buchanan, Director of the 56th Range management Office at Luke Airforce Base. “Seeing the remoteness of some of the installations and the challenges they face that are different than those we face in Phoenix really helps get the broader picture.”

The forum was an opportunity to compare challenges and network to share assets to accomplish the mission. For example, although YPG’s primary mission is conducting developmental testing of military equipment, the post also supports military training exercises. YPG is also part of the recently announced Army Permissive Test Range Expansion Initiative, which prioritizes commercial access to specialized environments ideal for testing unmanned aerial systems (UAS), counter-UAS technologies, long-range fires and low-cost interceptors at several facilities, including West Cibola Range, a newly opened component of YPG within YPG’s existing boundaries.

“That has dramatic implications into the future,” said Yuma Mayor Douglas Nicholls, who attended the event. “As we bring the amazing capabilities of YPG to bear for private industry, I think it will be a gamechanger for us for years to come.”

Multiple attendees noted the support the proving ground enjoys from the greater Yuma community, as well as the important role YPG plays in ensuring our nation’s defense. Nicholls gave a comprehensive presentation about what the city of Yuma offers early in the event.

“The military is important to our community and as a representative of the city I want to let everyone in the state know that Yuma is a community committed to the defense of our nation and preparing our warfighters,” said Nicholls. “It’s part of what makes Yuma, Yuma.”

items.title: When Disaster Strikes, Could AI Help? Q&A with Jessica Jensen
items.summary: Disasters are more frequent, more severe, and more costly. Pressure is mounting on emergency managers and the organizations that support them. Senior policy researcher Jessica Jensen discusses how artificial intelligence could help carry some of that burden.
items.body:
When Disaster Strikes, Could AI Help? Q&A with Jessica Jensen

Commentary

Sep 2, 2026

Evacuations in the Ravenswood neighborhood due to flooding after days of heavy rain in Indianapolis, Indiana, August 15, 2026

When disaster strikes, the public sees the most visible parts of the response: evacuations, first responders, rescue operations, and recovery efforts. But behind the scenes is a much larger network of people working to help communities manage through chaos.

That job is getting harder. Disasters are more frequent, more severe, and more costly. Pressure is mounting on emergency managers and the organizations that support them.

In a new RAND study supported by the Markle Foundation as part of the AI for Disasters and Emergencies Initiative (AIDE) , senior policy researcher Jessica Jensen and her RAND colleagues examined how artificial intelligence could help carry some of that burden.

Over more than two decades, Jensen has helped emergency management rethink how communities prepare for, respond to, and recover from increasingly complex disasters. Now, she is exploring how AI could help a field that's already stretched thin adapt to even greater demands.

What could AI realistically help emergency managers do—and how could that improve outcomes for communities?

AI can help with prediction and modeling, including when events are likely to occur and how severe impacts may be. It can also help bring together data from different groups, so people better understand what is happening during a disaster. If AI is used well, it can help communities get the right help at the right time without inefficiency or duplicated effort, ultimately saving lives.

Before disasters happen, emergency managers spend a lot of time on routine work like preparing plans, creating outreach materials, and managing grants. AI can speed up much of that work. That allows emergency managers to spend less time behind their desks and more time doing important public-facing work—helping people prepare, building community relationships, and focusing on the things that lessen disaster impacts.

If AI is used well, it can help communities get the right help at the right time without inefficiency or duplicated effort, ultimately saving lives.

Your team identified more than 1,000 AI-enabled products relevant to emergency management. What do these tools do, and what surprised you about your findings?

We were shocked by the number of tools out there. We thought we might find dozens. Instead, we found 1,179.

A lot of them support response. They support situational awareness, hazard monitoring, damage assessment, information sharing, and more. But the market is uneven, with more tools for response than for preparedness or recovery.

A big challenge facing emergency managers is that many of the products are very narrow. For example, many offer one piece of insight, but they do not connect different information streams or help create a fuller picture. That creates what we call a stacking problem. People would need to use multiple tools and would have to connect them. The products also tend not to facilitate interorganizational coordination, a hallmark of emergency management task areas.

What are the biggest barriers to using these tools—and what will it take for emergency management to adopt them more widely?

As we found, it's not that the tools do not exist. It is whether organizations have the capacity to evaluate them, buy them, integrate them, and keep using them over time.

A lot of these products require technical expertise. Often, you need someone with an IT background to set the tool up and provide ongoing support. Many jurisdictions don't have that kind of staffing. Many products also require internet connectivity, which can become an issue during response. A significant number depend on another product to work. And pricing is often hard to find—which makes procurement difficult.

Then you add privacy or cyber concerns, and the reality is that many offices are already stretched thin. One issue by itself may be manageable, but taken together, they can be overwhelming.

This is also where there is room for progress. Technology companies can design products more specifically for this field and prioritize transparency on pricing, access, and technical requirements—which will drive better adoption. Policymakers can make decisions about governance, procurement, and funding that make adoption easier. And emergency managers can build more familiarity with what these tools can do and where their limits are.

In your research, what role did large language models (LLMs) and AI chatbots play in emergency management today?

We found they could be especially useful for administrative and communication tasks in emergency management. They can help summarize reports, draft materials, translate information, and process large amounts of text more efficiently.

Those kinds of general-purpose tools stood out as one place the field may be able to realize benefits quickly, since they have broad capabilities, are user-friendly, and already available to some jurisdictions. For more complex emergency management tasks, though, there is still more research and real-world testing that needs to be done to determine LLMs effectiveness.

This study was supported by the Markle Foundation's AI for Disasters + Emergencies (AIDE) Initiative. How critical is philanthropic support in a fast-moving area like this?

One of the most important things philanthropies can do is bring together technology companies, the user community, and the researchers developing the underlying technologies, and facilitate conversations about how to balance everyone's interests. That convening role—and the ability to sustain those conversations—can make the difference between tools that sound promising and tools that actually help communities. That is exactly what the AIDE Initiative is doing—bringing the right people together to explore how AI can better support disaster preparedness, response, and recovery.

The AIDE Initiative is bringing the right people together to explore how AI can better support disaster preparedness, response, and recovery.

You've dedicated your career to emergency management. What's kept you in the field so long?

I've known I wanted to serve this field since I was 14. Around that time, a regular at the restaurant where I worked would talk about his job helping communities and organizations recover after disasters. What stayed with me was how many different people and systems have to come together to help a community heal.

Now, years later, this work feels even more meaningful. There is an incredible opportunity in emergency management to keep evolving the practice to better serve communities. And I care deeply about the people who do this work. They are hardworking, passionate, and committed—even when resources are scarce and the demands keep growing. In a world of increasing disasters and rising impacts, that work matters enormously. It's what keeps me going.

items.title: Countering Model Distillation
items.author: Brian A. Jackson
items.summary: Artificial intelligence model distillation (training new models on outputs of more capable ones) could affect U.S. frontier model advantage. New policy tools could augment such technical countermeasures as raising costs or reducing model quality.
items.body:
Limits and Alternatives

Michael J. D. Vermeer , Brian A. Jackson

Expert Insights Published Sep 2, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Artificial intelligence model distillation (that is, the process of training a new model on the outputs of a more capable one) poses a growing challenge to efforts to preserve the U.S. frontier model advantage. In this paper, the authors examine whether technical counter-distillation measures are likely to be sufficient to deter distillation. They argue that technical measures alone (such as by materially raising the cost of distillation or substantially reducing the quality of the resulting models) are unlikely to change the underlying incentives that make distillation attractive and that broader policy tools might be needed.

items.title: Operational reliance on AI in supply chains and emerging insurance risks
items.author: Sasha Romanosky
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded in supply chains. This report examines how that changes operational reliance, resilience, and insurance risk across logistics, transport, and warehousing.
items.body:
This report examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is being adopted across supply chains, including logistics, transport, warehousing, and inventory management. It explores how AI may create new operational dependencies, resilience challenges, and insurance risks, including correlated losses across firms, and considers implications for operators, insurers, and regulators.

Operational reliance on AI in supply chains and emerging insurance risks

Elie Alhajjar , Youmna Hashem , Alec Ross , Sasha Romanosky

Research Published Sep 2, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded in the digital infrastructure through which goods are forecast, routed, documented, stored, monitored, and delivered. In transportation, logistics, warehousing, and inventory management, AI is being used for forecasting, route optimisation, predictive maintenance, document processing, warehouse robotics, and anomaly detection. These applications may improve efficiency, visibility, and responsiveness, but they also create new forms of operational reliance on data, models, software vendors, cloud services, and automated decision rules.

This report examines how that operational reliance may translate into insurance risk, particularly where AI-related failures affect multiple firms at the same time. The focus is on transportation and logistics, and on warehousing and inventory management, with particular attention to aggregation risk: the possibility that shared AI weaknesses, common service dependencies, cyberattacks, or regulatory shocks generate correlated losses across policyholders and insurance lines.

The analysis combines a review of academic and industry literature, a desk-based review of AI-related incidents and lawsuits, stakeholder interviews across operational, legal, insurance, and technology backgrounds, and structured scenarios designed to test how AI-related losses could spread across firms and portfolios. The findings suggest that AI adoption in supply chains is likely to expand over the next five years, but unevenly. Lower risk uses such as monitoring, forecasting, and recommendations are likely to spread faster than automated execution. At the same time, insurers, operators, and regulators still lack settled approaches to identifying, governing, and underwriting AI-related supply chain risk.

Key Takeaways

AI adoption in supply chains is likely to grow, but unevenly

The strongest near-term growth is expected in lower-risk applications that can be added to existing digital workflows, such as monitoring, forecasting, optimisation, predictive maintenance, and document processing. More autonomous or execution-oriented uses are likely to expand more slowly and selectively because they raise greater safety, liability, integration, and business continuity concerns.

AI-related failures can create hidden dependencies and correlated insurance losses

Firms that appear independent at the underwriting level may rely on the same model provider, cloud platform, warehouse robotics system, mapping service, logistics software, or data feed. This creates aggregation risk: a shared AI weakness, service outage, cyberattack, or regulatory shock could generate related losses across multiple policyholders and insurance lines at the same time.

Governance and insurance responses are still evolving

Current AI use in supply chains remains more assistive than autonomous in many settings, with continued reliance on human judgement in higher-stakes contexts. At the same time, responsibility for AI-related failures remains difficult to allocate across operators, developers, vendors, and integrators. Insurers are beginning to adapt through changes to existing policy wordings, exclusions, and case-by-case assessments, but no settled approach to underwriting or covering AI-related supply chain risk has yet emerged.

Recommendations

Supply chain operators and AI and technology providers should establish baseline controls before AI systems become operationally indispensable, including AI-use inventories, meaningful human oversight, provenance tracking, runtime monitoring, staged deployment, and tested fallback procedures.

Insurers and reinsurers should incorporate AI into underwriting and accumulation management rather than treating AI use as a binary exposure. This should include asking where AI is used, what operational authority it has, which vendors and models are involved, whether updates are tested, and what human review, monitoring, and fallback arrangements exist.

National regulators should distinguish manageable portfolio aggregation from genuinely catastrophic AI risk and assess whether existing insurance and regulatory tools are adequate. Where private markets may not be able to absorb extreme correlated AI-related losses, regulators should examine options such as a public-private insurance mechanism, government backstop, or other coordinated response.

items.title: Super Garuda Shield 26 kicks off with multinational partners ceremony
items.author: PO2 Alfredo Marron and SGT William Rogers
items.summary: Super Garuda Shield 26 (SGS 26) began with an opening ceremony Aug. 31 2026, in Bandung, bringing together service members from Indonesia, the United States and 13 partner countries for a multinational exercise focused on strengthening relationships, interoperability and readiness.
items.body:
SOUTH SUMATRA, Indonesia — Super Garuda Shield 26 (SGS 26) began with an opening ceremony Aug. 31 2026, in Bandung, bringing together service members from Indonesia, the United States and 13 partner countries for a multinational exercise focused on strengthening relationships, interoperability and readiness.

Approximately 5,000 combined armed forces personnel are scheduled to participate in SGS 26 from Aug, 31 to Sept. 11 at multiple training locations across Indonesia, including Bandung, Bataraja and Lampung.

The U.S. Pacific Command-sponsored exercise demonstrates the shared purpose of participating nations while enhancing interoperability and providing realistic training in a variety of climates, terrains, and environments.

“SGS 26 is building valuable relationships and readiness with our Indonesian and multinational partners through challenging and realistic training,” said Maj. Gen. Patrick Ellis, commanding general of the 4th Infantry Division, “We are excited to work side by side with our partners this year to ensure we remain ready to rapidly respond to any contingency or crisis.”

SGS 26 provides opportunities for professional exchanges that strengthen partnerships through shared learning and training. Training includes engineering construction activities, staff training exercises, airborne operations, jungle training, air assault operations, a large field training exercise and combined arms live fire exercises, a Stinger missile live fire exercise, and a High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) live fire exercise.

The variety of training events allows participating forces to share their respective experiences and expertise while developing a better understanding of how partner nations plan, coordinate and execute military operations.

U.S. Army, Airforce, Navy and Marine Corps personnel will train alongside their Indonesian hosts and regional allies and partners to sharpen tactical readiness, test joint command-and-control systems and strengthen their ability to operate together. Training alongside partner nations builds the collective trust and interoperability necessary to strengthen defense relationships and support shared interests throughout the Indo-Pacific.

Beyond improving technical and tactical capabilities, SGS 26 provides opportunities for service members from participating nations to build professional relationships. Those relationships can improve communication and mutual understanding among forces that may work together during future operations, contingencies or crises.

Super Garuda Shield has developed into an important venue for multinational cooperation and professional exchange. Each iteration provides participating nations an opportunity to build upon existing partnerships while creating new relationships among service members throughout the region.

The United States’ participation in SGS 26 reflects its enduring defense relationship with Indonesia and its commitment to working alongside allies and partners. By training together, participating forces build the collective trust and interoperability necessary to respond to shared challenges and uphold their shared interest in a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Ellis reinforced the importance of building these partnerships during SGS 26 saying, “the trust that is required to execute these operations cannot be built in a briefing room; it is built in the mud, in the surf, in the cockpits, and in the operational command centers.”

Throughout the nearly two-week exercise, participating forces will continue training together across Indonesia, strengthening professional relationships and improving their ability to operate as a combined and joint force.

items.body:
Published Sep 1, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

The Department of the Air Force (DAF) confronts challenges on multiple fronts. RAND Project AIR FORCE’s (PAF’s) mission is to help DAF leaders make informed, research-based decisions to meet those challenges. We provide objective analyses of complex problems and effective solutions for confronting those problems. We clarify issues that are often clouded by uncertainty or disagreement and develop solid courses of action for the U.S. Air Force (USAF), the U.S. Space Force (USSF), and the DAF as a whole. Our standard of success is very high: we must earn DAF leaders’ trust in the quality and objectivity of our research; identify opportunities for positive action; and, ultimately, inform outcomes that benefit the DAF and the nation. This brochure describes PAF’s institutional values, research areas, expertise, and recent successes as well as how to access previous research, commission a PAF project, and engage with PAF leadership.

items.title: When Counties Invest in Early Childhood
items.author: Adaeze Ibeanu
items.summary: The authors evaluated the implementation of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in Harris County, Texas. ECIF provided $15 million to programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals.
items.body:
The authors evaluated the implementation of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in Harris County, Texas. ECIF represented a historic investment of more than $15 million to scale up evidence-informed programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals.

When Counties Invest in Early Childhood

Successes, Challenges, and Lessons from Harris County, Texas

Elaine Lin Wang , Karen Christianson , Jill S. Cannon , Jonathan Schweig , Adaeze Ibeanu

Research Published Sep 1, 2026

Includes Executive Summary

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

The Harris County Department of Economic Equity and Opportunity conceived of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in fall 2020. Funded primarily through the American Rescue Plan Act, ECIF represented a historic investment of more than $15 million to scale up evidence-informed programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals in Harris County, Texas. The long-term goal of ECIF, which was designed to fund six programs for two to three years each, was to strengthen outcomes for young children and families, particularly those considered vulnerable because of their income. This report presents the findings of RAND’s three-year evaluation of the implementation of ECIF.

The purposes of the evaluation were to assess progress toward initiative goals and inform future county decisionmaking. The authors formulated ten indicators to measure success across program selection, monitoring and supports for grantees, program implementation, participant satisfaction, and contributions to broader benefits for the early childhood system in Harris County. The evaluation approach included analysis of existing literature; program data; participant surveys; and interviews and focus groups with program leads, staff, and county administrators.

ECIF successfully expanded access and built some momentum for early childhood services in Harris County. The initiative demonstrated that public investment can expand early childhood supports for families and access to professional development for early childhood professionals. The initiative also highlighted system barriers—timelines, administrative complexity, and uncertain post‑grant continuation—that county leaders could address in future investments.

Key Takeaways

Collectively, grantees served far more people than initially targeted

Overall, ECIF‑funded organizations far exceeded service delivery targets. More than 30,000 children, 5,500 caregivers, and 8,500 early childhood professionals received direct benefits.

Programs reached all high‑poverty ZIP codes and primarily served Black and Hispanic families.

Many programs also provided wraparound supports and professional development for early childhood professionals.

Nearly 1.5 million meals were delivered to children and families.

Nearly 10,000 developmental screenings were provided to children.

More than 70,000 early literacy materials and resources were provided to children and families.

Participants were generally satisfied

About 90 percent of surveyed participants agreed that programs met their needs and were delivered respectfully and conveniently.

ECIF’s broader contributions were mixed

ECIF helped raise the profile of early childhood issues and efforts in the county and fostered some new partnerships.

About two‑thirds of grantees continued or expanded services after funding ended; smaller organizations faced sustainability challenges.

Program and county leads identified key lessons

Recruitment was more successful when programs actively addressed barriers to access for vulnerable families by working with community partners and providing direct support, such as transportation or translation services.

Participant feedback led to customized aspects that better addressed participant needs.

Programs needed up to one year for hiring; allotting sufficient time and resources would have helped programs scale more smoothly.

The grantee selection process should have better assessed early childhood service providers for a clear vision of goals, implementation capacity, budget assumptions, and readiness to manage public funds.

More thoughtfully structured performance indicators would have had more value for evaluating initiative success.

Recommendations

Harris County administrators should simplify oversight and reporting requirements—and provide technical assistance—to lower the burden on grantees.

Harris County administrators should plan evaluation data collection alongside program implementation to support more accurate assessment of initiative impact.

Harris County administrators should formalize and measure progress toward goals for networking and collaboration among grantees and potentially other early childhood organizations in the county.

Harris County administrators and grantees should plan for sustainability of programming and organizational capacity from day one.

Harris County administrators should invest in county-level data infrastructure to support evaluation of long-term outcomes and system-level change.

items.title: Not All ‘Magic’ Mushrooms Are the Same
items.summary: Millions of U.S. adults use Amanita muscaria mushrooms. But these distinctive fungi aren’t like other psychoactive mushrooms. What do consumers and policymakers need to know about them?
items.body:
Commentary

Aug 31, 2026

By Michelle Priest and Beau Kilmer

This commentary was originally published by San Francisco Chronicle on August 29, 2026.

Mushrooms are everywhere in California—literally and figuratively. Some are edible, some are psychoactive, some are toxic. And in the case of Amanita muscaria mushrooms, they can be all three.

You may not yet have heard of Amanita muscaria , also called “fly agaric,” but you certainly have seen images of it. The orange-, yellow- or red-capped mushroom with white spots is in everything from “Alice in Wonderland” to Super Mario video games. In our recent RAND report on the use of psychedelics , we estimated that about 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms.

Psilocybin mushrooms and Amanita muscaria are not the same. Given the growing popularity of so-called “magic” mushrooms for recreational and therapeutic use, as well as possible confusion between these different mushrooms, policymakers and health officials should not ignore health concerns related to Amanita muscaria .

This is especially true because of the media attention psilocybin has received. Emerging clinical research has shown promise in using psilocybin for treating a variety of mental health ailments. Yet despite growing public interest, psilocybin has not been approved as a medicine by the Food and Drug Administration and remains illegal under federal law. Federal prohibition has not stopped some states and localities from moving ahead. In addition to three states legalizing supervised psilocybin use, more than 30 cities and counties have “deprioritized” the enforcement of certain offenses related to psychedelics, including psilocybin.

About 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms.

Oakland was an early mover in this space. In 2019, the City Council passed a resolution making the investigation and arrest of adults “for planting, cultivating, purchasing, transporting, distributing, engaging in practices with, and/or possessing” psilocybin mushrooms and other naturally occurring psychedelics one of the lowest priorities for local law enforcement.

But not all psychedelic mushrooms are the same.

Unlike the vast majority ( PDF ) of mushrooms containing psilocybin, Amanita muscaria can be quite toxic . If not properly prepared, effects can include nausea and vomiting, with more severe cases involving seizures, coma and, in extremely rare instances, death .

Most people who use Amanita muscaria do not run into problems, but a recent international review highlighted some troubling anecdotes. In one case report , an older couple was rushed to the hospital after consuming Amanita muscaria . They both went into severe comas, and one had a seizure, in addition to other serious symptoms. Thankfully, after intensive medical treatment, each made a full recovery.

The main active compound in Amanita muscaria is muscimol, which acts primarily on neurotransmitters in the brain. The most common self-reported effects are an intoxicated feeling similar to alcohol, sleepiness (sometimes with altered dreams), and relaxation. Others report that it can help reduce substance use or alleviate anxiety, but no clinical trials have confirmed these health claims .

The mushroom is not hard to find.

Amanita muscaria grows in many parts of the country. The California State Parks Foundation website even features a picture of it growing in Salt Point State Park in Sonoma County. It is also sold in unregulated gummies, chocolates, and other products.

And, yes, people report using it to microdose, too.

Amanita muscaria is not illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act. And only one state, Louisiana, prohibits it. A 2024 assessment by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ( PDF ) found that it is not safe to eat or add to food, but minimal action has been taken to get these products out of brick-and-mortar and online shops.

Given its risk profile and legal status, there are concerns about unregulated products advertising with images of Amanita muscaria or claims that they contain it. These products may contain Amanita muscaria , or they may not. They may also contain a mix of other unregulated intoxicants that can be harmful. A 2026 review from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified 180 cases of severe illness in 34 states associated with eating mushroom-containing products, including some that contained compounds from Amanita muscaria and psilocybin mushrooms along with other substances. The California Department of Public Health has also raised concerns about the substances that are in widely available mushroom products.

The popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks.

State and federal policymakers have many options when it comes to Amanita muscaria and products claiming to contain it, and each has unique costs and benefits .

For example, prohibition is an option, although enforcing the law against those foraging for mushrooms would be difficult. Jurisdictions could also allow adults to grow and possess Amanita muscaria but prohibit retail sales, as Colorado has done with psilocybin mushrooms and some other nature-based psychedelics. If states decide to regulate production and sales, they’ll confront many decisions around child-proof packaging requirements, product testing, marketing restrictions, taxes, and how these products can be sold.

Regardless of any legal or regulatory changes, the popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks .

Not all mind-altering mushrooms are the same. In the current environment, consumers need to know that what they are buying is unregulated and may contain other harmful products.

Although Amanita muscaria isn’t as popular as psilocybin, it’s time for policy and public health conversations to include the other magic mushroom.

items.title: Mirror Life Is Theoretical. The Danger Is Anything But.
items.summary: With mirror life, scientists have given world leaders both the foresight and the time to address the danger. What's needed isn't alarm but action to ensure that mirror life remains just a footnote in human history—and not its final chapter.
items.body:
Commentary

Aug 31, 2026

Image by Ake Puttisarn/Getty Images

By Nidhi Kalra

This commentary was originally published by the Washington Post on August 31, 2026.

“This includes creation of mirror organisms.” These six bland words appear as a footnote in the White House policy for “Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research” ( PDF ) released in July—but they shouldn't be treated like one.

If you've never heard of mirror life—the more commonly used term for mirror organisms—there's a good reason: It doesn't exist. But this sci-fi-sounding form of life could theoretically be built out of biological molecules that are mirror images of the ones that exist naturally.

The idea emerges from the fact that nearly all biomolecules in nature have a kind of handedness—all DNA, for example, is built from right-handed sugars, and all proteins are made from left-handed amino acids. Thus, it's possible to imagine—and maybe even create—a living organism made of mirror-image counterparts to natural biomolecules. The first would probably be mirror bacteria.

That may not sound like reason for alarm. But scientists warn that mirror bacteria could devastate most life on earth. In 2024, dozens of them issued an urgent call to prevent mirror bacteria from ever being created, saying, “We cannot rule out a scenario in which a mirror bacterium acts as an invasive species across many ecosystems, causing pervasive lethal infections in a substantial fraction of plant and animal species, including humans.”

Yet we are edging closer to the threshold of mirror life. Over the past decade, biologists have engineered specialized tools for replicating and assembling mirror-image biomolecules. These tools could have some uses: For example, medicines made from mirror biomolecules could evade the processes that normally break them down, so treatments based on them might be longer-lasting than treatments based on regular biomolecules.

Certain advances could also become stepping stones toward mirror bacteria, and that's where the danger lurks.

But certain advances could also become stepping stones toward mirror bacteria, and that's where the danger lurks. Mirror bacteria might not be recognized by the things—immune systems, enzymes and other predator microorganisms—that keep normal bacteria in check. Outside of a lab, it might spread out of control, which is why no one should ever create it.

The good news is that the breakthroughs required to make mirror life are probably 10 to 30 years away , and very few scientists are even equipped to make the attempt. If the world's leading scientists desist, they will effectively deny the means to everyone else.

So here's the call to action: As Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in September to explore areas of cooperation, they should put prevention of mirror life on the agenda. If the two leaders seek a topic of global importance they can agree on, surely this is it. Mirror life is a shared existential risk with no credible upside for either country.

Instead, they can lay a foundation for universal restraint. A first step would be for the two countries to articulate a shared belief that there should be boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable research in this field. They could produce joint ethical standards for researchers, plus issue public statements that make it clear that mirror life is not a legitimate area of scientific pursuit.

Deciding exactly where to draw boundaries regarding mirror life research should involve collaborative discussions. The goals should be to determine when potentially beneficial early research steps onto a slippery slope.

As Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in September to explore areas of cooperation, they should put prevention of mirror life on the agenda.

For instance, some scientists have suggested that the mirror version of a ribosome—the machinery in cells that makes proteins—could make it easier to produce mirror proteins for medical use. But a mirror ribosome would also be a huge step toward creating mirror life. Instead, the United States and China might agree to prohibit the development of mirror ribosomes and work together on other ways to make mirror proteins.

This should lead to formal agreements not to pursue mirror life, along with jointly establishing economic and logistical barriers to its creation.

Some will dismiss hopes of such cooperation between strategic competitors as gross naiveté. But history has shown that cooperation among rivals is possible when the stakes are high enough.

In 1967, in the depths of Cold War animosity, the United States and the Soviet Union together championed the Intensified Smallpox Eradication Program. With joint leadership—money, logistics, and more than a billion Soviet vaccine doses—smallpox was successfully eradicated worldwide in 1980. Beijing and Washington can take inspiration from this example to protect the entire biosphere.

It's rare to meet a moment when the risks of a scientific breakthrough are so clear. More typically, it's too early to tell or too late to fix. With mirror life, scientists have given world leaders both the foresight and the time to address the danger. What's needed isn't alarm but action to ensure that mirror life remains just a footnote in human history—and not its final chapter.

items.title: Preparing Students for What Comes Next
items.author: Elizabeth D. Steiner
items.summary: The authors analyze data from three RAND survey panels to examine career-connected learning in kindergarten through grade 12 schools in academic year 2025–2026 using the perspectives of district leaders, school leaders, and high school students.
items.body:
The authors analyze data from three RAND survey panels to examine career-connected learning in kindergarten through grade 12 schools in academic year 2025–2026. They explore this topic using the perspectives of district leaders, school leaders, and school students. This report can inform policymakers and education leaders across the United States who are working to design or strengthen career-connected learning opportunities for students.

Preparing Students for What Comes Next

Educator and Student Perspectives on Career-Connected Learning in K–12 Schools

Benjamin K. Master , Melissa Kay Diliberti , Cristina Alvarez , AK Keskin , Elizabeth D. Steiner

Research Published Aug 31, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Increasingly, when employers hire entry-level workers, they are placing a higher value on candidates who have a variety of skills and experiences. As the labor market for young adults shifts accordingly, educators are facing a growing need to understand how kindergarten through grade 12 (K–12) students learn about and navigate college and career pathways. Research on how schools help students explore career fields and gain professional experience is therefore a key complement to research on traditional college preparation supports.

In academic year 2025–2026, the authors of this report gathered survey data from district leaders via the American School District Panel, from school principals via the American School Leader Panel, and from students via the American Youth Panel. These data included information about college advisory and preparatory activities and work-related learning. Together, the three survey panels offer a timely and nationally representative view of career-connected programming in K–12 public schools and students’ experiences with that programming. These findings can inform policymakers, workforce development coordinators, career and technical education directors, and school leaders across the United States who are seeking to design or strengthen these learning opportunities.

Key Takeaways

Career-connected learning in high school centers on pathways to college. Sixty-six percent of high school students reported hearing a lot of emphasis from educators about attending a four-year college, while other pathways received much less emphasis.

Most leaders described providing students with their first experiences with career-connected learning in middle school, with most districts offering some form of career exploration or planning support.

Students described making after high school plans late in their high school careers: By spring of their junior year, more than four in ten students had yet to make a plan or meet with their counselors about college and career plans.

Students’ plans for work-related learning consistently outpace their follow-through. By spring of their senior year, only 39 percent reported visiting an employer or workplace, even though 71 percent said that they had planned to do so; only 22 percent had actually participated in an internship or apprenticeship, even though 66 percent indicated that they had planned to do so.

Sixty-three percent of high schools set numeric targets for students to meet with guidance counselors about college or a career, and around half of high schools (52 percent) set targets related to students developing postsecondary plans. Few track whether students are accepted to college or secure employment after high school.

Students who do not want to pursue a bachelor’s degree rated their schools’ supports the most negatively. Students from lower-income families were also less likely to report that school supports are well-matched to their families’ financial situations.

items.title: The 988 Lifeline’s Integration Into the Broader Crisis Care Continuum
items.author: Ryan K. McBain
items.summary: The objective of this paper is to understand how 988 Lifeline centers are connected to the broader crisis care continuum, including 911, mobile crisis response, and community-based services.
items.body:
Stephanie Brooks Holliday , Samantha Matthews , Rachel Slover , James Liu , Joshua Breslau , Jonathan Purtle , Vikram Kilambi , Megan S. Schuler , Rajeev Ramchand , Beth Ann Griffin , et al.

Research Posted on rand.org Aug 31, 2026 Published in: AJPM Focus (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.focus.2026.100551

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Objective

To understand how 988 Lifeline centers are connected to the broader crisis care continuum—including 911, mobile crisis response, and community-based services.

Methods

The authors conducted a cross-sectional survey of 988 Lifeline centers in the U.S. between May and July 2025. A total of 159 centers (78%) completed the survey, which assessed transfer to/from 911, coordination with mobile crisis teams, capacity for referrals, and tracking dispositions and outcomes. Exploratory bivariate analyses were conducted to understand the factors associated with transfers to/from 911 and mobile crisis response team dispatch capability.

Results

Approximately 45% of centers reported bidirectional interoperability with 911. Among the 153 centers with a mobile crisis response team in their service region, 61% could dispatch the team directly. Exploratory bivariate analysis indicated that centers had higher odds of interoperating with 911 when mobile crisis services were present throughout their jurisdiction (OR = 2.10 [1.06, 4.20]) and could schedule appointments on callers’ behalf (OR = 2.88 [1.39, 6.23]).

Conclusions

Variation remains in centers’ ability to interoperate with 911 and dispatch mobile crisis teams. Centers with these capabilities were associated with having multiple referral, dispatch, and coordination capacities. Improving integration between 988 and other crisis services requires strengthened partnerships, sustainable funding, and investments in technology and data-sharing infrastructure.

Civic learning is having a moment. But what actually makes it stick as a priority in schools? New national survey data from the American School District Panel (ASDP)—a research partnership between CRPE and RAND—find signs of growing momentum: 20% of district leaders said their district had increased its prioritization of civic learning over the past year, while 18% reported increased school board support. But interviews with district leaders reveal an important wrinkle: support was strongest when civic learning was grounded in local engagement, and weaker when it was perceived as politically charged or connected to national debates. And support alone isn’t enough. Leaders who described civics as a clear district priority, woven into learning goals and other existing structures, had an easier time protecting a commitment to civic learning.

Unraveling Urban Building Fire Risk

Chenzhi Ma , Shengzhi Luan , Ensheng Dong , Lauren M. Gardner , Hongru Du , Thomas Gernay

Research Posted on rand.org Aug 31, 2026 Published in: Safety Science, Volume 205 (January 2027). DOI: 10.1016/j.ssci.2026.107411

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Building fires remain a major public safety concern in U.S. cities, threatening lives, property, and critical infrastructure. Despite substantial investments in fire protection, significant disparities persist, underscoring the need for a holistic, data-driven understanding of fire risk. In this work, we analyze more than one million fire incident reports and integrate them with community-level socioeconomic indicators, building inventories, weather conditions, and incident-specific characteristics. Our study makes two key contributions: a comprehensive framework that traces fire risk from occurrence to consequence, and a detailed city-level fire risk ranking system for U.S. cities. By examining the full progression of fire events, we identify structural, environmental, and social drivers that disproportionately endanger communities with older infrastructure and economic disadvantages. Socioeconomic disparities intensify both the frequency and severity of fire incidents, while incident-specific factors, such as ignition sources, ignition locations, and the presence of detectors or automatic extinguishing systems, substantially influence fire outcomes. Lower-risk cities generally exhibit more favorable socioeconomic conditions and a higher prevalence of fire safety features. By pinpointing high-risk communities and targeting critical vulnerabilities, this framework supports strategies that further improve fire safety and foster more resilient cities.

Jonathan P. Caulkins , Beau Kilmer , Peter Reuter

This Special Feature on illegal markets gathers, perhaps for the first time, papers by some of the world’s leading experts on nine different illegal markets. All are tasked with describing “their” market via a common analytic lens that focuses on the markets’ structure and how they operate. Two additional papers synthesize the main findings from these articles, focusing on analytic commonalities and implications for policy. Collectively, these 11 papers raise questions that may motivate other researchers to work on these topics, possibly spurring conversations about whether illegal markets should become a more prominent field of scientific inquiry.
